Kiwi’s experiment shows need for new UK passport ‘pointless’

New Zealand Herald July 23, 2026

Overseas applications for UK passports tripled after rule changes requiring British or Irish passports for entry. Photo / RNZ, Gill Bonnett

By Gill Bonnett of RNZ

New figures show people applying from overseas for United Kingdom citizenship and passports have soared after a change in rules for dual citizens.

New Zealanders with British heritage or families were caught by surprise at the start of the year, when they found they could no longer travel back to the UK on their New Zealand passport.

From late February, Britain and Ireland required all its citizens to use only passports issued by those countries when travelling to them, or pay more than $1300 for a “certificate of entitlement” to use in their New Zealand passport.

UK Home Office figures show overseas passport applications almost tripled to more than 300,000 in the first quarter of 2026. The British passport office had more than half a million applications in total in its system, the highest on record.

For some New Zealanders, it was the first time that they discovered they were classed as British citizens, as they had never previously owned a UK passport.

The policy change also coincided with the highest number of UK citizenship applications on record, in the 12 months to March. In the first three months of this year, 118,000 people applied – almost double the number at the same point last year.

Data from the UK’s 2021 census shows New Zealanders were the most likely migrants to have dual citizenship (49.2%), ahead of South Africa (49.0%), and Australia (47.4%).

The British Foreign and Commonwealth Office found that at least 80% of New Zealanders had some British ancestry – higher even than Australia.

RNZ has heard from dual nationals who have travelled to the UK without a British or Irish passport, as well as those not able to get one because of documents they could not track down or the high cost of applying and postage.

Many queries centred on whether border officials would have any way of checking whether a New Zealand passport holder also had UK citizenship.

Steve Horrell decided to try a real-world experiment, using an ETA (a $37 visa-waiver) he received last year to fly to London with his New Zealand passport. He took along the UK passport ($320 including postage) he purchased in February – in case it went wrong.

At two airport check-in points, no one queried whether he had dual citizenship; then he used the Smart Gate at border control in Heathrow without issue.

“I was actually very angry that my New Zealand passport was just accepted and I got the big green tick to enter the country,” he said in a formal complaint to the British Home Office. “Travel back to NZ was not an issue and I used my NZ passport throughout. So, my nice new shiny UK passport stayed in my travel wallet and has yet to see the light of day.

“How did the system not pick up that I was the holder of a valid UK passport and why did it not ask me to present it? Is the real reason that I was not challenged due to a shortage of staff to effectively police the border, or is it down to an ineffective computer system that is not fit for purpose?”

He told RNZ he planned to show an expired UK passport first if he was challenged at the border – to see if it was true that would be accepted as proof of his citizenship – then to produce his new British passport if that failed.

“It turned out to be a pointless exercise. The whole scenario is a complete nonsense and I am now absolutely sure that the UK authorities introduced this as a money-making scheme, because it would appear they were more interested in getting people through immigration by using Smart Gates so that they do not need to employ so many staff to check everyone manually.”

He sent follow-up emails after only receiving an automated acknowledgement to his complaint in May, which had promised a response in 20 working days. He said he felt conned, describing the Government’s statements about not allowing entry to British citizens using third-country passports to enter the UK as “fearmongering”.

The UK Home Office said British and Irish citizens are no longer able to get ETAs and the onus is on the individual to apply for the appropriate permission to travel. Its advice is still that it is the airline’s decision whether to allow dual citizen travellers to use an expired UK passport, if they also have a valid New Zealand passport.

The British Government had described the expired passport as a “short-term transitional measure” but it is not clear how long it will last. An article by an immigration lawyer on the UK law website Free Movement argues that ETAs issued to British dual citizens before online changes were made remain valid.

In research by the House of Commons library, it noted speculation that some British dual nationals would continue using their foreign passport by not declaring their British citizenship.

“Other dual nationals may travel to the UK as a foreign passport holder unaware that they have British citizenship. For example, a person who has never lived in the UK might have automatically acquired British citizenship through one of their parents by automatic operation of the law, without having had any formal interaction with the UK Government.

“In either situation, transport providers and staff at UK passport control wouldn’t necessarily know that a person travelling on a foreign passport also has British citizenship if the person didn’t volunteer that information. There is no central register of British citizens or dual nationals, and information about a person’s place of birth isn’t enough to confirm if they are British.”

The Home Office stressed that while British people would not be detained or separated from family at the border, the best way to ensure a smooth journey was travelling with a valid UK passport or a certificate of entitlement.

Meanwhile, the EU’s work on its own €20 ($39) visa waiver – known as ETIAS – is still continuing. It has been delayed previously and was due by the last quarter of this year. Authorities promised a specific launch date to be announced “several months in advance” and there is no indication whether that will now happen in time.

Plans for a Wellington super city have suffered a major setback, with Upper Hutt Mayor Peri Zee indicating her city is unlikely to join a proposed regional amalgamation.

Zee confirmed to the Herald she “signalled [her] position to the mayoral forum in confidence” at a meeting yesterday.

“What I can say is that we were waiting to see the financial modelling to determine the likely cost and benefits, and that modelling confirmed my scepticism around the potential benefit and also showed that it’s a high cost,” Zee said.

“I am not convinced that the benefits are likely to outweigh the costs of amalgamation.”

Local government leaders in the region have been working on an amalgamation proposal through the mayoral forum, discussing a potential super city-type merger to meet the Government’s deadline.

Ministers announced in May they were giving councils nationwide three months to come up with plans for mergers, as part of simplifying and strengthening local government.

“We are giving councils a clear choice, lead your own reform or we will do it for you,” RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said.

Zee had earlier appeared lukewarm on amalgamation, compared with other mayors in the region.

At a meeting last month, Wellington Mayor Andrew Little gave tentative support to a merger, and Lower Hutt Mayor Ken Laban and Porirua Mayor Anita Baker said they had the mandate from their communities to amalgamate.

Little confirmed Horowhenua, Wairarapa and Kāpiti councils are also unlikely to join forces with Wellington, following discussions.

He said the “core minimum” proposal would see Wellington City, Porirua, Lower Hutt and Upper Hutt councils merge.

If Upper Hutt chose not to participate, Little said, ministers could ultimately decide to include it in a reorganisation anyway.

“That would put Upper Hutt on the back foot in terms of what happens next,” Little said.

He said the discussions between the mayors had been “pretty robust on occasion, but actually pretty constructive”.

While Zee has indicated her position, her council will make its official decision on August 5, before the August 9 deadline.

Beehive bunker laptops malfunctioned during destructive storm

New Zealand Herald July 23, 2026

Operations room at the Civil Defence underground bunker at the Beehive. Photo / Marty Melville.

By Phil Pennington of RNZ

Documents show that with a destructive storm bearing down on the South Island last October, some laptops in the Beehive bunker could not access the emergency management system.

The National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) says now that it didn’t matter, that staff had other devices that did work.

The problem has come to light in a Department of Internal Affairs review released under the Official Information Act of how Nema was shifted from the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to the DIA late last year.

The reshuffle, costing just over its $2 million budget, was effective but done hastily over three months, and a host of difficulties were underestimated.

“The transfer was framed as a ‘lift and shift of NEMA’ ... The reality was substantially different to ‘lift and shift’,” said the review done last November.

“The post-transfer technology support and project structure was underestimated.”

In one case this meant that a vendor company failed to fully finish a job, leading to the problem with new DIA laptops staff had been issued.

This was not apparent until states of emergency were declared in late October in Canterbury, Southland and parts of Otago.

“It became apparent in the lead-up to an emergency activation that some aspects of the transfer had not been adequately completed by the vendor, meaning NEMA staff were unable to access the emergency environment in the bunker through their DIA devices,” said the short review.

But other laptops linked to the National Crisis Management Centre (the bunker under the Beehive) did work.

“Our response activities weren’t impacted, which is a good thing,” Nema told RNZ.

“Staff had full access to all applications and tools required to support response activities, and there were no impacts to response operations, support to [Civil Defence] groups or access to systems.”

DIA said it was accountable for making sure the tech worked. Since then it had got Datacom to make technical changes to allow access.

Nema made the shift between departments in just 10 weeks when it had a lot on its plate.

It had recently embarked on a five-year overhaul of old, fragmented disaster response technologies and introducing new ones, such as a new national warning system, in response to Cyclone Gabrielle. An internal report suggested that alongside the tech it must also helm a really big and uncertain cultural shift to be sure of lasting change in the previously fragmented sector.

Last week the agency’s fledgling tech failed under pressure, with the civil defence website crashing during a tsunami alert near Te Anau, and its just-launched emergency mobile alert map not quickly updating about either the tsunami or flooding the previous week in Wairoa.

Emergency Management Minister Mark Mitchell said he would be meeting Nema this week to make sure the website was fixed.

Last year’s shift demanded that four agencies co-operated, including Treasury.

Cabinet agreed in April 2025 on the shift and wanted it done fast, starting in June and done by September 25.

“Agencies successfully completed a significant level of work to transfer people, data, and information,” said the 10-page review.

“The overwhelming feedback from NEMA staff is the transfer was well communicated, the products and services are of a high standard, and the project was delivered by DIA in a very tight timeframe with minimal disruption to NEMA’s core business.”

However, there was a very big “but” – the review’s section on what went well had seven bullet points and what did not go well had 28 bullet points, for instance:

The lessons learned for future such shifts revolved around not underestimating the scale of it and making clear who was in charge.

Youth charities say they are “incredibly disappointed” at Claire Achmad not being reappointed Childrens Commissioner, effectively reducing her original term by one-and-a-half years.

The Herald understands Achmad reapplied for her role but was not selected, despite many children’s organisations holding her in high esteem.

A petition has now been created by youth advocates who are pushing to keep Achmad in the role.

Nikita Van Dijk said she and petition co-creator Jaden Movold were “distraught and angry” when they found out Achmad’s term as commissioner would be finishing at the end of the month.

“Her [original] appointment was supposed to last five years, so it’s been cut 18 months short, which erodes trust in an already vulnerable community,” she said.

While other commissioners had “led from a distance” and “said a whole lot without being seen”, Van Dijk said Achmad was “on the ground with youth all the time” and had a “grassroots leadership style”.

Movold said Achmad was an “exceptional” Children’s Commissioner.

He knew her in his capacity as a disabled youth advocate, and praised her for always remembering their prior conversations, following up on the things they discussed and reflecting youth experiences in her recommendations to Government.

“This petition isn’t simply about keeping one person in a role,” he said.

“Youth did not have a genuine opportunity to be heard about who represents them and who fights for their rights,” Van Dijk added.

Movold and Van Dijk said their concern was not with incoming Children’s Commissioner Jane Searle, but with the loss of continuity and the lack of consultation with young people who viewed Achmad as a trusted advocate.

Achmad was made Chief Children’s Commissioner in 2023 for a five-year term.

It made her one of five commissioners that sat on the Children and Young People’s Commission, which was abolished by the current Government last year through the passing of the Oversight of Oranga Tamariki System Legislation Amendment Bill.

The Bill fullfilled part of the Act-National coalition agreement.

In a press release at the time, Minister for Social Development Louise Upston announced Achmad would continue in her role until July 31, 2026 to oversee the transition from a panel of commissioners to a sole commissioner.

“By returning to a single Children’s Commissioner, the Bill makes it crystal clear to children and young people who their advocate is,” Upston’s press release read.

Advocates questioned why Achmad, who went from the chief commissioner to the only commissioner, was not allowed to see through her full term until 2028.

Instead, a different Children’s Commissioner was chosen for a new five-year term this year.

The Herald understands Achmad applied for the role but was not selected.

Upston did not respond to the Herald‘s questions about Achmad, instead pointing to a press release from earlier this month where she said Achmad had “led the organisation through a period of significant change, and passionately championed children’s rights”.

“I thank her for her dedication and wish her very well for the future,” the statement said.

Achmad declined to give the Herald comment but said she had “really hoped she would get to continue to serve [rangatahi]” as Children’s Commissioner in a video posted to the Commission’s social media pages.

Safeguarding Children Aotearoa chief executive Willow Duffy called Achmad “incredible” and said she was “exactly what a Children’s Commissioner could be”.

“I’m incredibly disappointed that she won’t be continuing.”

Duffy said she “loved working with Achmad”, who was “always approachable and available”.

She was aware of the petition to keep Achmad and said she “understood [young people] putting their voice to their disappointment”.

Duffy said she looked forward to working with the incoming Children’s Commissioner and wished her the best with her new role.

VOYCE Whakarongo Mai posted on social media to acknowledge Achmad’s “profound advocacy for tamariki and rangatahi in care”.

“Claire has brought warmth, integrity and an unwavering commitment to children’s rights,” their LinkedIn post read.

The charity said Achmad would show up wherever young people gathered and created spaces where they could be heard, always asking the question: “What do our young people need me to hear?”

Janhavi Gosavi is a Wellington-based journalist for the New Zealand Herald who covers news in the capital.

Dave Letele says “a perfect storm of hatred” drove his decision to abruptly leave embattled supplement retailer NZ Muscle one week after he took over the top job.

The former professional boxer resigned as NZ Muscle’s chief executive on Monday after an intense online backlash to the move, including death threats and the leaking of his home address and number plates.

Appearing on Ryan Bridge TODAY, Letele clarified that he’d “walked away” from NZ Muscle rather than quitting, saying he “learned a lot in that one week” as chief executive.

“I learned who my friends were. I also learned that I’ll never ever go into politics, that’s because I can imagine that’s what it’s like.

“It was like the perfect storm of hatred. Even though ... I didn’t make the mistakes, and I was just trying to fix them.”

He wrote earlier on his Brown Buttabean page: “I came in with the best of intentions, to help a business front up and fix things properly.

“I’ve realised I can’t help in the way it needs, and the right thing is to be honest about that.”

NZ Muscle was unwittingly thrust into the spotlight last month when the owner of a rival supplements brand released a YouTube video raising concerns about the supplement brand’s packing, labelling and regulatory processes.

An internal review subsequently confirmed that several whey protein and creatine products had been sold in “non-compliant” packaging, while others were found to have been “relabelled inappropriately”.

The company was forced to recall products due to an undeclared milk allergen, coinciding with a New Zealand Food Safety (NZFS) investigation into public complaints.

Letele conceded today that NZ Muscle handled the fallout “really poorly”, which he’d made known to them, and soon realised he wasn’t the right person to turn things around.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

“Once I left, I felt instant relief, and I knew I’d made the right decision.”

He said an appearance on Raniera Rewiri’s Planting Seeds podcast made him realise what decision he needed to make.

“It ended up being a therapy session where he said to me, ‘Dave, why are you doing this?’ And I said, ‘I can’t, I can’t quit. I don’t want to let these people that are hating on me win.

“And he said, ‘Well, they are winning, look at you.’”

Founder Dion Roosenbrand, who started NZ Muscle in 2006, took responsibility for the company’s failures and announced on July 13 that he would “step back” from the role to “work through regulatory issues”.

Letele took his place, vowing to review operations and earn back their customers’ trust.

“The people who buy from NZ Muscle, they deserve a fair go,” he said at the time.

“The staff who rely on NZ Muscle to pay their rent, put food on the tables, they deserve a fair go, and that’s what I’m about.”

Salman Rushdie testifies at terrorism trial of man convicted of stabbing him

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 21:33:08 GMT

Author testified for second time about near-killing four years ago during event at New York amphitheater

Four years after being stabbed on an amphitheater stage, Salman Rushdie on Thursday sat across a courtroom from his convicted attacker and told jurors for a second time about the ambush that nearly killed him.

The prize-winning writer recalled feeling what he thought was a punch under his chin, then feeling blood coming from his neck.

Soon, he said, “I was on the stage, lying down, with an enormous pool of blood all around me,” Rushdie testified. “It was an enormous and expansive lake of blood.”

A Buffalo federal court jury watched Rushdie fixedly as he testified – and at one point removed his glasses to show his now-sightless right eye – at Hadi Matar’s terrorism trial. Matar has pleaded not guilty.

Matar was already convicted of a state-level attempted murder charge in the 2022 attack at a cultural institution where Rushdie was poised to speak about threats to writers and artists. Federal prosecutors say Matar was acting on such a threat: an Iranian leader’s 1989 call for Rushdie’s death because of his novel The Satanic Verses.

“I can’t say what his ambitions or his aim was, but the wounds were dispersed across my body,” Rushdie testified.

Rushdie, 79, was composed and straightforward during just more than an hour on the witness stand. He outlined the attack – which blinded him in the right eye, damaged his liver , paralyzed his left hand for a time and briefly put him on a ventilator – and his lengthy recuperation and enduring injuries.

“The knife was a millimeter from my brain,” said Rushdie, whose attacker had climbed on stage, approached from behind him and then slashed the author 15 times as the Chautauqua Institution audience gasped. Spectators and another speaker, Henry Reese, scrambled to aid Rushdie and restrain Matar, who was arrested by law enforcement officers assigned to the event. Rushdie had described the stabbing and recovery previously during Matar’s earlier trial, in a memoir and in interviews with the Associated Press and other outlets.

As Rushdie testified, Matar, 28, looked down at the defense table, sometimes rested his hand on his chin or turned to speak to his lawyer, looking toward the author only as Rushdie walked out a door. The writer glanced at Matar fleetingly, if at all.

Matar’s defense has argued that prosecutors can’t prove his intent or mindset at the time of the attack – a key element in their claim that it was an act of terrorism motivated by allegiance to Iran’s government and the Iranian-backed Hezbollah militant group. Matar, currently serving a 25-year state prison sentence, faces a potential life sentence if convicted of federal charges that include engaging in an act of transnational terrorism.

When defense lawyer Nathaniel Barone asked whether Rushdie believed the defendant had ties to terrorism, the author replied: “I had no knowledge, but I had my suspicions.”

Iran’s late Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini issued the 1989 fatwa, or religious edict, calling for Rushdie to be killed over The Satanic Verses, which includes a dream sequence about Islam’s prophet Muhammad that some Muslims considered blasphemous. The novel sparked often-violent protests against Rushdie, who was born into a Muslim family, and the fatwa drove him into hiding for years. He gradually emerged after the Iranian government distanced itself from the order in 1998, though the fatwa was never officially repealed.

“For two decades or more, I led a public life without a hint of trouble,” Rushdie testified on Thursday.

Barone repeatedly asked Rushdie whether he had anticipated blowback from the book.

“Probably, but I don’t believe the book to be on trial here. I believe someone else is on trial,” Rushdie said. At Barone’s request, the judge struck the comment from the court transcript.

Prosecutors say Matar was animated partly by comments that a former Hezbollah leader, the late Hassan Nasrallah, made about Rushdie and the fatwa in 2006. The US-born Matar also holds citizenship in Lebanon, where Hezbollah is based, and Matar’s mother has said a 2018 trip there left him moody and withdrawn.

Matar started researching Rushdie in 2020 and eventually wrote to himself, “We need to kill him ASAP,” said assistant US attorney Timothy Lynch in an opening statement on Wednesday. Matar cast the killing as part of what he considered a jihad, or holy war, Lynch said.

Matar’s New Jersey bedroom and electronics held photos and other material showing his regard for Hezbollah, and he carried a fake driver’s license with a name similar to that of a Hezbollah figure, said Lynch. The US government designates Hezbollah as a terrorist organization.

Matar’s lawyer has said the government is asking jurors “to connect the dots” in a case without hard evidence about what he was thinking on the date of the attack. In a seeming effort to scrutinize how much the fatwa was on anyone’s mind by 12 August 2022, the defense also has asked some witnesses about the relatively light security around Rushdie that day. A state trooper and a sheriff’s deputy were assigned to the event.

Matar declined to testify at his state court trial but may do so at the federal trial, Barone said outside court on Thursday.

Rushdie was born in India, raised in Britain and is now a US citizen. He won the Booker prize in 1981 for his novel Midnight’s Children. His most recent work is The Eleventh Hour, a book of short stories and novellas published last year.

Iran’s government denied involvement in the 2022 stabbing, but its foreign ministry’s then-spokesperson suggested Rushdie invited trouble by insulting Islam. Hezbollah’s Nasrallah did not comment on the attack.

It’s not just a No 10 in the north, it’s an engine for growth throughout the whole UK

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 21:30:55 GMT

Power has been too centralised in Britain and tackling that is key to progress and prosperity. This initiative is ambitious: we’re remaking the state

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

On Monday, while the cameras were fixed on that famous black door in Downing Street, something important was happening 165 miles away. A small team of officials and advisers were walking into an office building in Manchester to set about the remaking of the British state.

This was the beginning of No 10 North: the first major act of this government and what I hope will be seen as its most defining.

Over the course of the past 40 years, Britain has taken a series of wrong turns. In the 1980s, political power was centralised, economic power was privatised and communities were deindustrialised. Many of the places most affected have not recovered since and are still in decline. They have been unable to turn things around because they simply do not have the necessary power to do so. This feeling of neglect has lain underneath the increasingly fractious politics that has bedevilled Britain in recent times.

Solving this problem is crucial for the cohesion of our country. It is something with which it has wrestled for a long time but never got right. We have seen gimmicks, such as levelling up. We have seen the shifting of bits of the British state around the map to no great effect.

Why has none of it worked? It is partly because, even though Whitehall departments have set up outposts, decision-making power has remained in London. It is also because, in the very centre of government itself, Nos 10 and 11 have not been sufficiently aligned – particularly on growth.

This is what No 10 North is seeking to correct and, if we succeed, it could bring the much-needed sea change in the way Britain is run. It is about driving growth from the most powerful office in the land and doing so in close alignment with the Treasury. It is about taking power down and placing it in the hands of people who can use it best.

No 10 North will be responsible for accelerating devolution. It will drive reindustrialisation and growth across every postcode of the UK. It will remove barriers to regeneration, from council housebuilding to public transport infrastructure. Crucially, No 10 North will bring the whole of Whitehall together behind places rather than standing in their way. Our long-term ambition is clear: to achieve equivalent living standards across all the regions and nations of the UK.

Giving places their own power matters because, without it, they cannot do those things. Growth cannot be imposed from the top down, but instead has to be nurtured from the bottom up. Britain has spent decades trying unsuccessfully to do the former and now, through No 10 North, it is about to give the latter a proper go.

People will have heard me talk about wanting the nation to face the same way and pull together. That example has to be set by government. Whitehall departments need to stop fighting turf wars and start pulling together behind the places that desperately need their support.

I know change is not always easy and that this is the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen. When I entered Downing Street, I told staff that the era of fighting devolution is over. No one in government loses when power is shared. When you lift up a place, you lift up Britain.

I know the power of devolution is real. A decade ago, I left Westminster to go back home and try to change things for the better. And we did. We brought buses back under public control. We created new opportunities for young people. We built a city-region with twice the economic growth of anywhere else in the UK. What we did in Greater Manchester, we can do across our nation.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Tomorrow, from No 10 North, I will chair the first meeting of the National Economic Council, bringing together senior ministers and regional mayors. Through this forum, we will ensure every department in Whitehall gets behind the growth and devolution ambitions of every region.

I want Britain to believe again. That means creating a country where everybody feels a part of what is happening and everybody feels heard. This government will demonstrate to everyone that they are part of the story.

Later this year, we will bring forward a 10-year plan for Britain, laying out a path from where we are now to where I believe we all want the country to be. Our plan will set out how we bring the essentials in life back under stronger public control to make them affordable again; how we reindustrialise every part of Britain; and how we build more council homes and solve the housing crisis.

I know people cannot wait forever to see change. So we will do smaller things too to provide some breathing space. We have already done this with two tax cuts: one on VAT on electricity bills for households over winter and another on business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues.

The new government has shown in its first five days how it is prepared to take the small steps to make life easier now and the big ones to put Britain back on the right long-term path. Both are needed simultaneously if we are to carry people with us.

I am under no illusions about how hard this is all going to be, but I have a clear plan and I know how to get things done. And this week has left me in no doubt that the civil service is ready to come on this journey with me too.

Andy Burnham is the prime minister of the United Kingdom

Regional mayors to take key roles in UK policy decisions as part of No 10 North plans

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 21:30:55 GMT

Burnham says ‘no one in government loses when power is shared’ as he revives Brown-era national economic council

It’s not just a No 10 in the north, it’s an engine for growth throughout the whole UK | Andy Burnham

Regional mayors are to be given a leading role in the UK’s economic policy, Andy Burnham has said, as he called the opening of No 10 North “the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen”.

The new prime minister has revived the national economic council [NEC], first set up by Gordon Brown to put the government on a war footing during the 2008 financial crash, arguing that economic growth requires the same level of urgency, focus and collective action.

In an article for the Guardian, he wrote: “When I entered Downing Street, I told staff that the era of fighting devolution is over. No one in government loses when power is shared.”

Burnham will chair the inaugural meeting of the council on Friday, bringing together senior ministers and regional mayors to put devolution at the heart of his government’s mission.

Burnham wrote: “Even though Whitehall departments have set up outposts, decision-making power has remained in London … This is what No 10 North is seeking to correct and, if we succeed, it could bring the much-needed sea change in the way Britain is run.

“It is about driving growth from the most powerful office in the land and doing so in close alignment with the Treasury. It is about taking power down and placing it in the hands of people who can use it best.”

As he becomes the first British leader to run the government on a weekly basis from Manchester, Burnham will face calls to prove that the operation is not tokenistic.

Earlier this week, he created a powerful new prime minister’s department taking in parts of the Cabinet Office, Treasury and housing ministry to become the “dominant driver of the UK’s economy” – an apparent tension with the No 10 North plan.

In one of his first acts, Burnham set up the Office for the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, to be led by his ally and enforcer Louise Haigh, which will oversee No 10 North in Manchester, the No 10 operation in London, and parts of the Cabinet Office.

Haigh, along with the education secretary, Lucy Powell, and the communities secretary, Angela Rayner – who both have Greater Manchester seats – are planning to spend some of their time working from No 10 North, while teams of civil servants are expected to be relocated there.

With regional mayors invited to sit round the table, Downing Street argues that devolution will be cemented at the centre of economic decision-making, maintaining the prime minister’s pledge that decisions will be taken with local leaders, not just for them.

Operating from Heron House in Manchester’s city centre, the home of GCHQ in the north-west, No 10 North is intended to bring together the levers of local economic growth and devolution under one roof for the first time, working from a single plan rather than competing ones.

Burnham is expected to work from No 10 North each week so that decisions about the country’s economic future will no longer exclusively be made in Westminster, with other ministers also working regularly from the building.

Dave Penman, the general secretary of the FDA union which represents senior civil servants, has welcomed the changes to the structure of government but cautioned that relocation was a big decision for staff.

after newsletter promotion

At least seven Greater Manchester Combined Authority employees, including Burnham’s deputy chief of staff, Caroline Simpson, and longstanding aide Kevin Lee, are already moving into the temporary building, while a brownfield site is developed. The Heron House office will be led by Sam Lister, a senior civil servant who has worked across several departments.

The NEC’s attenders will change at each meeting, depending on the issues under consideration, bringing together business leaders, trade unions and other partners where their expertise can help drive decision-making.

Under Gordon Brown, the body met twice a week and acted as the focus of his government’s effort to stave off recession, the global crisis in the financial markets and volatile prices, although there were concerns at the time that it could clip the wings of the Treasury.

The new committee was quickly described as an economic version of the Cobra emergency committee. It included key figures such as the then chancellor Alistair Darling and former business secretary Peter Mandelson, and was instrumental in coordinating emergency banking sector bailouts.

In his article, Burnham suggested that the Manchester department would be crucial to his aim to “drive reindustrialisation and growth across every postcode of the UK”.

He went on: “It will remove barriers to regeneration, from council house building to public transport infrastructure. Crucially, No 10 North will bring the whole of Whitehall together behind places rather than standing in their way.

“Our long-term ambition is clear: to achieve equivalent living standards across all the regions and nations of the UK.”

London Spirit begin new Hundred era with Tinie Tempah and double defeat

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 21:07:51 GMT

The Hundred put on a show at Lord’s but the hosts’ men’s and women’s teams both lost to Manchester Super Giants

London Spirit launched their new era with double defeat at Lord’s, and though they may have new owners, new coaches and new players it seems they’re still getting the same results. For the fifth time in their six-year history the men started their season with defeat, losing by seven runs a game of the Hundred that Liam Livingstone came very close to turning into The One.

The Spirit captain took responsibility for 20 of the last 25 balls of Manchester Super Giants’ innings, shouldering what should have been the hardest part of the bowling burden, and finished with two wickets for just 14. Then, with his team flailing in pursuit of 139, he scored 69 off 40 to keep them in the contest until the moment he swung at its antepenultimate delivery and was bowled by Sonny Baker.

They had been helped by a run of drops and misfields by the Super Giants, most notably when Livingstone heaved Noor Ahmad to deep midwicket where Tim Seifert – whose 67 off 45 ultimately decided the match – let the ball bounce off his hands and into the boundary padding for six. But on the pitch that four days earlier allowed England and India to score 747 runs between them in a ODI batters in both games struggled, and even Seifert soared for only part of his innings. His team’s knock was a curiosity, with 26 runs and one wicket coming in the first 25 balls and six wickets falling for just 22 in the final 26, while in between they rampaged to 90 at nearly two runs a ball.

Of the crowd of 23,847 some will have come for the women’s game, some for the men, and others presumably for early-noughties chart-topping rapper Tinie Tempah. That said, it seems extraordinarily unlikely that anyone will have shelled out the £55 required for an adult ticket to watch 20 minutes of twixt-game entertainment.

From pony racing to spear-throwing, from being requisitioned by the RAF to Jack Leach scoring 92 as a Test opener, Lord’s has witnessed a few unlikely sights over the years and that of Tempah, jets of fire screaming skywards behind him, was another to add to the list. But despite at one stage uttering the dreaded words “Lord’s, this is a brand new one” he produced a masterclass in scepticism-obliteration.

Helpfully, he spent very little of it on his heavily branded stage, favouring wading into the crowd to hug mildly bemused paunchy white blokes. “He was,” Eoin Morgan later enthused on Sky, “magnificent.” This might not have been the future Tempah envisaged when Pass Out was conquering the charts 16 years ago but it was one he embraced with winning enthusiasm.

Southampton’s Utilita Bowl will host a men’s Ashes Test for the first time next year with the men’s and ⁠women’s series against Australia again running concurrently, the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) announced.

Trent Bridge will host the first men’s Test, starting on 18 June, while the ⁠first match of the ⁠multi-format women’s series, the ​sole test match, begins at Headingley on 24 June.

Southampton will host the fourth men’s Test starting on 21 July. England last played a Test match at the venue, ⁠also known as the Rose Bowl, in 2020 when Pakistan were the opposition during the Covid pandemic. The World Test Championship final was also played at the ground in 2021 when New Zealand beat ⁠India.

A packed summer of cricket in England will also include 10 ODIs for the England men’s team, the final of ​the World Test Championship at London’s Oval and England ‌men’s Mixed Disability team hosting Australia.

The ‌men’s and women’s Ashes were also held at the same time in England in 2023, boosting crowds for the women’s ‌fixtures. Reuters

It was not so much Pass Out as fail and out for London Spirit’s women, even if they started beautifully, with Grace Harris hitting the opening delivery for four. But that was very much as good as it got: by the end of the powerplay they were 23 for four and having to reset their ambitions to mere survival.

In the end they did not manage that, bowled out after 91 balls having scored just 80. No team in the history of the women’s Hundred has successfully defended a score below 106 and Spirit never looked likely to become the first, Super Giants cantering to a total that was neither of those things in just 59 balls to win by seven wickets, with Paige Scholfield carrying her side over the finish line with a four and a six off successive Josie Groves deliveries and in the process becoming the game’s top scorer with just 22.

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 19:34:45 GMT

Residents in Ladera Ranch in Orange county voice concerns after six children diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Concerns are growing in southern California over a cluster of “exceptionally rare” cancer cases that has sickened multiple children in a suburban community.

Families living in the Orange county neighborhood of Ladera Ranch, home to about 26,000 people, have reported that six children in the community were diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma, Katrina Foley, the vice-chair of the county board of supervisors, said in a statement.

Ewing sarcoma is a rare cancer that primarily affects bone and soft tissue and is largely seen in young adults and children.

At a community meeting this week, hundreds of residents turned up to voice their concerns, including several who spoke about additional cancer cases in adults and pets. While the American Cancer Society reports there are “no known lifestyle-related or environmental causes” of Ewing sarcoma, many residents believe the cancer cases are linked to the use of herbicides and pesticides.

“We’re very concerned about pesticides that are being sprayed all around the community,” Liesl Heizt told ABC7. “There’s so many times that I walk around and they’re spraying, and I ask what they’re spraying and they’re not telling us.”

During the meeting, Brian Dalton spoke about his daughter Lily who died earlier this year after being diagnosed with the same rare cancer as the other cases, KTLA 5 reported.

“I don’t want another mother holding her child’s hand through endless treatments, praying for one more birthday, planning a funeral instead of a future,” Dalton said.

In a letter sent last week, Foley urged the state to expedite a review of the cases and give residents “timely, transparent updates”.

“Ladera Ranch families deserve answers, transparency and urgency from the state,” Foley said. “We do not yet know what caused these cancers, but that uncertainty demands a comprehensive review of every credible factor, including possible environmental exposures, along with direct communication and the public release of the findings.”

Kemi Badenoch ‘has to adapt’ her rhetoric to take on Andy Burnham

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 18:14:51 GMT

Conservative leader is becoming more confident and forging a message for her party, but faces a new opponent

“So, Andy Burnham seems like a nice guy.” Those were the slightly unexpected opening words of Kemi Badenoch’s first speech since the change in prime minister. But make no mistake: she was there to bury her opponent.

Even Badenoch-sceptics inside the Conservative party and farther afield agree the Tory leader is becoming more confident, and has been able to forge an increasingly coherent message for her party, one based on a promise of economic competence.

She does, nonetheless, face a different challenge now Burnham has replaced Keir Starmer.

Aside from being a fresh face with a likely polling bounce, the former Greater Manchester mayor is more of a media natural, with the ability to deflect Badenoch’s jibes using self-deprecating humour, such as a viral social media response last month after the Tory leader dismissed him as a “pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt”.

“She has to adapt – it’s like with anything when your opponent changes,” one senior Conservative said. “As a personality, Burnham is much more likable [than Starmer], and comes with a fair degree of popularity. She needs to wait for weaknesses, and one immediately seems to be: where is the money coming from for all these giveaways?”

And that was one of the main themes of Badenoch’s speech on Thursday morning, held in muggy sunshine on a rooftop terrace in central London.

Labelling Burnham’s philosophy as “cap one price and send the bill somewhere else”, she repeatedly questioned how the new prime minister would pay for his early flurry of policies. The other central theme was ambition, Badenoch calling Burnham a prime minister “with small answers to big problems”.

Such message discipline would be necessary in taking on the new operation in No 10, one senior Conservative MP said, especially given Badenoch’s occasional tendency to get caught up in culture-war debates.

The MP said: “When she first became leader there was a bit of a worry that she would just talk endlessly about culture-war issues. But that hasn’t happened. The focus should be on the economy and jobs, which it currently is.”

A manifestation of Badenoch’s increased confidence is a schedule of regular press conferences and lengthy media Q&As, often without a particular policy to announce. It is notably similar to the timetable maintained last summer by Nigel Farage – before his byelection battle and anxieties over questions about his finances scuppered this.

And while she still maintains a largely take-no-prisoners approach, Badenoch now has rhetorical registers other than the sometimes caustic antagonism she used on Starmer and, in a speech which some Tories say began her turnaround, towards Rachel Reeves when she eviscerated the then-chancellor’s budget with almost startling ferocity.

Such an approach would not necessarily work against politicians more relaxed in their own skin, said Luke Tryl, the UK director of the pollsters More in Common, who is a regular observer of its focus groups.

“If Burnham is seen to just laugh it off it might be less effective than against brittleness,” Tryl said. “The reason it worked so well against Reeves, and her budget response got such rave reviews, was in part because Reeves looked so shellshocked. I suspect [the new chancellor] John Healey and Burnham won’t.”

Bigger questions remain for Badenoch, not least why her own improved personal poll ratings have yet to translate into more support for her party, and whether her mission to reshape the Tories in her muscularly rightwing approach could put off some more moderate voters.

But for now, much of the coming weeks will be devoted to pinning down how best to tackle a PM who is a notably more slippery target that his predecessor.

“She has a summer to figure this out,” the senior Tory said. “But she has to be nimble – what works in July might not by September.”

Chelsea paid Aston Villa £117m for Morgan Rogers. Is he the right fit?

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 18:00:51 GMT

The England attacker thrives when he can gallop into space but Xabi Alonso’s best team built attacks slowly

By Opta Analyst

It quickly became apparent this summer that Aston Villa would not be holding on to Morgan Rogers. Having helped the club finish fourth in the Premier League and win the Europa League, the 23-year-old was in demand.

Arsenal looked like his likeliest next destination, with the champions eager to strengthen the left side of their attack. The charm offensive came from many angles, with Martin Ødegaard, Mikel Arteta and the club’s England players trying to sell the idea to Rogers. But, with Arsenal reluctant to meet Villa’s asking price, Chelsea intervened and made Rogers the most expensive British player ever, surpassing the £116m that Manchester City paid Nottingham Forest for Elliot Anderson earlier this summer.

Xabi Alonso is new to Chelsea, so it is difficult to know exactly where Rogers will play. The versatile forward, who started out at West Brom before moving to Manchester City, Middlesbrough and then Villa, will probably be used in a variety of roles – often starting from the left but having opportunities to take up various attacking positions.

Alonso predominantly used a 3-4-3 formation at Bayer Leverkusen and a 4-2-3-1 at Real Madrid. If Chelsea play with three at the back, Rogers will be the left-sided No 10 in the team; if they use a four-man defence, he will start slightly wider but with the freedom to come inside – or he might even occupy the central role.

If Alonso goes with the style he used at Leverkusen, Rogers might not be the best fit. During Alonso’s two full seasons in the Bundesliga, the team averaged 62.1% (2023-24) and 59.6% (2024-25) possession. During their title-winning campaign in 2023-24, they went unbeaten all season while dominating the ball and moving up the pitch slowly.

They were set up to patiently build with lots of passes, win back possession quickly if they lost it and keep the ball as close to the opposition’s goal as possible. They made 367 high turnovers, which was 54 more than any other side. This system works best with attacking players who are tidy and intricate in tight spaces. However, Rogers is at his most effective when he can use his pace and gallop into space.

His dribble completion rate last season was 34.2%, which was nothing to shout about. And his completion rate for passes under pressure was 73.4% – again not exceptional. Of the 161 forwards and midfielders who attempted at least 300 passes under pressure last season, Rogers ranked 143rd. The statistics suggest he is not particularly effective in close-quarters engagements.

With space to attack, Rogers is a threat. He made 223 progressive carries last season, the 10th highest among Premier League forwards, wingers and attacking midfielders. Only Cody Gakpo (41) and Matheus Cunha (35) had more carries that ended in shots than Rogers (30). He also created 16 chances for teammates after a carry: only 11 players created more. Rogers’ combined 46 chances created and shots taken following carries put him behind just Jérémy Doku (58), Gakpo (57) and Bukayo Saka (56). Alonso’s passing style may not bring the best from Rogers.

There are reasons for optimism though. Rogers is frequently on the move and that makes him difficult to track. Only four players made more off-ball runs in the league last season; his 160 off-ball runs ending in the box was the eighth highest in the division.

He also has the potential to form a good relationship with João Pedro. The Brazilian will probably be the focal point of the team and he is not a conventional No 9. He likes to drop deep, link with teammates and be a creator almost as much as a finisher. With Pedro dropping back, there will be room for Rogers to exploit beyond him: he made 258 runs in behind last season, the 12th highest in the league.

Rogers’ strong relationship with Ollie Watkins bodes well for Chelsea. He created 20 open-play chances for Watkins last season, which was the second most from one player to another in the league. Wherever he has played, Rogers has developed an understanding with his teammates. He already has a close friendship with Cole Palmer after their time together in the Manchester City academy.

Rogers’ other great attribute is his ball-striking ability. Since he made his Premier League debut in February 2024, Rogers has scored 21 non-penalty goals from 14.7 non-penalty expected goals. His overperformance of +6.3 is the 10th highest in the league.

Rogers has a great strike on him and it could be a gamechanger for Chelsea, particularly when they play teams employing a low block. His five league goals from outside the box since his Villa debut is bettered by only six players. Few players are as accurate when shooting from distance. It was his shot against Norway that led to Jude Bellingham’s winning goal in the World Cup quarter-final.

Chelsea have paid an incredible amount of money for Rogers and there are reasons to wonder if the move will work tactically. But Rogers has a habit of making an impact regardless of the context. He’s not a right winger but he still made his presence known for England against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final, setting up Anthony Gordon’s opener from the right.

Is he a £117m player? Perhaps not. Will he succeed playing the same way he played at Villa? Perhaps not. But it’s hard to imagine him not making a significant impact at Stamford Bridge.

Lobbying firm pressed for details about payments to journalists for favourable stories

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 17:52:11 GMT

MPs and others condemn behaviour of CT Group, which offered cash for positive coverage of clients

A political lobbying firm secretly paying journalists for articles favourable to its clients is facing calls to reveal full details of the payments, after the practice was denounced as a dangerous “attack on democracy”.

MPs, senior lobbyists and transparency campaigners all condemned the behaviour of CT Group, the firm co-founded by the campaign strategist Lynton Crosby, an election guru previously hired by David Cameron and Boris Johnson.

There were calls for an overhaul of lobbying rules and demands for CT Group to reveal the full extent of the practice, exposed after a four-month Guardian investigation.

“Lobbyists paying journalists to produce apparently independent articles is an attack on the ethics of journalism, public relations and, indeed, on democracy,” said Alastair McCapra, the chief executive of the Chartered Institute of Public Relations. CT Group is not a member of the body.

“Anyone can practise public relations in this country without belonging to a professional body or answering to a code of conduct. The majority do that ethically but these reported practices undermine our profession and erode the credibility on which responsible lobbying and public relations depend.”

Lobbyists for CT Group told an undercover reporter they had paid journalists to place apparently independent stories in newspapers. They also offered hundreds of pounds in cash incentives to do the same for a property industry client and said that in return for the payment, CT Group would have increased editorial control.

Jemimah Steinfeld, the chief executive of Index on Censorship, said: “To spin what is lobbying as journalism is shortsighted and frankly dangerous.” She called on CT Group to launch an internal investigation.

Steve Goodrich, the head of research and investigations at Transparency International UK, said: “When lobbyists secretly pay journalists to write favourable coverage for their clients, it undermines the integrity of the press. This investigation raises serious questions about the conduct of CT Group, and about how widespread these hidden arrangements are across the lobbying industry.”

Luke Taylor, a Liberal Democrat member of parliament’s public administration and constitutional affairs committee, said there should now be “full transparency on when money has changed hands when it comes to reporting”.

“Across the board we are seeing worrying signs of our democracy being in peril,” he said. “A truly free press is a fundamental pillar of a healthy democracy and so we must do everything in our power to maintain it.”

Sam Carling, a Labour MP on the committee, said: “If secret payments or other ethical failings are taking place widely, then the government ought to consider giving the Office of the Registrar of Consultant Lobbyists regulatory powers to hold lobbyists to account.”

Rupa Huq, a Labour member of the Commons media select committee, said: “We need more transparency in lobbying which almost feels like the wild west, such is the lack of regulation.” She added: “I hope the new Andy Burnham government can grip this issue.”

The Guardian began investigating the arrangements after CT Group approached a freelance journalist and offered to pay him to pitch a piece to a British national newspaper about problems caused for the housebuilding industry by the Building Safety Regulator, set up in the wake of the Grenfell Tower fire that killed 72 people.

CT Group is a lobbying company with a £40m-a-year turnover whose recent clients include the tobacco firm Philip Morris and the owner of the football club Manchester City.

In a statement, CT Group said: “We do not comment publicly on work we do for clients and we therefore cannot respond to the specific allegations you have made.”

It said the events had been “deliberately mischaracterised” and that it had not engaged the undercover journalist to do anything and did not pay him anything. It said the journalist was looking for work and “chased us relentlessly over a period of more than six months”.

The investigation has also raised concerns about the vulnerability of freelance journalism, which can often feature irregular and low-paying work.

“If reporters are being paid to place stories in papers by private companies this breaches the essential buffer zone between lobbying and journalism,” said Martin Bright, a senior lecturer in journalism at the University of Essex.

“The market is very tough for freelance journalists in the present media climate. They should never be exploited in this way.”

Southport killer Axel Rudakubana moved to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 17:51:41 GMT

Exclusive: Clinical assessments concluded Rudakubana could not be safely managed in prison, sources say

The Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has been moved from prison to a psychiatric hospital after clinical assessment, the Guardian can disclose.

He was transferred to Broadmoor high-security hospital from the category A prison Belmarsh this week after it was concluded that he could not be managed safely in a prison environment, sources confirmed.

People in psychiatric units such as Broadmoor are treated as patients rather than prisoners. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said he would remain locked up and is unlikely to ever be released.

The move is likely to anger many of the families of his victims, who will argue he was assessed as fit to stand trial in January 2025.

It means the cost of his incarceration will rise. Costs for patients in hospital secure units are more than £300,000 each a year, compared with about £60,000 for prisoners, Whitehall sources said.

Rudakubana, 19, from Banks, Lancashire, was jailed for life in January 2025, with a minimum sentence of 52 years, for the “sadistic” murders of Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and nine-year-old Alice da Silva Aguiar.

He attacked eight other children, the class instructor Leanne Lucas, and businessman John Hayes, who had tried to disarm him at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024 in Southport. He was also found guilty of producing the biological toxin ricin and of possessing an al-Qaida training manual, an offence under the Terrorism Act.

Alder Hey children’s NHS foundation trust confirmed Rudakubana had been under its care as a mental health patient between 2019 and 2023, when he “stopped engaging”. He was referred to them after taking a knife to school and later saying he had done so “to use it”.

He was also referred to the UK’s counter-extremism programme, Prevent, because he had been researching school massacres on a computer at his next school, the Acorns.

There were two other referrals to Prevent, but none were progressed as Rudakubana had no clear ideology behind his obsession with violence.

In May 2025, Rudakubana attacked a prison officer with boiling water, sparking an internal inquiry at Belmarsh.

Responding to the move to Broadmoor, Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the POA union, which represents prison, correctional, and secure psychiatric workers, said his members believed he was “playing the system” so he could move to a more comfortable environment.

He said: “[Rudakubana] is not mentally unwell. He is playing the system and is nothing more than evil. He should spend his entire sentence in solitary confinement staring at four walls.

“It is appalling to think that he will now enjoy all the freedoms a secure hospital is forced to give him and even more unjustified is the taxpayer actually paying him benefits because he is now classed as mentally unwell.

“It is POA members who will now have to carry out the wishes of those who think he can be cured. This is a sickening development and my thoughts are with the families of the victims and all those who have been affected by his atrocious crime.”

Broadmoor, in Crowthorne, Berkshire, is the oldest of England’s three high security psychiatric hospitals. It has been used to hold some of the UK’s most notorious murderers, including Peter Sutcliffe, the Yorkshire Ripper.

Patients remain locked up, with conditions heavily regulated by strict physical security including locked wards, monitored by staff and 24-hour CCTV. They receive mandatory therapeutic and rehabilitative programmes. If offenders no longer require treatment in hospital, the 1983 Mental Health Act provides for a swift return to prison.

If an offender presents an increased risk and cannot be managed safely in a prison environment because of a mental disorder, a request to be moved to a secure psychiatric unit can be made by clinical professionals.

Sources said the act and the clinical assessments meant ministers had no choice but to accept the request to transfer the prisoner in this instance.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country’s heart for ever and our thoughts remain with them.

“The offender who carried out these vile crimes will rightly spend the entirety of his 52-year custodial sentence locked up, and is unlikely to ever be released.

“High secure hospitals are not places of freedom. He will remain under constant supervision in a high-security psychiatric unit, and be returned to prison as soon as possible.

“The transfer of an offender follows a robust independent clinical assessment.”

One task awaiting new energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh is devising a plan to avoid a crisis by the end of the decade

Welcome to the energy secretary job, Miatta Fahnbulleh. You have a politically tricky decision to make on whether to approve production at the Jackdaw gasfield and the Rosebank oilfield. But here’s another one that can’t wait much longer: what is the broader plan to ensure Britain avoids a gas supply crisis in 2030?

By way of reminder, one of the more alarming reports published by the energy department under Ed Miliband was the one that warned of “an emerging risk” to gas supplies at the turn of the decade if an important piece of kit – an import terminal, say, or the critical 725-mile Langeled pipeline from Norway – were to be out of the action during a severe cold snap.

“In the unlikely event of the loss of the single largest piece of gas infrastructure, gas supply falls short of demand for all pathways in 2030-31,” said the report from the government’s in-house adviser, the National Energy System Operator (Neso). Unlikely maybe – but the risk can’t be wished away, which was the point of the report.

Now here comes Centrica, owner of British Gas, warning that it will close its Rough gas storage facility off the coast of Yorkshire unless it can agree a long-term financial support deal with the government to back a £2bn expansion. Rough is Britain’s largest such facility and, although Centrica has been issuing dire warnings for a while, it clearly means it this time. It has set a date for closure next April, in the absence of a deal. The company isn’t even injecting gas into Rough for this winter.

“I think this [Rough] is essential for the UK energy security,” said Centrica’s chief executive, Chris O’Shea, on Thursday. “I think it would not be good if this was to be allowed to close, and that’s why it’s really a decision for government now. What we hear a lot is that this is a commercial decision for Centrica. That is patently not true.”

On his commercial point, O’Shea is clearly correct. The economics of storage rely on buying low and selling high, but winter/summer spreads are often narrower these days. Disruption caused by the closure of the strait of Hormuz worked in Centrica’s favour at Rough as it made a £57m top-line profit at the facility in the half-year, but last year it lost almost as much. That is not a basis on which to sanction a £2bn investment without some form of regulated return.

Whether Rough is the right storage project for the country is another matter. Gas folk refer to it as “a big balloon with a small straw”, meaning it can hold large volumes but extraction can be slow at the moment they’re urgently needed. Maybe that feature could be re-engineered away if the £2bn investment happens. Or maybe a different storage solution would be preferable – more on-shore salt caverns, for example, which comprise most of the rest of Britain’s storage capacity. Or the economics favours other ideas in the Neso report: expanding interconnector capacity to the continent, or building more liquefied natural gas import terminals (Britain only has three). Or a combination of the above.

The future of North Sea gas production is not incidental to this debate either. The basin may be in long-term decline, but the rate of decline matters (and Jackdaw alone would be 6% of domestic production). If the gas system operator knows the stuff is coming, that is storage by proxy.

The point is that a joined-up strategy is needed. Gas still accounted for 35% of the UK’s total energy demand in 2024, according to government statistics. Even if it dwindles to next to nothing for the purposes of electricity generation by 2030 with the rollout of renewables, demand for gas for domestic heating will be slower to shift, as there are 24m households with a gas connection.

The short-term question for Fahnbulleh, then, is whether to pay Centrica to fill Rough for this winter. The argument in favour is that storage on the continent, which Britain usually taps during the cold months, is projected to be low after the Hormuz disruption. There is a risk of price spikes. A fuller Rough might dampen them.

The longer-term issue is the overall strategy to decide where the gas will come from in 2030. The storage question is central, and so is the policy on North Sea production. There is a strong sense that both have been dodged until now.

The government’s interim response to its own “gas system in transition” review is due within weeks. Real choices have to follow because none of these projects – more connectors, more terminals, or more storage – will be quick to build if they are needed. In the meantime, that “emerging risk” of a supply crunch has, presumably, already emerged a bit further.

Rugby brain injury case reaches crisis point as judge retires to consider 95% strikeouts

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 17:36:45 GMT

Senior Master Cook says case in ‘uncharted territory’

Judge blames solicitor Richard Boardman for situation

The landmark legal action over brain damage in rugby is on the brink of collapse as the managing judge weighs whether to strike out 95% of the first batch of 561 claimants on the grounds they have failed to comply with a court order to disclose all available documents relating to their neurological testing.

After two days of hearings at the Royal Courts of Justice, Senior Master Cook said the case had entered “uncharted territory” because he was unable to find any legal precedent for what to do next before retiring to make his judgment.

It’s unclear how long he will take. Cook said that, given that absence of precedent, he needed to operate in “a careful and considered manner”. The court is due to break for summer next Friday, 31 July.

The defendants – World Rugby, the Rugby Football Union and the Welsh Rugby Union in one case, and Rugby Football League and British Amateur Rugby League Association in the other – all pressed to have these cases struck out on the grounds that there had been “wholesale and widespread non-compliance” with the court order to disclose all the documents.

Cook agreed with this at the high court on Thursday, but was unequivocal that it was the solicitor until this week in charge of the case, Richard Boardman of Rylands Garth, who was at fault rather than the claimants themselves. “The only complaint in this case is against the way Mr Boardman has handled the material,” Cook said. “No claimant in this case can be said in any way, shape or form to be responsible for the deficiencies in the way this case has been presented.”

Boardman has notified the court of his intention to “come off the record” in the case after the claimants unanimously agreed to terminate their dealings with Rylands Garth.

They are in the process of appointing new solicitors, but until they have done so Boardman remains notionally in charge despite being absent from court for the last day and a half of hearings. The firm Leigh Day has been consulting on the case since February, and is considering whether to take it on.

Cook said he felt this change “raises more questions than it answers”. There are still second tranches of stayed cases in both league and union, which could conceivably proceed to trial even if this first tranche is struck out. But as the barrister representing the Rugby Football League, William Audland KC, said in court: “There may be no one that is prepared to pick up this mess.” Even if they were, it would probably necessitate more delays and expenses in a case that has been running for six years and has cost millions.

Yet Cook was mindful of the severity of strikeouts, which would deny the claimants the opportunity for justice. He described them as passengers in a vehicle being driven by somebody else. “The point is simply this: you have three buses full of passengers, all going to the same destination. The first bus, the driver takes them off the edge of a cliff, with the result they do not get to their destination. The other two buses get to the destination. Let’s say they are successful, buses two and three. What of those on board bus one?”

Cook told the court the case had only reached this crisis point because Boardman had given misleading evidence about whether or not he had successfully complied with the court order. The defence have been provided with thousands of documents relating to the testing, and the claimants argue that these ought to be sufficient. But there remain significant gaps, despite Boardman’s insistence in court that there were not.

“Mr Boardman should have said he had complied as far as he was capable instead of making these bland statements that the order had been complied with to the letter,” said Cook.

“But that’s the evidence he has chosen to put here, with not a bit of mea culpa.”

The dispute led to the 74-day 1982 Falklands war, where 649 Argentinians and 255 Britons were killed.

“It’s disappointing when politics gets mixed with sport,” Alexander told the Guardian regarding Argentina’s banner. “We are here to compete and represent our country. We keep politics out of it.”

Alexander, who moved to the Falkland Islands from South Africa eight years ago, said representing the British overseas territory had been a rewarding experience. “I am fairly new to the Falkland Islands but I am enjoying [living there],” he said.

Argentina’s celebrations prompted the now former prime minister of the United Kingdom, Keir Starmer, to back calls for Fifa to investigate whether any rules were breached when the banner was displayed.

Bowls is one of the original six sports on the Commonwealth Games programme and it has been played at every Games since 1930, with the exception of the 1966 Games in Kingston, Jamaica, where no bowls facilities were available. Team England did not give a reason for her withdrawal, although it is expected that several athletes are prioritising next month’s European Championships in Birmingham amid a congested schedule.

The three-time Olympic medallist Asher-Smith had been due to compete in the women’s 4x100m relay, while Hudson-Smith, Neita and Anning were all expected to strengthen England’s medal prospects.

In response to the high-profile absentees the chief executive of the Games, Phil Batty, said he was focused on the quality of talent competing in Glasgow, while also looking at athletes for whom the event will be a springboard to future success.

Niamh Emerson replaces Johnson-Thompson after previously winning Commonwealth bronze behind her in 2018, while Renee Regis, Ebuka Nwokeji, Tara Simpson-Sullivan and Tom Keen also come into the team. The withdrawals follow the Olympic champion Keely Hodgkinson’s decision to skip the Games. The athletics programme begins on Monday.

The Guardian view on Europe’s demographic crisis: the young must not be left to deal with the consequences

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 17:22:27 GMT

A new Brussels study highlights the pace at which EU countries are ageing. A more informed public debate is overdue

Europe is ageing at pace as birthrates fall and people live longer. A new report by the European Commission, published this month, notes that 2012 marked the first year in which fewer people were born in EU countries than people died in them. By the middle of this century, nearly one in three EU residents will be 65 or older. The numbers of those over 80 will almost triple from 6% to 15%. The old continent is getting visibly greyer.

The transition to a “longevity society”, as the report’s authors describe it, is something to be celebrated. Many people are enjoying healthier, richer lives for longer, and redefining the meaning and possibilities of old age. But the statistics and direction of travel also point to immense social challenges, with implications for the way we work, intergenerational fairness and the future funding of care. Sadly, amid fraught and at times toxic debates about immigration and the cost of welfare, Europe’s politics is struggling to meet the moment.

A relative decline in the size of the working-age population underlines the crucial role that non-EU migrants will continue to play in easing demographic pressures. The zero-net-migration future dreamed of by far-right parties would leave the EU’s population an estimated 32% smaller by 2100, dramatically increasing the fiscal burden on those in work. Yet mainstream politicians avoid highlighting this inconvenient truth, and devoting the necessary resources to fostering integration, while competing with the far right to create an ever more hostile environment for asylum seekers.

On welfare, the framing of the debate is increasingly dominated by the idea that Europe’s postwar social model – conceived in an era of population growth – is no longer affordable. That is a politically dangerous calculation. Since the 2008 crash, resentment at austerity programmes introduced across Europe has been instrumental in the rise of the authoritarian populism which imperils the EU’s democratic values and social fabric. In deeply unequal societies, the message that the less well-off will simply have to work harder and longer for less will further fuel the politics of the far right.

The argument for more cuts is also economically flawed. Future growth and productivity in demographically challenged communities will depend on making it easier for more people to participate in a flexible and accessible labour market. From the reform of social care to offering affordable childcare and sustained help for the long-term unemployed, that will require renewed investment to unlock dormant potential. The related issue of rural depopulation and decline will also need to be addressed, as the young increasingly gravitate to cities in search of opportunities that can no longer be found where they grew up.

The factors underlying what is a global fertility crisis are complex. But this is a problem that is here to stay. In Europe, public policies designed to increase the birthrate have signally failed to shift the dial, and the European Commission’s study indicates that the pace of demographic change is quicker than anticipated. Nevertheless, beyond controversies over changes to retirement ages, the long-term consequences and implications continue to fly under the radar.

A bigger, more high-profile debate is overdue. It cannot be left to younger generations to pick up the pieces of a broken social model which should have been renewed and redesigned while we had the chance.
