The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 17:21:30 GMT

Sadiq Khan’s heat-ready plan for London is a sensible strategy for adaptation that should provide a roadmap for other cities

“Our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe from the outside is under threat,” the geographer Sam Johnson-Schlee writes in Hot House, his recent book on how heat has transformed domestic life. This summer, high temperatures have become inescapable. People have coped with makeshift solutions: keeping curtains drawn, placing foil over windows or – for those who can afford one – plugging in an air-conditioning unit. Planning experts warn that, with only about half of councils requiring new buildings to include cooling strategies, many homes will become “death traps” as temperatures rise.

Britain’s homes weren’t built to cope with this. The country’s historically mild climate allowed developers to build houses without insulation, while industrialisation supplied plentiful coal to burn when temperatures dropped. Many homes are consequently drafty in winter and sweltering in summer. Unlike those in Mediterranean climates, British homes lack shutters and shaded communal spaces. While Ildefons Cerdà, Barcelona’s masterplanner, was designing housing blocks with cool courtyards and chamfered edges to allow breezes to flow, Britain’s Victorian builders were throwing up rows of terrace houses – many without cross-ventilation – and giving little thought to the movement of the sun.

A new approach is overdue. Insulation would help to keep properties cool, but schemes to encourage it have languished. The promising green homes grant, launched in 2020 as part of Boris Johnson’s pledge to “build back greener”, was the victim of a political culture that prized soundbites over meaningful policy. The scheme gave upfront vouchers to homeowners and landlords to upgrade their insulation, but collapsed after just six months, with the public accounts committee saying that it had been “set up to fail” owing to an impossible timetable and rushed design.

With no national strategy for dealing with oppressive heat, many homeowners have installed air conditioning. There are now twice the number of air-conditioned homes in Britain that there were three years ago. While this technology has a role to play, it should form part of a broader cooling strategy alongside less energy-intensive techniques. Adopted en masse, air conditioning raises the urban temperature by expelling hot air, making life even warmer for people without it.

A recent plan from the mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, sketches a welcome alternative. The capital is more affected by extreme temperatures than anywhere in Britain due to its distinct heat island effect. London’s heat-ready plan puts forward a collective response based on sensible measures that should serve as a roadmap for other cities, such as retrofitting homes with shutters, installing air conditioning in schools and other public buildings, planting more trees for shade, and providing more swimming spots where people can take a dip.

There is much to admire here. But Sir Sadiq’s plan collides with a political reality that poses severe challenges to adaptation. In a fiscal climate hostile to public investment, it will demand many billions of public money to deliver, particularly since such changes, its authors note, “do not always translate into clear financial savings or returns”. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has made much of his vision for a politics that is more attuned to place, but has so far remained quiet about the climate crisis. Its terrifying impact on the places where we live should make this threat an urgent priority.

Trump made his remarks on Thursday as oil prices once again surged past the symbolic $100 for a barrel of Brent crude, the international benchmark, and amid indications the price could go higher still.

He acknowledged that such a decision would have consequences but said he had not yet made a final determination. Israel “would join in two minutes if I ask them to”, he added, before saying: “We don’t need anybody.”

Trump’s comments followed the earlier threat of “major military punishment” against Iran and the Houthis, after the Iran-backed Yemeni militia’s attacks on two Saudi Arabian oil tankers in the Red Sea.

Underlining the sense of a region increasingly approaching an abyss, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, told the security council that the Middle East was being pushed to the “edge of the unimaginable” amid mounting fears over the trajectory of the conflict.

“The situation is getting out of control. It is teetering on the edge of the unimaginable. The region is being pulled into an ever-widening circle of confrontation. One crisis feeds another. One escalation triggers the next,” Guterres told a security council meeting.

“As this dynamic spreads, the political objectives are becoming increasingly obscured by the confrontation itself.”

The UK announced it was temporarily withdrawing diplomatic staff from Iran on Wednesday, and the German military announced on Thursday that it would withdraw two vessels from the Red Sea.

And as Israeli cities opened bomb shelters, the US state department warned Americans living in the region that flights may be cancelled.

In a separate development, Trump clarified on Thursday that an announced agreement that the US would help Saudi Arabia with its civilian nuclear programme would require the kingdom to normalise relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords, a move Saudi Arabia has long resisted until there is demonstrable movement on Palestinian rights and statehood.

It emerged later that Trump had not spoken to Saudi Arabia about the new condition.

The Houthi attacks threatened the safety of a second major maritime route connecting the Suez canal to the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. They also came amid reports that Iran had sent military advisers and drone parts to the Houthis 10 days ago.

Quoting four sources, including two Iranians, Reuters reported on Thursday that Iran had transferred ​Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps personnel and military-related equipment on a flight from Tehran to Yemen on 13 July, as Tehran was calling for the Houthis to blockade the Bab el-Mandeb strait.

Ships had begun turning back from sailing through the narrow strait this week after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports, most notably the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which Riyadh has been using to ship oil to Asia during the conflict that has all but halted shipping through the strait of Hormuz.

The maritime data and analysis firm Lloyd’s List Intelligence said the Houthi attacks put Saudi oil shipments from Yanbu at risk and presented a “double whammy” on top of the Hormuz disruptions, , adding that the Houthi threat “raises questions on the viability of this route”.

Trump wrote on social media: “If [the Houthis] do this again, the US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a Surrogate and/or Proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves.”

The Houthis’ Saba news agency said the rebels had struck two tankers, the Encelia and the Layla, causing fires on both. There were no reports of casualties in their first reported attack on a vessel since they announced the blockade of Saudi-linked shipping.

The Bab el-Mandeb is a vital shipping chokepoint connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. About 12% of the world’s trade, including a fourth of global container traffic, passes through there, moving between Europe and Asia via the Suez canal at the northern end of the Red Sea.

Trump has been escalating his rhetoric against Iran in recent days, hinting the US is prepared to bomb an underground tunnel complex at the “Pickaxe mountain” site where Israel alleges Tehran has hidden centrifuges used in uranium enrichment.

As Trump has struggled to get a grip on the spiralling crisis, during which Iran has occasionally launched lethal strikes against US bases and Washington’s Gulf allies, he appears to have been sucked into an “escalation trap”, threatening ever more violent retaliation.

On Wednesday, Trump said the US would destroy one bridge or power plant every time Iran shot at a ship in the strait.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Trump was seeking a “head for an eye” after the recent deaths of several US service members in an Iranian strike on the Muwaffaq Salti airbase in Jordan.

However, speaking on the outskirts of the Asean conference in Manila, Rubio said Iran was “begging for a deal”, and insisted “they need to come to their senses” and that they will “pay a very heavy price for the things they are doing” – all claims US officials have made before.

With Trump’s poll ratings in freefall, and his war against Iran deeply unpopular at home, the president and his administration are running short of time before the autumn midterm elections to find a resolution to the conflict on Washington’s terms.

Underlining Trump’s growing political problems, the US House of Representatives narrowly passed a resolution on Thursday to halt US military action in Iran, the second such warning to the president.

Raymond Briggs’s library goes on sale at his local Oxfam shop

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 16:52:51 GMT

Books belonging to the beloved creator of The Snowman and When the Wind Blows were donated by his estate after his death

The book collection of the creator of The Snowman and Fungus the Bogeyman has gone on sale at Oxfam’s Hove bookshop in East Sussex and online.

More than 1,000 books from the collection of Raymond Briggs, the beloved British author and cartoonist, were donated by his estate after his death aged 88 in 2022.

Briggs’s personal library spans comics, illustration, novels and social history, including works by Peanuts creator Charles Schulz and Winnie-the-Pooh illustrator EH Shepard as well as a signed first edition of Graham Rawle’s Woman’s World, the 2005 book composed of fragments from women’s magazines.

Other illustrators featured in Briggs’s library include Shirley Hughes, Aubrey Beardsley, Edward Gorey and Posy Simmonds. There are about 30 comic annuals from the 50s, offering “a glimpse into the visual world that shaped Briggs’s style”, according to Oxfam.

“What’s fascinating is the range,” said Oxfam Hove bookshop volunteer Martin Hill. “You begin to see connections between the books Briggs created and the books and artists he chose to have around him.”

“There are great illustrators and cartoonists, but then you find books about ageing, bathrooms, domestic life, old annuals and wartime milkmen,” he added. “It is serious, funny, ordinary and sometimes rather dark – which feels very familiar to anyone who knows Briggs’s work.”

The collection includes pamphlets on nuclear disarmament, a subject explored in Briggs’s 1982 graphic novel When the Wind Blows. A 1974 book by Monty Python’s Terry Jones and Michael Palin, Bert Fegg’s Nasty Book for Boys and Girls, is also listed, along with a set of John Constable’s reproduced sketches and a first edition copy of Riddley Walker, the post-apocalyptic novel by Russell Hoban.

Born in Wimbledon in 1934, Briggs later spent more than 50 years living beneath the South Downs near Hove. The area inspired the 1978 picture book The Snowman, which features Brighton’s Royal Pavilion. Briggs taught illustration at Brighton School of Art from the early 60s to 1986.

He became known for picture books that subverted conventions of children’s storytelling, in the likes of 1977’s Fungus the Bogeyman and 1973’s Father Christmas, which imagines a cantankerous Santa Claus.

“I liked to find fantastical creatures and treat them realistically,” said Briggs in an interview with the Guardian in 2019, on the publication of his illustrated memoir Time for Lights Out. “I don’t see any difference between doing children’s and adult books. My attitude is exactly the same. I just do the book as I want it to be.”

The animated adaptation of The Snowman first hit screens in 1982, and has been broadcast almost every Christmas since.

After Briggs’s death, children’s author Michael Rosen said that “we have been lucky to have read and watched such great work from a great artist with a great heart”.

The Oxfam collection “offers a wonderful glimpse of the visual and intellectual world of one of Britain’s most distinctive illustrators”, said Hill. Prices for the books on the online store range from £5.99 to £400 for the first edition of Rawle’s Woman’s World.

Essex police were called by the ambulance service at 5.35pm on Wednesday after reports of the incident near Seaview Avenue in West Mersea.

DCI Al Pitcher confirmed that a mother and daughter had died, saying: “My thoughts, and those of my team, are with the friends and family of the woman and girl who died yesterday. We can now confirm they were a mother and daughter from London and we are supporting their family in what is an unimaginable time.

“Since yesterday we have been working to establish the circumstances which led up to this incident. At this stage we believe they were trying to help a seven-year-old boy who had got into difficulties.

“The boy was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical condition, but the woman and teenage girl, sadly, died. All the people involved in this incident are related to each other.

“As part of our investigation we are working through speaking to dozens of witnesses and taking their accounts, and we are building a picture of what happened.”

Mishba Uddin, a family friend, said he believed the mother and teenage girl “were not very good swimmers”. He said that those involved came from east London, with one family based in Barking.

Matiur Rahman, the brother-in-law of Shalina Rahman, told the BBC: “We all feel very bad, my four brothers, my sister … My whole family – we are speechless. We are very shocked.”

Rahman was told in a phone call from his brother about the tragedy. “They went in Colchester, [to the] seaside, and they were near water and playing with them, then suddenly a big wave came,” he said, adding that about 10 family members were on the day out.

Carl Powling, of Colchester council, said his daughter was one of three teenage waitresses at a local cafe who had tried to help. “Members of the public witnessed it, called the emergency services, helped starting to pull people out, then they went into the Seaview cafe to ask for assistance,” he said.

A woman, who did not give her name, told PA Media that the incident had happened at high tide, which caught the small group on a sandbank.

“It comes in very quickly and you have to be careful,” she said, adding that there was “quite a commotion” and “just total panic”. She said helicopters were deployed and the air was filled with the sound of sirens.

“That was quite alarming, for a small place like this, I think that’s why so many people are shocked,” she said. “The beach was packed with people, they were coming down to see what was going on.”

The woman said the emergency services “worked diligently” to deal with an “absolutely tragic” incident.

There have been at least 29 accidental deaths in open water across the UK since the middle of May, according to the National Water Safety Forum.

The area in Essex is known for its strong currents, though the local MP, Bernard Jenkin, told the BBC that “we don’t think of West Mersea beach as a dangerous beach”.

Anyone who was in the area at the time and has information or footage that may assist the investigation is asked to contact the police on 101 and quote incident 1090.

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:46:14 GMT

Government agency announces status in north Wales and Upper Severn after series of heatwaves and lack of rainfall

Parts of Wales are now in drought and all other areas of the country are experiencing prolonged dry conditions, with this month on course to be the driest on record for nearly 200 years.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said on Thursday that record-low river flows, back-to-back heatwaves and widespread wildfires have prompted the declaration of drought status in north Wales and the Upper Severn.

As of Thursday, several fires were still burning across the country after more than a week, leading the Welsh government to activate “crisis” plans amid concerns over a lack of firefighting helicopters.

The declaration of drought in Wales comes as a new scientific analysis finds that extreme heat, supercharged by the human-caused climate crisis, is sucking Europe dry in summer and intensifying the drought hitting the continent.

Deadly wildfires have raged through Spain and France, and rivers are running low across Europe. On Monday, the National Drought Group – the members of which include the Met Office, the National Farmers’ Union, water companies and expert bodies – declared parts of southern, central and eastern England to be in “prolonged dry weather”.

The two areas now in drought in Wales have received less than 2% of the expected rainfall for the month so far, and the rivers Clwyd, Alwen, Alyn, Clywedog, Dyfi and Conwy in north Wales, as well as the Wye, have recorded new monthly minimum flows or are approaching record lows.

The hot and dry weather over recent weeks means July is on course to be the driest on record in Wales for nearly 200 years, causing problems for fish, wildlife and crops.

NRW announced last week that north and south-east Wales were moving to “prolonged dry weather” status, the stage before drought, triggering extra checks on waterways and protected wildlife sites as well as the release of reservoir water into struggling rivers.

Rhian Thomas, the sustainable water and nature manager at NRW, said the hot and dry spell was “having serious impacts on the environment across parts of Wales”, adding: “We have seen rivers fall to exceptionally low levels, groundwater continuing to decline, and increasing reports of environmental impacts affecting wildlife, fisheries, farming and sensitive habitats. The recent wildfires across north Wales and south-east Wales are one of the clearest and most visible signs of how dry our landscapes have become.”

Drought has no official threshold criteria, but is measured by NRW as “a combination of indicators showing a significant shortage of rainfall and water availability, resulting in impacts on rivers, groundwater, ecosystems, agriculture and land management”.

While Welsh Water has reported that reservoir levels remain healthy overall, the company has implemented a hosepipe ban in parts of west Wales. People across England and Wales are being urged to be mindful of water usage. About 23 million people will have been banned from using hosepipes by this weekend.

In England, eight areas are in prolonged dry weather, the National Drought Group said this week. England has received only 3% of its long-term average July rainfall, with the south and east having nothing at all so far – the longest spell without rain since the mid-1990s.

Some rivers are at lower levels than during the heatwave last summer. In the south-west the Dart and Tor flow is lower than this time last year. In central and south-eastern England the Coln in Gloucestershire and the Soar in Leicestershire both have lower flows than this time last year.

Farmers have had to begin their harvests early, with warnings that cereal yields will be lower than expected.

Drought was declared across much of England, Wales and eastern Scotland last summer – conditions that did not officially end until March, after a wet autumn and winter replenished rivers and reservoirs.

The Met Office predicts that climate change will make UK summers 1C-6C (1.8F-10.8F) hotter and up to 60% drier by 2070, compared with 1990.

Hannah Cloke, professor of meteorology and climate science at the University of Reading, said: “Unless the UK collectively gets its act together, and builds greater resilience into its water system at every point, we face a more uncertain future in which the tap could run dry. There is a better future, where we use water better where it falls and don’t waste as much. But we need a fundamental shift in understanding from almost everyone to get there.”

The Swedish owners of a Viking longship replica that features in the Hollywood blockbuster The Odyssey say they feel “forgotten” after film-makers allegedly returned the vessel damaged and failed to foot the bill for repairs.

In nearly three decades at sea, the warship Glad av Gillberga – based on a wreck from around 1040 found in Denmark’s Roskilde fjord – has successfully sailed the North Sea, the Baltic and even voyaged to Canada.

But after six months in the hands of Universal, which according to its owners promised to cover the cost of any repairs, it allegedly sustained considerable damage including to the stern and the mast.

Vikingaleden, a nonprofit Viking centre in Värmland, western Sweden, said that when it invoiced Universal for the materials used to repair their ship (they did not charge for their volunteer labour), no payment arrived.

A year later, while the Christopher Nolan epic starring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Anne Hathaway and Zendaya storms global box offices, taking $264m (£196m) in its opening weekend alone, it says it is still waiting for its $6,000 payment.

Peter Olausson, chair of the Vikingaleden association, said that although he felt proud that the ship was featured in the film, that feeling had been tinged with injustice after the film giant’s alleged failure to cover the cost of damages.

“We are only charging for the material cost, not the labour,” he said. “Of course Universal can afford this $6,000. We feel forgotten.”

The ship is now back in action but Olausson accused Universal of going back on their word. “The agreement was that we would fix it and get financially reimbursed.”

Olausson said that to Universal, the outstanding sum would be comparatively small, but for the 200-member association that runs the Viking “village” and museum, it is a significant amount.

The critically acclaimed film, which reportedly cost $250m to make, is based on Homer’s ancient Greek epic poem about the king of Ithaca, Odysseus, on a 10-year sea journey home from the Trojan war.

The Glad av Gillberga was used as one of the escort vessels in the flotilla, which are thought to have been similar to Nordic Viking ships.

The main ship, Odysseus’s boat, was the 35-metre-long Norwegian replica Draken Harald Hårfagre.

Its Swedish captain, Björn Ahlander, said life on the ships filming for six months around Greek and Italian islands was not easy for the 30-person crew. He told the broadcaster SVT: “We rebuilt the ship into an ancient Greek ship. We removed the tents and all the modern things and had an open deck that we lived on during this time. It was quite tough.”

A Universal spokesperson said: “Our records show that all invoices relating to the Glad av Gillberga were paid in full, including repairs. The studio and the production have contacted the association to clear up any misunderstanding.”

Elon Musk says he got ‘carried away’ with Trump – but still holds on to contentious political views

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:27:52 GMT

In interview, billionaire says instead of running ‘Doge’ he should’ve ‘worked on my companies’ and shares extreme predictions

Elon Musk has admitted he became too consumed by politics during his volatile alliance with Donald Trump and his brief appointment as the president’s financial axman, running the so-called “department of government efficiency” (Doge).

The world’s richest person, and briefly its first trillionaire after his SpaceX company floated on the New York stock exchange in June, made the confession in a wide-ranging interview with the Economist published on Thursday. He shared his positions on subjects from foreign wars to AI, and made a number of eye-opening predictions for the future.

“I got carried away, frankly,” Musk said of his relationship with the president, whom he helped get elected in 2024 with $200m in financial backing, then served during his controversial tenure as head of Doge, overseeing $150bn in “harmful” budget cuts and forcing tens of thousands of people out of federal jobs.

The owner of Tesla did not expand on the statement, but appeared cognizant of the impact of his dalliance with the levers of power in Washington DC.

In December, he offered in a podcast with Katie Miller, wife of Trump’s White House adviser Stephen Miller, that his wrecking-ball approach to the federal government had been only partially successful, and that given the opportunity he probably wouldn’t do it again.

“I think instead of doing Doge, I would have basically worked on my companies,” he said at the time.

Talking to the Economist, however, he appeared to relish the attention his political involvement had garnered, and the influence he believed he exerted. “People don’t realize that what I’m saying will come to pass,” he said, the outlet referring to Musk – at least in his own mind – as a modern-day Cassandra.

The interview, a 90-minute conversation for the publication’s video platform The Insider, recorded at a Tesla factory in Texas, was Musk’s first since the SpaceX flotation, in which his personal wealth briefly topped $1.25tn before dropping back to a relatively penurious $750bn.

He reflected on moving from “exhilaration to terror” in a single day, but was not referring to the SpaceX share price. Instead, he was talking about artificial intelligence, which he believes will ultimately render work by humans “optional”.

AI systems and robots will eventually handle most digital and physical jobs, he said, and the merger of his own AI venture with SpaceX will allow him to develop systems to perform cognitive tasks such as software programming while Tesla manufactures humanoids.

Musk, the Economist said, plans to power his AI venture with datacenters in space, which experts have warned will be “catastrophic” for Earth.

Within five years, Musk said, AI intelligence systems may surpass the sum of all human intelligence. Within 10 years, robots in the workplace will help usher in an era of such “amazing abundance” that money will become meaningless.

It was, however, Musk’s political views, and predictions, that were perhaps the most contentious parts of the interview. The UK, a country he has not visited for years, but whose politics, especially on immigration and race, have become a recent obsession, will become engulfed in a civil war within 20 years, he claimed.

Asked if he was anti-Muslim, Musk attacked the questioner, a policy of diversion similar to that which has served Trump well, and which he has employed previously, notably calling the Guardian “irrelevant” when it decided to withdraw from his “toxic” social media platform X.

“I’m against rape and murder. I’m against the imposition of rules and laws that are contrary to what we’ve come to accept in the west,” he said. “It’s a crying shame that traditional media, like you, don’t recognize this.”

He described the media’s characterization of Europe’s far right as “false, misleading and nonsense”, and argued that it was made up of “normal people” seeking safe cities, secure borders and sensible spending, the Economist said.

In an analysis piece accompanying the interview, the outlet acknowledged that Musk was a divisive figure. “His political views, disseminated to his 240m followers on X, strike many as plain-speaking and strike many more, including The Economist, as plainly bigoted,” it wrote.

“But he is also one of a handful of men who are pioneering AI and who thereby have an outsize influence on its trajectory. When he speaks, he reflects the debates they are having. His datacentres in space could power AI’s future.

“For all his political polemics, he has a record of being right about technology in fields such as electric cars, rockets and satellite communications that confounded other engineers and entrepreneurs.”

Another Musk prediction: after AI destroys jobs, there may need to be a large-scale wealth redistribution to create “universal high income” for humans.

He said he would be willing to pay “trillions in tax” then, conversely, argued that money will become irrelevant inside 10 years. In which eventuality, he said, governments should “issue people cheques”, because, he said, amid an infinite supply of goods and services produced by machines, deflation will be a bigger problem than inflation.

He also shared thoughts about the Ukraine war, in which his Starlink satellites have been used to help that country’s military against Russia’s aggression. Despite this, Musk said any peace deal should include territorial gains for Russia.

The interview concluded with an assessment by Musk of his achievements and ambitious current projects, in AI and in space, a field in which he has also made a number of bold predictions. He said in 2024 that humans could set foot on Mars by 2028 (currently Nasa is targeting 2028 for a return to the moon, which many analysts think is unlikely).

The universe, Musk said, according to the Economist, could be a computer simulation created by aliens. “The things I’m doing are so preposterous that it’s hard to believe they’re real,” he said.

Iran crisis is not solely a product of Trump’s rule

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:26:17 GMT

Focusing on Donald Trump’s defects risks making war appear as an aberration rather than as a recurring feature of American power, writes David Eaton. Plus letters from Blaine Stothard and Harvey Gilbert

Simon Tisdall’s article (Trump, not Iran, is the world’s greatest danger. He’s a one-man weapon of mass destruction, 18 July) is a forceful polemic, but it risks turning a structural problem into a personal one. If Donald Trump is uniquely reckless, that deserves criticism. Yet the article implies that America’s present predicament is chiefly the consequence of his character, rather than asking why successive administrations, Republican and Democrat alike, have repeatedly resorted to military intervention in the Middle East. To focus on Trump’s defects risks making war itself appear as an aberration rather than as a recurring feature of American power.

The same applies to the strait of Hormuz. Its strategic importance does not begin or end with one president. It reflects a global economic order that depends on secure energy supplies, trade routes and the projection of military power to guarantee them. That broader context is largely absent.

The article also assumes that a more competent president, acting with Congress, allies and international law on side, would have avoided today’s crisis. History offers little comfort. We have been here before: the Iraq, Afghanistan and Libya conflicts were carried out under far more conventional presidencies.

Trump may be the spectacle, but he is not the problem. The article focuses on the drama rather than the system that keeps producing it. David Eaton Sunderland

Simon Tisdall is right to identify the dangers to the world presented by the Trump administration and the president himself. Tisdall enumerates the recent damage, death and destruction that the Trump administration has presided over, seeing current excesses and abuses of power as dangers to the rest of us, as indeed they are. But the current excesses, overt and covert, can be seen as a continuation of American history and practice that not only has led to the 20th century being seen as the American century, but also as the century of US wars.

Since the end of the first world war, we have seen the US initiate the war for oil, the war against communism, the war against drugs, the war against terror and the war against Islam. All continue to have negative impacts on the rest of the world, and perpetuate American foreign policy arrogance and belligerence. All these wars failed to achieve their supposed aims. They have also provided cover for other tyrannical governments to act in similar, if less universal, fashion. I’m not sure we should see Trump as an aberration – more as a more shameless manifestation of what has always been there. Blaine StothardLondon

I agree wholeheartedly with Simon Tisdall, but he didn’t answer his own question: who will stop Donald Trump? The polls show his weakness, but the upcoming elections may not because the Democrats are so weak and Trump will inevitably confuse the results to his own benefit. The answer to the question must lie in the Republican party itself. Surely there are enough right-thinking Republicans to turn votes against him and force some control over his behaviour. It is beginning to happen.

This may be the way to begin to bring him to heel, but it creates further issues before any real resolution. The immediate problem for the American people and the world is twofold. First, as the “wounded bear”, Trump will continue to do catastrophic damage before November’s elections. And second, Marco Rubio to take over? God save us all. Harvey GilbertMilton Keynes

Regulation cannot eliminate surrogacy risks

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:25:56 GMT

Lexi Ellingsworth of Stop Surrogacy Now UK responds to news that the rise in the use of surrogates abroad is leaving more babies at risk of becoming stateless

Your article (Rise in overseas surrogates ‘increases risk of stateless babies, 19 July) suggests that the solution lies in better regulation to make surrogacy safe and ethical. But regulation cannot remove the central ethical problem: every surrogacy arrangement begins with the deliberate separation of a newborn baby from their mother, who they have naturally bonded with throughout the pregnancy.

Regulation is also not able to eliminate the physical risks borne exclusively by surrogate mothers. A study in Canada has suggested that surrogate mothers are more likely to experience severe complications including postpartum haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia than women who conceived naturally or with IVF.

Regulation cannot eliminate the risks and realities of surrogacy, and the evidence referenced in the article should give decision-makers pause. Countries and US states that have introduced detailed regulatory frameworks continue to report concerns about the exploitation of economically vulnerable women, inadequate informed consent and difficulties with oversight and enforcement. Laws may change the way that surrogacy is organised, but they have not consistently prevented abuses or addressed the inequalities that drive many women to engage with surrogacy.

Rather than assuming that better regulation will make surrogacy ethical, we should ask whether a practice that depends on separating a baby from their birth mother, while exposing women to significant medical risks and creating opportunities for exploitation, can ever truly be made safe. Lexi EllingsworthFounder, Stop Surrogacy Now UK

Aid cuts will harm lives and livelihoods in Somalia

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:25:42 GMT

Humanitarian support keeps families buying food, shops trading and clinics open when crisis hits, says Abdullahi Nur Osman

Foreign Office figures showing that the UK will almost halve bilateral aid to Somalia by 2029 (Report, 16 July) come as families across the country brace for yet another climate emergency.

Forecasters are warning that rains in Somalia in October could bring catastrophic flooding, displacing thousands. The World Meteorological Organization has flagged a heightened risk of extreme rainfall, which will strike communities still recovering from a severe drought that has left 6 million people facing high levels of acute food insecurity.

For Somali families, this means facing yet another major disruption to their lives and livelihoods, and having less humanitarian support available to those affected.

Britain has long supported Somalia through some of its hardest years, and its ambition to use trade, investment and private sector partnership to support Africa’s development is welcome.

However, the decision to channel available funds into multilateral funders like the World Bank cannot happen at the expense of aid provision. Humanitarian support keeps families buying food, shops trading and clinics open when crisis hits. Without it, each crisis will leave less for businesses and investors to build on.

Aid and investment must go hand in hand. One helps countries weather the emergency ahead; the other helps build the strength to face the next. Britain cannot expect investment to succeed if it withdraws aid too soon. Abdullahi Nur Osman Chief executive, Hormuud Salaam Foundation

No matter your age, you can always enjoy a rave

Brian F Nattrass went to a festival to celebrate his 80th birthday, started dancing and suddenly felt ageless. Plus a letter from John Parry

Thanks for an inspiring and timely article (The rave secret: why middle-aged women are larging it – and seeing big health benefits, 20 July). My 37-year-old daughter recently invited me to a festival to celebrate my 80th birthday. There were raves each night for three nights in a row. I learned to dance in the late 50s and 60s, during the era of Elvis Presley and the Beatles. I used to absolutely love dancing and used to party in clubs well into my late 30s. But reading your article, I realised that I hadn’t danced in over 40 years!

When my daughter invited me to a festival, naturally I had all the self-doubts and concerns you mentioned in your article, including “internalised ageism”. But I love and trust my daughter. She said: “Dad, you’ll do great!” So I went, and I did – dancing with total strangers until 4-5am every night for three nights.

It was so incredibly fun. Feeling my body move to the beat was so tangible and felt so right, and it was so energising. I was initially afraid that the dance style I learned 60 years ago in the age of rock would look really out of it. But nope. Things on the dancefloor haven’t changed that much. And once I started dancing and felt the beat of the music, I completely forgot my age of 80 years; I became ageless.

Dancing awakened a sense of physical vibrancy that I had forgotten. I definitely intend to rave on. It feels so good!Brian F Nattrass Gibsons, British Columbia, Canada

As a 63-year-old man who still goes dancing, there were no surprises in this article for me. Around 10 times a year I go clubbing or to festivals with dance stages/tents. The shared feelings of euphoria with polite and kind people from every generation far outweigh the tiredness the day after. I’m thoroughly convinced of the extended health benefits of raving for six-ish hours (in my case with ongoing rheumatoid arthritis). And leaving the club (or wherever) as dawn breaks just makes me feel completely alive. If you like dancing, go dancing. It’s lovely. John ParryTorremolinos, Spain

​’Ian Curtis didn’t have a chance’: the Durutti Column on departed friends, Factory Records and fun with Morrissey

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:16:19 GMT

As they release their first album in 16 years, the Vini Reilly-fronted band answer your questions on sandpaper record sleeves, having Harry Styles as a fan and inventing a new style of guitar music

Vini, you’ve created some of the most beautiful, ethereal music of the last 40 years. Is it true that in your youth you were in a violent Manchester street gang? Songy24Vini Reilly [guitars, vocals, keyboards]: Gangs then had a different meaning. It was just “their lot” and “our lot”. We’d sling insults at each other. Then you’d play football in the park and realise you were playing with the local thugs. They were actually very funny, and I could have fun with them because I was so little. At the time I’d been going through a recurring depressive illness and felt I didn’t fit in at home, so I left without any clean clothing. I wanted to end my life so I decided to go to Moss Side, where the gangsters would shoot me. Of course they didn’t. I’d had a very happy childhood until my father died when I was doing my O-levels, but I’ve come to the conclusion that the really bad things gave me more than they could ever take. How can you know happiness until you’ve known deep sadness?

Bruce Mitchell [drums]: Vini does kick off, though, properly battles. We had to section him once, and six people had to hold him down.

Legend has it that Joy Division helped cut and glue the sandpaper sheets on to the famous original cover of The Return of the Durutti Column. Were you involved? Gomgom71VR: I walked into Factory Records to find Joy Division gluing them all. It was mortifying, so I escaped as quickly as I could.

BM: Vini denies this, but Hooky [Peter Hook] always says that Vini quickly stopped gluing them so he didn’t damage his nails. Joy Division had no cash, so they were paid to do it, which they did while watching porno movies. Alan Erasmus at Factory Records had got a load of thrown-away sleeves from an album of steam train noises: you can tell it’s an original edition because if you peel the sandpaper back you’ll find a steam train.

Is there a story behind your Blood Orange collaboration, The Field? nobblehobbleKeir Stewart [producer]: Dev Hynes [Blood Orange] has been a fan for a long time, and he sampled [the 1998 track] Sing to Me and made a tune out of it. He asked permission for the sample, and when we met we had this two-hour babble about the Durutti Column and all sorts. Durutti have all these famous covert fans: Stewart Lee, Chris Morris, Max Richter, Richard Ayoade, John Frusciante from the Red Hot Chili Peppers, Chris Martin from Coldplay, AG Cook, Caroline Polachek, loads of artists on the hyperpop scene. It’s great that Vini’s been able to harvest this recognition in his lifetime, but he keeps it all outside his door. He wants to remain unpolluted.

VR: I’ve never heard of most of these people, but it’s very nice.

Which guitarists did you listen to growing up? TroykatooVR: One of my favourite guitarists was Al Casey, who played with Thomas “Fats” Waller: really sparse melodies and harmonic progressions. I had this notion that whether you went to a big orchestral performance at the Free Trade Hall or a folk club in Sale, you knew exactly what the audience would look like, because people identify with genre. So I wanted to create something that wasn’t a recognisable form. When we were trying to get into Canada, the customs guy asked what kind of music we played and I piped up: “Avant garde jazz classical.” It was a joke, but it stuck.

How do you feel about the recent For Vini – A Tribute to the Durutti Column show in London? NickJMorganKS: Harry Styles told Radio 1 that the biggest influences on his new album are LCD Soundsystem and the Durutti Column. Then he was asked to curate the Meltdown festival, so we were asked if there was any way Vini could do a show. There wasn’t, so we got the musicians together for the tribute. I played guitar – I can’t play like Vini but put in a lot of practice! When Bruce came on to play drums, everyone was cheering. A promoter’s already asked if we could do a UK tour, so we’ll see.

VR: It’s fantastic that they’re doing it, but I couldn’t bear to see it. If Bruce is involved, it’s always right. Whenever we played together we didn’t rehearse, but we had such chemistry he always knew when a song would end. It worked every time.

Could you tell us your memories of Ian Curtis and the inspiration behind the song The Missing Boy? PhilshawknightVR: Ian and I were getting to know each other – we both worked for different parts of the civil service. We were planning to do some music together but never told anyone in case people like Mark E Smith called it nepotism. Then I was staying with Tony [Wilson, Factory boss] and Lindsay [Reade, Wilson’s then wife]. I answered the phone and it was Ian. He wasn’t making any sense. He fluctuated from being really positive to the opposite. He was angry that Tony had called him a poet. When I saw all the pills Ian had been prescribed for epilepsy, I knew he didn’t have a chance. Also his marriage was falling apart, he had a little girl … I wasn’t surprised when he killed himself: it’s all there in the songs, but nobody – not even Tony – ever asked him about them. There’s an anger to The Missing Boy because it’s like I’m gritting my teeth.

BM: I was living round the corner. Vini said he needed someone to go in the studio with him to record a memorial for someone who had died. He played it for the engineer, then played once more, leaning over to play the grand piano while his guitar went through a space echo. That second take is on the record.

Who is Paul in Detail for Paul? UncleheinrichagainVR: A friend I had for a long time who’d been at art school. Really intelligent, good guy. Then he got a job in advertising which went against his socialist principles. One day he just didn’t show up. I miss him. People always assume my songs are named after girlfriends, which they’re not at all. Jacqueline is Bruce’s wife, a fantastic artist. Quite a few are named after my nieces or cousins. Do they feel honoured? Oh no. My family are terribly insulted.

What was the best and worst thing about Tony Wilson? dramaaghVR: There wasn’t a worst. The best is that he was a true altruist, and that never changed. Factory was conceived with the money his mother bequeathed to him after her death, and he was determined he was gonna do something out of respect for her. He made loads of recordings possible. A lot are very precious to me, because without him people would have never got to hear them.

Without Mercy is absolutely beautiful – a modern classical classic. How do you rate it among your work? FarmyardManureVR: It was a nightmare to make, but I don’t regret it. Tony said: “Will you do an album for me?” How could I say no? He’d decided that Keats’s poem Without Mercy [La Belle Dame sans Merci] was the same formula as a pop song – boy meets girl, girl dumps boy – and wanted a musical interpretation. I don’t really like it [laughs], but I’m glad that Tony did, because it was a way of trying to thank him.

Was the name the Durutti Column deliberately or accidentally misspelt from the Spanish civil war anarchist Buenaventura Durruti and La Colonna Durruti? somna123VR: The name was Tony’s idea. He felt that since anarchy was the basis of punk, we should go back to that idea. But he decided not to explain that to people, which was great for me because it meant I could waffle on talking absolute nonsense about it. It was probably misspelled by Factory as a mistake, but even in Spain some people think it looks better with one “r”.

What was it like to work on Viva Hate with Morrissey, and would you work with him again? deFaoiteKVR: Certainly, because he’s so ridiculously gifted. I remember him talking about the Moors murderers and how he could have been one of those [murdered] kids, which never left him. On the song Late Night, Maudlin Street you really felt that doomy power. But also we never stopped laughing.

BM: I dropped Vini off at the studio half-expecting to pick him up again after half an hour, because all the musicians and engineers were eating at this long table, and right at the end on his own was Morrissey. But they got on so well that when I eventually picked him up, Vini said: “Can we take Mozza?” They were nattering in the back seat all the way. It was like listening to two old ladies on Coronation Street.

Renascent is released via London Records on 31 July

My first relationship just ended. How can I expect to find someone else when it took 15 years to find her?

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:00:48 GMT

To stay open-hearted and optimistic, you need hope, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. That’s not the same as expectation

Read more Leading questions

I’m nearly 30 and my first serious relationship just ended a month ago. It lasted eight months, she was my first girlfriend and first kiss, etc. She broke up with me in a very kind and respectful way, and I have been … OK, I guess.

The thing is, everyone has been saying to me, “But you must feel so much more confident now.” I don’t. My self-esteem and confidence wasn’t exactly soaring before I met her, but now I feel even less so. It just feels like most people are less tolerant or accepting of my shortcomings.

If this wonderful, understanding person couldn’t see me as worth it, or enough or whatever, how can I expect to find someone else when it took 15 years to find her?

Eleanor says: A person declining or ending a relationship with you is not a scorecard on your value. I know it sure feels like it.

But it’s really important to separate the pain of being rejected from the pain of being proven “not worth it”, because although they feel nearly identical, only one has actually happened.

People end relationships because of the relationship itself: they felt you were not a fit with them. The same trait that makes you not fit with one person can make you a perfect fit with someone else. And in the search for love, that’s what we’re really after: not approval, not having lots of people like us, nice though that would be. We want to find a relationship that fits. The fact this lovely person felt you didn’t quite fit together isn’t evidence of your objective value, any more than learning that your neighbour doesn’t like porridge would convince you that porridge is bad.

The bad news is, we can’t predict if or when we’ll find that fit. You asked: “How can I expect to find someone else when it took 15 years to find her?” and I can’t give you that. I can’t give you proof that you can expect to find someone else.

But do you need it? To stay open-hearted and optimistic, you need the hope, not the expectation, you’ll find someone.

It might feel daunting to do the things that would help you find someone new – putting yourself out there; giving new connections the benefit of the doubt – when you’re not even sure they’ll work. But nobody’s sure they’ll work. Hope can be the motivation where expectation can’t be. You don’t need to know that it’ll work out. You can be led by the possibility that it might.

In fact, that’s what everyone has to do in the search for love, no matter how many relationships they’ve had. Don’t think of yourself as unlucky in love, such that you alone have to subsist on hope when everyone else gets to dine on sumptuous certainty. A very long romantic history doesn’t get you across the line to knowing you’ll find a relationship, or even that the one you’re in will last. Everyone, no matter how historically well-liked or beautiful or charismatic, faces ineliminable uncertainty that can only be bridged by choosing to pay attention to the possibility that love might work out instead of the possibility that it won’t.

Remember, too, that self-esteem and esteem from others have to be separable if either is to last. You said you feel like “most people” are less accepting of your “shortcomings”. You might be right, but double-check to make sure it’s not you who’s withholding the acceptance you want. Often we feel things are happening relationally when in fact – or as well – they’re happening within us.

Other people’s love and acceptance is worth wanting – everybody wants to feel cherished. But try hard to separate uncertainty about whether you’ll find that with another person from whether you can feel it for yourself. Relationships are about finding a fit; self-esteem is about recognising worth. Neither one can replace the other.

The roaring 20s: how the current decade revolutionised cinema

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 15:00:48 GMT

Pre-Covid, the movie landscape was dramatically different: YouTubers weren’t dominating the box office, video game spin-offs rarely made an impact and Winnie-the-Pooh wasn’t yet the star of a slasher movie. Why such a flurry of innovation – and what will be next?

Cinema has always been a medium of research and development. At any given point, the industry is searching for yet another breakthrough that can drive it into the future. Synchronised sound in the 1920s. Technicolor in the 1930s. The invention of the modern blockbuster in the 1970s.

Conversely, the consensus is that, if the 2020s has a defining trend, then it is one of decline. The theatrical experience is under attack from all angles: streaming, YouTube, a once-in-a-century health crisis that shut cinemas down entirely. And yet, if you look closer, this has actually been one of the most innovative decades that cinema has ever seen. Whether down to technology or desperation, the film industry has spent these last few years figuring out new ways to make films that simply could not have existed even at the turn of the decade.

Currently, the most notable of these is the way that cinema has become a conversation with YouTube. Back in 2005, when Jawed Karim uploaded the first video (the 19-second Me at the Zoo) to the platform, YouTube felt like a novelty. It was cheap and cheerful, a collection of cat videos and people falling over. How things have changed. Not only has it become the largest streaming platform in the world, but the first generation of adults who grew up with YouTube has come of age.

As we speak, the seventh and eighth biggest films of 2026 have been directed by people who learned their trade making content for YouTube. Obsession (worldwide gross: $442m) was directed by Curry Barker, a 26-year-old who dropped out of film school to make YouTube videos and TikToks. Meanwhile, Backrooms (worldwide gross: $384m) is even more explicitly internet-inspired. Directed by the then 20-year-old Kane Parsons, the film is based on a series of shorts he began uploading to YouTube in 2022, which in turn were inspired by some creepypasta (web-based horror content) that has been floating around online since 2019.

A decade ago, studios would have got this disastrously wrong. Ask them to adapt a YouTube video and they would have hired Michael Bay and Rihanna to make David After Dentist: The Motion Picture; it would have baffled anyone who didn’t watch YouTube – and appalled anyone who did. This is the first time that the industry has trusted natives to make the films they want to make. Clearly, given the enormous financial returns, it will not be the last. Steven Spielberg is now producing Alex Kister’s The Mandela Catalogue, based on a terrifying analogue horror series that has run on YouTube since 2021.

This would also be a good time to mention the rise of the copyright expiry movie. In 1998, the Copyright Term Extension Act was passed in the US, which extended protection to works to 95 years after they were first published. (In the UK, the rules are different; copyright extends to 70 years after the creator’s death.) This effectively meant that two decades went by without anything going out of copyright. When things finally caught up in 2019, freeing up anything made in 1923, there was a goldrush.

Now, let it be said that it wasn’t a particularly good goldrush. First out of the blocks was 2023’s Winnie-the-Pooh: Blood and Honey, a low-rent slasher movie whose only original thought was to have Winnie-the-Pooh in it. Then came The Mouse Trap and Screamboat (both based on Steamboat Willie, the first element of the Mickey Mouse character to have lost copyright protection), along with Popeye the Slayer Man and Bambi: The Reckoning. Without exception, these films are cheap, exploitative and burn out their premise long before the end credits – but more are to come.

Next year, if you can wait that long, will see the release of something called Poohniverse: Monsters Assemble, which will star – deep breath – Winnie-the-Pooh, Tigger, Bambi, Peter Pan, Tinker Bell, Pinocchio, Sleeping Beauty and the Cheshire Cat. It is also worth pointing out that King Kong enters the public domain in 2029, which will be brilliant news for anyone who has been longing to see a low-rent horror movie starring an unusually large gorilla.

Now, here is where I may lose you, because I am about to name Sonic the Hedgehog as the most important movie of the decade. Please bear with me. One of the most pervasive trends of this decade has been the way that, for good or ill, audiences have hijacked movies to their own ends. The biggest example is obviously Barbenheimer, in which Barbie and Oppenheimer were released on the same day, kickstarting a phenomenon where people bought tickets to see one straight after the other. Nobody in the film industry expected this, but the publicity from this grassroots celebration drove receipts of both films through the roof.

The flipside to this is Morbius, a terrible film that inspired no end of ironic online mockery – but what was hilarious was that Sony mistook the irony for sincere support, and rereleased the film on 1,000 screens to cash in. It goes without saying that nobody watched it. Also, think of all the extra teenagers who bought tickets for Minions: The Rise of Gru, purely so they could watch dressed in suits and babble nonsense to participate in the Gentleminions trend, or the people who went to see A Minecraft Movie exclusively to scream and chuck stuff about when Jack Black said the words “chicken jockey”.

No film, arguably, has benefited from fan reaction quite like Sonic the Hedgehog. The first we saw of it was a nightmarish trailer featuring an unrecognisable main character. Sonic had bizarrely human proportions, as well as tiny eyes and teeth that looked as if they had been stolen from someone’s mouth while they slept. It was awful, and the internet wasted no time in saying that it was awful. In times gone by, studios would have simply taken the hit and released the film as quietly as possible, writing it off as another godawful video game adaptation destined to die on impact. But this time, producers listened. The trailer was released on Tuesday. By Thursday, the director had tweeted that the character would be completely redesigned. Six months after that, New Sonic was unveiled, and fans were delighted.

With a character that people could actually stand to look at, Sonic the Hedgehog went on to become the sixth biggest film of 2020. Nobody saw this coming. Until Sonic, video game adaptations were universally written off as the lowest form of cinema. Think of the dismal live action Super Mario Bros movie, or Mark Wahlberg’s baffling Max Payne, or Uwe Boll’s irredeemable Postal. About 46 English language video game adaptations were released between 1993 and 2019, and they made a combined total of $5.4bn. But A Minecraft Movie made close to a $1bn on its own. The animated Super Mario Movie released in 2023 ended the year second only to Barbie. At time of writing, The Super Mario Galaxy Movie is the biggest film of 2026 so far worldwide. By demonstrating to other film-makers how to give people what they actually want to see, Sonic has turned the video game adaptation into a licence to print money.

As you will agree, this makes Sonic the Hedgehog by far the most important film of the decade. And the future will only bear this out further, once Mr Beast signs on to direct Sonic the Hedgehog 5 and someone makes a rubbish horror film about a blue hedgehog, as soon as the rights lapse in 2087.

Murdoch and Musk in the crosshairs at Venice film festival

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 14:58:18 GMT

Danny Boyle’s drama about the acquisition of the Sun and a four-hour Elon Musk documentary will premiere alongside new films from Martin McDonagh and Werner Herzog – but only one female director has a movie in competition

The Venice film festival promises to take a swing at media moguls of the print and digital era this year, with Trainspotting director Danny Boyle’s new film about Rupert Murdoch’s acquisition of the Sun and a new documentary about Elon Musk included in the lineup of the films for the festival’s 83rd edition.

In Boyle’s Ink, which will open the festival on the Lido on 2 September, Australian actor Guy Pearce plays compatriot newspaper tycoon Murdoch, whose purchase of the Sun in 1969 sensationalised the media landscape and transformed public life in Britain. The script is written by Olivier award-winning playwright and screenwriter James Graham (Dear England, Brexit: The Uncivil War).

Oscar-winning veteran film-maker Alex Gibney profiles the wealthiest person in the world, rightwing agitator and owner of social network X in his four-hour documentary Musk, which will be screened out of competition in Venice.

In recent years, Venice has sought to profile itself as the glitziest and starriest of the big three European film festivals when compared with artistically challenging Cannes and politically charged Berlin.

This year’s lineup, presented by long-running artistic director Alberto Barbera this week, will still draw major stars to Venice’s waterways.

British-Irish director Martin McDonagh will showcase his new film Wild Horse Nine, in which John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell are two unlikely CIA agents in action in Chile on the eve of the coup led by Augusto Pinochet. Steve Buscemi, Tom Waits and Parker Posey also star in the awaited return of the director of In Bruges, Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin.

Robert Pattinson will grace the Lido as the lead in A24’s Primetime, a psychological thriller inspired by the US reality TV show To Catch a Predator, directed by Lance Oppenheim.

Real-life spouses Penélope Cruz and Javier Bardem star in French playwright-director Florian Zeller’s Bunker, in which a publisher-architect couple move to London and are invited by a millionaire to design a building that could withstand a nuclear bomb.

Real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara star in Bucking Fastard, the first dramatic feature film in seven years by German cult director Werner Herzog. The film was originally announced as a biopic of Freda and Greta Chaplin, twins from York who spoke and moved in unison and gained notoriety after a brush with the law. It seems to have since veered off into a direction more familiar from the maker of Aguirre, the Wrath of God and Fitzcarraldo, centred around a mission to dig a tunnel through a mountain range “in search of an imaginary land”.

Barbera said that Liam and Noel Gallagher had confirmed their attendance at the festival, for the premiere of Oasis reunion documentary Don’t Look Back in Anger, while Russell Crowe is expected to attend a screening of What Love Builds, a feature-length documentary about his band Indoor Garden Party.

But there is some more serious fare on the Lido this year. Russian-born film-maker Ilya Khrzhanovsky will show the latest film to emerge out of his Dar project, likened to a Stalinist Truman Show and inspired by a Soviet research institute that contributed to the creation of the first atomic bomb.

Ukrainian director Sergei Loznitsa will bring his documentary Imperium, about a film that was commissioned by the Italian Communist party to glorify the triumph of the Soviet Union but ended up revealing its contradictions.

Laura Poitras’ latest documentary They’re Here, made with Rachel Mueller, dives into ICE’s intervention in Minneapolis and the killing of Renée Good, with some previously undisclosed footage.

Tragicomedies such as Caro Diario and The Son’s Room have made Nanni Moretti one of Italy’s most revered film-makers, but for the last two decades he has preferred to show his new works at Cannes rather than Venice. Showing in competition this year, Succederà Questa Notte (It Will Happen Tonight) will be Moretti’s first film in Venice since 1989.

After Tunisian director Kaouther Ben Hania made a mark on last year’s festival with The Voice of Hind Rajab, there is a dramatic drop in female directors in this year’s competition. After six female directors competed for the Golden Lion in 2025, Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhy’s drama Woman Unknown is the only female-directed film among the 20 titles in the main competition.

How to Launder Money But Not Like Me, by George Cottrell (as imagined by John Crace)

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 14:38:02 GMT

The Guardian’s parliamentary sketch writer imagines Nigel Farage’s right-hand man’s thinking behind his book, How to Launder Money

Anti-money-laundering laws are supposed to stop the illicit flow of money. So far, they seem to have stopped next to nothing. About 5% of the global economy is illicit and only 0.05% is stopped by AML laws.

Which makes me, George, something of a rarity. The idiot member of the 1% who actually got done for conspiring to launder money. Just think, while 99% of criminals were getting away with it, I had the bright idea of telling an audience of undercover members of the US Internal Revenue Service in Las Vegas how I could clean up their drug money for them. Much to my surprise, they didn’t take me up on my offer. I was arrested on money-laundering charges at Chicago airport. Still, I did a plea bargain and the charges were reduced to wire fraud and I did eight months in prison. So no harm done.

Anyway, that’s all water under the bridge. And in my book How to Launder Money I tell you how you can get away with it by not making the same mistakes as me.

Er, excuse me, co-author Lawrence here. I thought we were supposed to be writing a book to inform the authorities on how to prevent money laundering.

Gosh, sorry Lozza. There seems to have been a misunderstanding. Of course. We’re all definitely against money laundering. I’m all for cleaning up the global economy. It would be terrible if the system got so opaque that it was nigh on impossible to discover how political parties were being funded. Not that it would be illegal. Obvs.

First, we need to think of the nature of money. Money is something you can spend onthings. Not many people realise that. In my time I have spent money on lots of things. Like renting a house near Buckingham Palace that I can make available to Nigel Farage – or Daddy, as I choose to call him – whenever he needs somewhere to stay. I like having lots of money. The key to having a small fortune, as my friend Dicky Tice likes to remind me, is to start with a large one.

We should also be clear that there is a big difference between money laundering and grifting. Grifting is entirely legal. That is what Daddy does when he offers to make personalised Cameo videos for £80. As he often likes to say, every little counts. Of course, the best money is the money you get for doing nothing.

Or in Daddy’s case, a Thai crypto billionaire who coincidentally gifts you £5m just a short while after you have said you need £1m a year for the next five years if you are going to stand for parliament. Any suggestion that Daddy might owe income tax on this should be referred to his accountants. And it’s obviously deeply distressing to hear the £5m was reported to the National Crime Agency (NCA) over money laundering concerns.

Anyway, back to me. Here are several hundred pages of really boring anecdotes of money laundering from Roman times to the present day. Try to look on this book as a cure for insomnia.

One easy way to rinse dirty money is to get someone to paint a fake Van Gogh. No one will notice if another picture of some sunflowers comes on to the market. Then you buy it yourself at an international auction house and donate the painting to a museum. Lo and behold you have suddenly transformed a few thousand quid in dirty money into an asset worth tens of millions. Job done. What could possibly go wrong? Another thing that can work well is bribing people. Though you have to make sure the people you are trying to bribe aren’t undercover agents! If you get my drift.

Perhaps the best way of cleaning money is to become prime minister. That way you don’t have to worry about going through customs with gold ingots or large bundles of high denomination notes. Instead you can just walk on to the private jet with a couple of suitcases and hand them over to Vladimir Putin during a bilateral meeting at which no special advisers are present. With the right person in No 10, the UK could become the world centre of illegal finance. Just think of the boost that could give to our economy.

Of all cryptocurrencies, 99.9% are an outright scam. But don’t let that bother you. Just buy the ones that Daddy recommends as they are obviously legit because they are being run by Kwasi Kwarteng. And don’t think that any monies being donated to Reform UK are dodgy just because they are subject to a Suspicious Activity Report to the NCA.

Make no mistake, no one would be more horrified than me to discover that money from overseas – Montenegro, say – had been used to fund a British political party.

The desire to be loved is a natural human emotion. I long for Daddy’s attention and was thrilled when he allowed me to answer his emails even when I definitely had nothing to do with the day-to-day activities of the Brexit party and Reform. But sometimes it is best to seek anonymity in your financial dealings, regardless of whether your activities are illegal or not. That’s why when I was offering to launder drug money in Vegas I went under the pseudonym Graham Cottrell. No one would ever think of linking that name with my own.

Everything else is quite straightforward. Buy some houses via shell and offshore companies – not that there is anything wrong with these – and leave a trail that is too complicated for anyone to bother to trace. Best of all, you can place bets on the crypto polymarket that you know you are going to lose. That way your illegal money instantly disappears. And the Feds never suspect you of deliberately squandering your assets. This also works well with making legal money disappear. I recently lost £1m on the date of Keir Starmer’s resignation and Donald Trump bombing Iran.

So that’s it. All you need to know to get your criminal activities up and running. I mean, for the authorities to clamp down on money laundering. Thank God my own financial affairs are now so transparent. Happy washing day everyone.

MoD cancels army training in Kenya over powers to prosecute British soldiers

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 14:06:01 GMT

September exercise called off after Kenya raises concerns over funding and jurisdiction for criminal offences

The British army has been forced to cancel training for its troops in Kenya after the Kenyan government refused to ratify a bilateral defence agreement.

While the UK government wanted to renew the existing agreement, Kenyan lawmakers had sought changes to give local authorities greater powers to hold British soldiers accountable for any offences committed in the country.

According to the Kenyan news outlet the Daily Nation, the dispute centres on which cases Kenya will retain primary jurisdiction over, while the amount of money Britain pays Kenya to host the training camp has also been a sticking point.

The chair of the Kenyan national assembly’s defence, intelligence and foreign relations committee, Nelson Koech, said the two governments were “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues”.

As a result of the Kenyan government’s decision, a planned exercise involving the 1st Battalion the Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, which was due to begin in September, has been cancelled.

A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: “The UK highly values its relationship with Kenya, which is underpinned by mutual benefit, respect and cooperation. The UK-Kenya Defence Partnership is one of the great strengths of our relationship. Our joint training and operations with the Kenyan Defence Forces are keeping both Kenyan and British people safe.

“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming. As a result, the planned training will now be conducted at an alternative location outside Kenya.”

Kenya also benefits from training of its own armed forces at BATUK, the British army base near Nanyuki, and the presence of British troops is valuable for the economy.

The MoD spokesperson added: “We recognise the disappointment this decision will cause for those who would have benefited from the economic activity generated by the exercise.”

They said the UK government remained “committed to our defence partnership with Kenya”, adding that the UK would “continue to engage closely with the Kenyan government to support the resumption of training in-country at the earliest appropriate opportunity”.

However, there has been sustained pressure from Kenyan people opposed to the British army’s continued presence. Last year, a report to the Kenyan parliament into the base alleged human rights violations, environmental destruction and sexual abuse by British soldiers.

The most high-profile case linked to the base is the death of Agnes Wanjiru, in which a British soldier has been charged with murder. Kenya has retained jurisdiction in the case and an extradition hearing is due to take place in November. Robert Purkiss denies the single charge of murder.

Legal proceedings had stalled since Wanjiru’s death in 2012, but advanced under John Healey’s tenure as defence secretary. As shadow defence secretary, he had called on the previous government to do more to progress the case.

Koech said the committee had called for “stronger accountability measures, including jurisdiction over serious offences, enhanced protection for local communities, and implementation of recommendations arising from the BATUK inquiry”.
