Like Trump, I went through a home-renovation obsession. The results are often disappointing

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 14:00:46 GMT

We are now a nation of homogenized open concepts and curb appeal. It’s an approach that leads to anxiety and isolation

Recently, Jonathan Swan – one of the authors of a new tell-all about Donald Trump’s second term – told the hosts of The View that if you had a pie chart of Trump’s mind, “a pretty substantial slice is devoted to interior decorating”. He also revealed that Trump is engaged in “design wars” with Melania and moved furniture she had selected into his spaces. The commander-in-chief apparently has even been caught supergluing gilded accents to the Oval Office mantel himself. Though Trump claims taxpayers won’t be on the hook for the costs of his renovations, the New York Times reported that the White House’s 18 major remodeling projects – from the botched Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool to the paved-over Rose Garden to the looming “Arc de Trump” – will probably come with a price tag of $1.2bn.

Of course, Trump’s renovation compulsion didn’t start this year. The president celebrated winning his first term, in 2017, by ripping out the Oval Office’s royal blue carpet with the presidential seal and replacing it with a Mar-a-Lago peach version, accented with – what else? – gold. But in his second term, he’s gotten bolder, both politically and aesthetically – and more addicted. By the autumn of his first year back in office, he went ahead and tore down the East Wing entirely.

And, OK, I get it. In January, my husband and I bought a money pit of a house. In this economy, we counted ourselves lucky. But, within the first 24 hours of ownership, we had a fire, a leak, and the boiler burst, filling the basement with several inches of rusty water. There went the aesthetic tweaks we’d planned, not to mention the furniture. The problem was that my Instagram algorithm had already picked up on my new life stage. Soon, I was plagued by an irrational, unyielding fear of ugly rooms. I wanted nothing but to designmaxx. I began to give up an inordinate amount of my brainpower to rules like: “One throw per sofa, draped not folded. Folded is a store display. Draped is a home.” I actually battled it out with my tween over the “rule of three”. In desperation, one day, encouraged by a Zillow study about which hues raise property values, I painted a room sage green only to realize all my furniture clashed. (I believe they call it “scope creep”.) If, at that moment, I’d been supplied with an Ikea hack for transforming discount chair cushions into a padded room, I would have felt I’d alighted upon the perfect decorating scheme.

In other words, this stuff could make anyone crazy. In one survey, 12% of new couples (together five years or less) considered separating or divorcing during the remodeling process. In another, more than two-thirds of millennials reported moderate to high stress amid remodeling, with 40% saying it strained their relationships. Yet so many of us keep coming back for more. What began with the Puritans and their stonewalls, their European notions of private property, has spawned an entire channel devoted to renos. On HGTV, the Property Brothers alone have 10 spin-offs. When Edith Wharton tried to sell her interior design guide, The Decoration of Homes, in 1897, it was rejected by publishers. No one, they told her, would be interested. But the interior design market hit over $185bn globally in 2025 – and is projected to reach $298bn by 2033. We are now a nation of open concepts and curb appeal and pops of color, of mid-century and farmhouse sinks and shiplap and Homegoods, homes that look “good”, yes, but often strikingly the same.

In a recent essay for the New Yorker, Jia Tolentino describes a similar homogenizing phenomenon with faces, surgically or AI-enhanced, “increasingly, more technically beautiful but more spiritually unattractive”. Trump’s design choices may not be your standard Joanna Gaines style, but, in Washington DC, the decorating analogue for Mar-a-Lago face is massive, gilded anything. All this uniformity is enough to make you long for Jerry Seinfeld’s cluttered cereal shelves or the Friends’ violet walls or even Archie Bunker’s threadbare wing chair.

Why do any of us put ourselves through this torturous process? Is it all for resale value? To keep up with the Joneses? Or for the positive emotional effects of built environment factors like natural light, wood furniture and high ceilings? Most perplexing of all: why is Trump, in the middle of a war, plunging approval polls and an inflation crisis, devoting mental space to the future of a home he doesn’t even own? Is it a classic response to feeling out of control, or perhaps an attempt at denying reality? (“Like the Administration,” writes Tolentino, “Mar-a-Lago Face locates power in the spectacle of dismissing reality altogether.”) Or is Trump just the most extreme version of our narcissistic instinct to put our stamp on spaces, to claim ownership, like a boy with a Sharpie tagging everything around him?

Unfortunately for our president, one thing I’ve learned is that on the other side of a reno does not always lie satisfaction. Only 52% of couples reported feeling happier in their newly renovated homes. In the HBO show DTF St Louis, the female lead’s raison d’être is a redo of her son’s bedroom decor. Spoiler alert: she gets it but loses a lot more. And Annetta Grant, now an associate professor at Bucknell University, confirmed this kind of disappointment in her 2023 study, with a nod to HGTV’s impact. Americans, she learned, have stopped designing their houses for themselves. Because of home-improvement media (read: everything from Better Homes and Gardens to Pinterest), increasingly, the changes homeowners are making are for resale value, or as she puts it, “a market-reflected gaze” – and that means they decorate in a more and more homogenized style. It’s an approach that leads to anxiety and isolation, as homeowners worry about being judged by visitors at the same time that they don’t feel their homes reflect their own preferences.

Recently, I started to lust after the kind of homes where no one is thinking about the proper way to size a rug – homes you can relax in, homes covered in Legos and board game pieces. I blocked social media on my phone in an attempt to limit the kinds of Instagram visits that convince me I need a custom monogrammed cross stitch kitchen towel. Instead, I started reading Middlemarch. In it, George Eliot writes that a “betrothed bride” often “dictates” changes to her future home before marriage only to discover: “The mistakes that we male and female mortals make when we have our own way might fairly raise some wonder that we are so fond of it.” We may think what we want is what we want, but it’s often not what we need at all.

Trump, for his part, may think what he needs is a new ballroom complete with bunker or just one more gilded vase, when what he really requires is a gut reno of his relationship with himself – and the American public.

Jackie Delamatre is a freelance writer based in Providence, Rhode Island

‘Unbearably sexy in his rodenty way’: Benedict Cumberbatch’s 20 best films – ranked!

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 12:00:44 GMT

To mark the two-time Oscar nominee’s recent 50th birthday, we rate his finest screen roles – from hyper-British patricians and seething serpents, to ghastly Yanks, tragic codebreakers and sci-fi scoundrels

Benedict Cumberbatch does his considerable best opposite the equally prestigious Olivia Colman in this souped-up marital-breakdown dramedy, essentially remade from the 1989 movie with Michael Douglas and Kathleen Turner. This time, though, it’s all about the Britons – indicating the supposed classiness of the affair. But the film is overwrought and unconvincing; it never convinces us that the couple were once passionately in love and now passionately in hate. The below-par script has the effect of bringing out an unrewarding kind of coldness in Cumberbatch, technically assured though he always is.

Here is an example of Cumberbatch’s presence signalling a film’s purposeful seriousness – and he does indeed give an honest, intelligent and well-intentioned performance in an otherwise self-conscious and contrived study of grief and emotional breakdown. He is the writer and illustrator whose wife has died, and who is visited by a gigantic hallucinatory crow (raspingly voiced by David Thewlis) symbolising the agony of loss. Cumberbatch’s performance, however, looks a little refined and dry for the material.

An interesting, subdued appearance from Cumberbatch in this film version of Tracy Letts’s award-winning play about an explosive family reunion. It is an example of how his theatrical accomplishment, technique and distinctive appearance, when married up to material that doesn’t overstate things, can work well. In fact, it is the rest of the cast, headed up by Meryl Streep, who bring the fireworks; Cumberbatch, playing the shy, depressed cousin Little Charles, delivers a less-is-more premium.

Popcorn movies like this, as opposed to upmarket Masterpiece Theatre-type productions, allow Cumberbatch to have some fun – and here he is, playing in motion-capture as the terrifying dragon Smaug and the equally daunting Necromancer, in Peter Jackson’s LOTR prequel-triple. Within the confines of motion-capture, his Smaug – a little like Ian McKellen’s Gandalf – delivers authentic British vocal richness and theatrical hamminess, evil and yet lonely.

Nowadays, a Tudorbethan romp with Cumberbatch would have to cast him as Henry VIII or Thomas Cromwell at the very least. In Justin Chadwick’s enjoyably gossipy and saucy what-if period drama about Henry’s illicit relationship with Anne Boleyn’s sister Mary (played by Scarlett Johansson), Cumberbatch has to content himself with the more self-effacing role of Henry’s courtier and Mary’s husband, William Carey, who is a step away from the real action. But Cumberbatch’s theatrical credentials are important to the film’s integrity.

Cumberbatch gives some serious moustache action in this espionage drama-thriller, based on a true story. It’s not as good as his appearance in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, but Cumberbatch is very good at conveying something that for most actors is just the pretext for comedy – a certain kind of simmeringly significant British uptightness. He plays Greville Wynne, a mousy 1960s businessman, always going to Moscow on boring business and who is asked by MI6 to make contact with a possible Soviet defector. And so, with his fusty homburg and moustache, he makes his appointment with destiny.

One of Cumberbatch’s distinctive supporting roles is in this bold and starrily cast version of the Ian McEwan bestseller about a tragic lie that changes lives. Cumberbatch is Paul Marshall, a well-spoken young man who visits an aristocratic country house before the second world war, and whose sexual assault of a girl there forms part of a calamitous misunderstanding and untruth. Cumberbatch does sterling work, but this is one of the lesser roles that he tended to get before TV’s Sherlock catapulted him into the big league.

Cumberbatch can play comedy, although he rarely gets the chance. He displays those skills in this small but perfectly deadpan role, as the special branch negotiator who has to talk to the potential suicide bombers in Chris Morris’s acidic black comedy about jihadist extremism. The character’s stolid professionalism coexists with a certain kind of cluelessness almost comparable to that of the bumbling terrorists themselves.

No self-respecting English actor shrinks from the challenge of an accent – and in Scott Cooper’s Black Mass, Cumberbatch does an entertainingly studied version of south Bostonian: posh, but with a hint of the mean streets. In this true-story mob drama, he is Massachusetts senator Billy Bulger, at home in the cigar-smoky gentleman’s clubs and bars exchanging worldly badinage with the great and the good. But his brother is gangster Whitey Bulger, played by Johnny Depp, and Billy finds himself under pressure to persuade Whitey to become an informant. Cumberbatch is very good at showing how infatuated Billy is with his own prestige.

As befits the title, this movie demonstrated Cumberbatch’s horse-riding chops and the elegant figure he cuts in the saddle. As the blusteringly patriotic Maj Jamie Stewart, he is every inch a clenched member of the officer class, giving a fierce speech to his men before a deeply misjudged cavalry charge in which the British are cut down by German machine guns. Cumberbatch looks and sounds the part, and you can fully imagine that gimlet-eyed fanaticism on the faces of actual officers of the time. But it’s a slightly cartoony character in a slightly cartoony film.

A very early movie role for Cumberbatch, in which – perhaps before the industry quite realised what a thoroughbred they were dealing with – he was cast in an almost slapstick role as the pop-eyed, geeky butt-of-the-joke. In this version of David Nicholls’ novel about students competing in the TV quizshow University Challenge, James McAvoy is the fresher at Bristol Uni, mad keen to be on the team. But he is unbearably patronised by Cumberbatch’s team captain – a pompous postgrad – and their confrontation ends in chaotic violence. It’s a very tasty, broad comic role for Cumberbatch – and it’s a shame he hasn’t developed that side of his career.

Cumberbatch’s second performance as a ramrod-straight commanding officer in the first world war. His contribution here is smaller than in Steven Spielberg’s War Horse, but it is a very powerful cameo and in some ways more realistic. He is Col Mackenzie, to whom two desperate young lance corporals have to deliver a vital message to call off an attack the cunning Germans are attempting to lure the British into making. His Mackenzie is a fierce martinet, careworn by slaughter and by the burden of command, and with a poignant hint of despair.

Cumberbatch had one of the trickiest, knottiest roles of his career in this John le Carré thriller, playing Peter Guillam – an intelligence officer low enough on the food chain to have escaped suspicion of double-dealing, but nonetheless little liked by his superiors. He has, however, a close relationship with Gary Oldman’s spy chief George Smiley and, by virtue of the semi-protected status this gives him, has a somewhat cool and insolent manner. Cumberbatch amusingly carries off a cuff-shooting style with a rather absurd mop of a haircut, and a dandruffy three-piece suit.

Cumberbatch deserves a massive supervillain role and perhaps the sheer obviousness of this possibility means that he hasn’t really had one. (He could be a Bond villain – but, then again, he may be more interesting as Bond himself.) At all events, he was a watchable turn as the blankly named John Harrison, AKA Khan Noonien Singh – the enigmatically cool foe of Kirk and Spock in JJ Abrams’ 2013 follow-up to his great reboot of the sci-fi pop classic. His role here is a little light on dialogue, and Abrams’ intention was probably more to let us simply luxuriate in that mysterious face: unbearably sexy in its rodenty way.

Writer-director Dictynna Hood’s little-known indie drama gives us one of Cumberbatch’s most interesting and fully realised performances, notable because there is less of the slant, quirk or mannerism that many other directors and writers would contrive for him. He plays David, a schoolteacher and decent guy married to Claire Foy’s Dawn, living in a quiet English village. Their home life is upended when his troubled brother Nick (Shaun Evans) returns from the army and reveals some uncomfortable family secrets. Cumberbatch’s David shows that he himself is not the cool customer we thought. A finely detailed and well-judged performance.

Cumberbatch was genius casting as Doctor Strange, arriving at what now, perhaps, looks like the end of the Marvel superhero golden age. Strange is a brilliant but arrogant neurosurgeon who achieves his superpowers – in time-honoured fashion – through an accident, but has to be schooled in a distinctively Zen kind of mastery by an enigmatic mentor (played by Tilda Swinton). With this, and 2022 follow-up Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness, Marvel gave Cumberbatch a massive global cineplex audience for his unique charisma, theatricality and unconventional handsomeness.

Perhaps it is odd that Cumberbatch has only been in two Wes Anderson films: this Oscar-winning short for Netflix, and The Phoenician Scheme two years later. The elegance and British idiosyncrasy of Cumberbatch would make him an obvious candidate. Henry Sugar gives Cumberbatch another side to his underappreciated comedy style: the deadpan pose, which is here an almost Keatonian stoneface. His Sugar is a wealthy, greedy man with an inscrutable manner, who discovers in himself magic powers (which are, however, not quite superpowers in the Marvel sense) that he is able to exploit for gain in casinos all over the world.

Cumberbatch played the most insidiously culpable role in Steve McQueen’s Oscar-winning slavery drama – the true story of Solomon Northup (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a black man abducted in 1841 from freedom in the US north into slavery in the south. Northup has two masters: the apparently thoughtful and liberal William Ford, played by Cumberbatch, who then sells him to the sadistic and odious Edwin Epps, played by Michael Fassbender. Ford is supposedly the good guy, and yet he is all the more despicable for being so blandly complicit in the situation, and for his weakness in selling Solomon to a man he knows is evil just to clear his personal debt. His chief emotion is a kind of sorrowing and worldly self-pity.

Here is the one movie that really gave Cumberbatch a chance to develop the Sherlockian persona that had made him an international star. He plays Alan Turing, the genius mathematician and wartime codebreaker who was later persecuted as a gay man in the 1950s, in the middle of a seedy moral panic led by Churchill’s home secretary, David Maxwell Fyfe. Cumberbatch is excellent at showing the young Turing’s brilliance, his abruptness and tactlessness (which may now be attributed to autism spectrum disorder), and also his sensitivity and loneliness. There is a rich, romantic melancholy in the fake heterosexual relationship that Turing confects with his fellow codebreaker and friend Joan Clarke, played with energy and charm by Keira Knightley. Sherlock was fictional, but the equally exceptional Turing was real, and achieved more than Sherlock ever could.

Ironically, Cumberbatch’s greatest film to date is a western – and this most English of actors plays the nastiest US roughneck imaginable. He is the boorish and charmless Phil Burbank, who runs a ranch in remote Montana with his brother George (Jesse Plemons). Phil is more than just ornery; he is a sociopath and a bully, obsessed with mocking his brother’s pretensions to culture and refinement, but profoundly dependent on him emotionally. And so, when George marries sensitive widow and single mother Rose Gordon (Kirsten Dunst), Phil starts harassing and abusing her – there is a bizarre scene where he strums derisively along on a five-string banjo while she is trying to play the piano. In his dysfunctional, childlike way, he is clearly unable to stop thinking about the fact that his brother and this woman are enjoying sexual relations. Phil himself would appear to be a virgin. Or is he? He also begins to take an oppressively strange interest in Rose’s teenage son, offering to teach him to ride and take him out into the remote hills to school him in the rancher ways of manly self-reliance. It is a huge role for Cumberbatch, and his wild-eyed magnetic and sinister aura floods the screen.

‘My life’s work was being delightful. That really hurt me’: breakout Americana star Brennan Wedl on freeing herself through song

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 11:30:42 GMT

​With her roots stretching from the Catholic church to riot grrrl, the US singer-songwriter explains how sobriety and self-analysis powered her classic new Waxahatchee-produced album

The songwriting on Brennan Wedl’s new album is so ironclad that I kept checking the credits to see if any of its songs were actually covers of peak Lucinda Williams tracks that I’d somehow missed. Nope: all originals by a 29-year-old songwriter whose radiant, hooky, tough Americana puts her toe-to-toe with genre godheads such as Williams circa Car Wheels on a Gravel Road, or Sheryl Crow had she grown up playing church basement punk shows; also, a vision of Courtney Love in cowboy boots.

“I love Lucinda’s very earnest way of looking at daily life, and I hoped to achieve that on this record,” says Wedl, calling from her Nashville home, surrounded by vintage magazines and tchotchkes. Wedl is warm and dudely; she answers almost every question with an exuberant “toootally!”. She cites her favourite of her new songs, the absurdly immediate Just Another Daddy Who Did Me Wrong, a bittersweet number that questions her self-destructive appeal. “It’s a very harsh look at reality, but also about how our minds can create so much fantasy around reality. I’m working on not projecting too much on reality these days.”

You could reasonably say Wedl doesn’t have too many reasons to fantasise Her new, self-titled record was produced by Waxahatchee (AKA Katie Crutchfield) and her longtime producer Brad Cook, who asked to make the album after Snail Mail’s Lindsey Jordan put them on to Wedl’s music.

“I just couldn’t wrap my head around her voice,” says Crutchfield, who had never produced before. “It’s immediately iconic, so timeless and confident – for someone who was, at the time, so undiscovered.” When Crutchfield heard an early version of Two Dollar Pistol, a loving, windows-down nudge to someone frustrated by ambition, “I was like, this person’s writing huge melodies that can be played in arenas. This is a really different level of songwriting.”

Wedl puts the fully formed nature of the album – her third solo release after more muted outings – down to never having known herself better. Combining newly written songs and others from her 20s, “it’s a lot about communicating between various versions of you, time-travel with music; conversations with the unknown, dialogue with large themes like the man, God, Jesus, the trope of ‘daddy’.”

Like many of the US’s best young alternative songwriters, Wedl comes from a religious background – but, unusually, she hasn’t rejected it wholly. She grew up in Missouri with nuns for aunts. “I’m really grateful to have seen a lot of different sides of the Catholic church,” she says. “I saw nuns devoted to service, to education. But I also saw the assault of young boys. My grandfather is a huge advocate for female priests and says we can’t keep brushing this under the rug – the church will die if they do not change their ways. So, coming from elders in my family who have really made Christianity their own, it inspired me to put a little pagan twist on it in my adult life.”

Wedl discovered riot grrrl when she attended the She Rock She Rock summer camp at age 12, and found common ground between the church and punk in their impetus to come together “to build the new era of something”. Minnesota offered a great local soundtrack in the Jayhawks, the Replacements and Prince (members of the New Power Generation, his backing band, played in her grandparents’ church band), and Wedl played both with her uncle and her first band, Sex Education. (Not something they actually got much of in high school.) “As I get older and listen to these artists, it really makes me dream of the day that I’ll move back to Minnesota and be with family,” she says.

She first left home to attend Berklee College of Music in Boston, where she studied songwriting and co-founded the playful queercore outfit Dazey and the Scouts. They lasted just over two years, then became a minor pandemic TikTok sensation when a kid dancing to a Morrissey-impersonating verse in their song Wet went viral. “TikTok has its dark sides, but the discovery factor does bring people together – being able to see yourself in some kind of art or music, no matter where you are, is magic,” says Wedl.

Get music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every week

after newsletter promotion

Music also helped Wedl see herself more clearly. Her album’s rockiest moment, Pretty Little Fantasy, attacks perceptions of her as “somebody’s daughter … prim and proper”. Growing up as the eldest and only girl, she says, “I wanted to be so helpful, and I think girls are taught that a lot. But then I was introduced to riot grrrl and Marina Abramović and disgraced women throughout history, and it took most of my 20s to come to the conclusion that I was still carrying the self-imposed life’s work of being delightful, and that doesn’t help anyone – actually, it really hurts me. I think ‘delightful’ is the mask I wore out of not dealing with my own shit – and so if I was a delight, no one would have to investigate further.”

On stage, Wedl cultivated being “dead serious about having fun – the ambition to live the life I want”. It filtered into the rehearsal space, then her everyday confidence. Recently, she was reminiscing on an earlier version of her solo project. “There was an upright bass player and an electric bass player because I didn’t want to hurt someone’s feelings by saying they couldn’t play,” she says, laughing. “I’m sure that sounded horrible!” That was 10 years ago now. “Being the leader of a band is a constant crash course in people-pleasing, self-assuredness and respect, and I’m so grateful that I get to learn these huge life lessons through music.”

She also credits “various 12-step programmes” with breaking these moulds. “Twenty-one has found me sober,” she sang on her last album, 2019’s Holy Water Branch. “A lot of my life boils down to: how do my daily habits make up who I am?” she says. “When I was drinking, I was really focused on the next time I was gonna do that, who was gonna be there – this mental obsession with the wrong things.” Quitting drinking didn’t erase her problems, but it made them clearer. She realised she had become someone who wasn’t writing, neglecting “this shortcut for when I couldn’t really explain what’s on my heart to others; I could explain it to my guitar and to my journal.”

Writing, she says, “can be how we communicate with what we don’t see, what contracts we sign with ourselves. What we want to bring into this reality can be done with pen and paper a lot of the time. It’s really magical.”

From first hearing Brennan to making the record to now, I kind of still can’t fully wrap my head around her existence. She’s unique. Three or four years ago, Lindsey Jordan [AKA Snail Mail] was at my house and we were going back and forth, playing each other stuff. She put on I Wanna Be Your TV, by Brennan, and didn’t give me any context, and I had to stop her and be like, what is this? Is it recent? Did somebody young make this or is this an old song I’ve never heard? She told me Brennan was from Nashville. I couldn’t stop listening to her – I listened to that song a million times.

Shortly thereafter, she put out some singles with [west coast label] Kill Rock Stars, a handful of which we re-recorded. Eventually, we got in contact and I got to know her, then got to watch her play music in a studio, her technique, her approach. At every turn, she impresses me – she’s so talented and so humble but not in a grating, overly precious, shucks, I shouldn’t be here kinda way. She has the absolute perfect amount of confidence. She can really write a hook. The melodies are amazing. As I got to know her better, [I saw that] her lyric writing is really strong, too. It’s all influenced by my favourite stuff: it’s Kathleen Edwards, Lucinda Williams, Tom Petty – the people’s songwriters.

Brennan Wedl is released via Anti- on 21 August

One day, your life and future may depend on a jury. The integrity of that legal process is in peril right now

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 11:00:42 GMT

When a barrister is cited for contempt because of his argument to a jury, as happened in a Palestine Action trial, the risks affect us all

Palestine Action barrister’s prosecution criticised as ‘chilling’

Within days of Mr Justice Johnson’s decision to seek contempt proceedings against Rajiv Menon KC because of that barrister’s closing speech to the jury in a Palestine Action criminal damage trial, I happened to be making a closing speech to a jury. Neither the case nor the personnel of my case are relevant to what happened next, but it is telling that counsel for the prosecution appeared to invoke Mr Justice Johnson’s imprimatur to rebuke me for stepping over the boundary as to what was acceptable to say to the jury.

Thankfully, nothing of substance came of that. Not so for Menon. On 22 June 2026, Mr Justice Johnson handed down his approved judgment in Menon’s case such that he now faces a possible two-year prison sentence for defending his client in what was, it seems to me, in accordance with his professional duties and obligations.

As a highly experienced and successful member of the English bar, Menon was giving his closing speech in a case that involved pro-Palestine activists who broke into an Elbit Systems UK arms factory. The trial judge alleged that Menon deliberately ignored directions and misled the jury by discussing jury equity and the war in Gaza.

The judgment is significant not only for those directly affected by practising in the criminal courts but society as a whole because it starkly demonstrates how words spoken by those defending their clients – the traditional fortress of forensic freedom – can attract the machinery of contempt. The seriousness of that needs to be understood. The prospect of contempt proceedings is in danger of imposing a chilling effect on the willingness of defence advocates to test, for example, institutional misconduct themes robustly before a jury.

As I experienced first-hand, the risk will discourage advocates from deploying precisely those tools that the adversarial system contemplates. Defence counsel in cases involving allegations of police misconduct, for example, must be able to put credibility challenges with vigour, to name dishonesty where the evidence supports it, and to invite jurors to engage empathetically with the defendant’s experience. If such language can attract a contempt referral, advocates will face an unwelcome calculation: whether to advance the strongest case open to them or to temper their rhetoric in order to insulate themselves from future jeopardy.

The right to a fair trial, protected by article 6 of the European convention on human rights and embedded in the common law long before that instrument was enacted, encompasses the right to effective legal representation. Effectiveness, in a jury trial, requires more than the formal presence of counsel; it demands that counsel be free to deploy every legitimate forensic tool available to challenge the prosecution case. Public confidence in the criminal justice system depends upon the perception – as much as the reality – that proceedings are conducted fairly and that no party enters the courtroom at a structural disadvantage.

A climate in which defence advocates self-censor out of fear of contempt undermines that perception. If it becomes publicly known that counsel in cases involving police misconduct temper their submissions to avoid personal exposure, reasonable observers will question whether the adversarial process retains its integrity. That erosion of confidence is corrosive: the legitimacy of jury verdicts – acquittal and conviction alike – rests in part upon the assurance that they were returned after the defence case was pressed as fully and fearlessly as the evidence permitted.

The quality of jury deliberation is also imperilled. Jurors are lay decision-makers. They depend upon counsel to distil complex factual and legal questions into accessible, persuasive narrative. A closing speech that is moderated by the advocate’s anxiety about personal sanction is likely to be less effective. The result is not necessarily that the jury reaches the wrong verdict, but that it does so with a thinner and less complete presentation of the defence case than the evidence would have supported.

The risk of wrongful conviction must be a key factor here. It is an uncomfortable but empirically grounded observation that a disproportionate number of wrongful convictions in England and Wales have involved some form of police misconduct, whether in the gathering of evidence, the presentation of testimony or the suppression of material. Cases of that kind depend heavily upon vigorous adversarial challenge in the closing speech. If that challenge is muted, the risk that a factually innocent defendant is convicted is materially increased. The chilling effect of Menon’s case thus carries a direct, if unquantifiable, contribution to the wrongful conviction risk that the system as a whole must bear.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

As for barristers themselves, if senior advocates perceive that hard cases carry a personal professional hazard not faced in more conventional litigation, the rational response is to avoid that kind of work. Defendants in such cases will find themselves represented by advocates who are either less experienced or less willing to advance their case with full forensic force. What price, then, the quality of justice?

But what is most fundamentally at stake is the constitutional value of fearless advocacy itself. The principle that counsel must be free to advance a client’s case without fear of personal retribution is not a professional privilege; it is a constitutional safeguard. It reflects the understanding, embedded in centuries of common law, that the state – which commands the resources of the police, the Crown Prosecution Service and the wider apparatus of prosecution – should not also be able to deter challenges to its own witnesses through the threat of proceedings against the advocate raising them.

When the contempt is used or threatened in the context of advocacy, that constitutional equilibrium is disturbed.

Society has a collective interest in maintaining it – not for the benefit of the bar, but for the benefit of every person who may one day stand accused, and for the integrity of the process by which guilt or innocence is determined in their name. That vigilance should start here.

Imran Khan KC is a practising solicitor

‘Cockroach’ protests: India’s Modi promises to punish officials over exam leaks

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 10:31:50 GMT

PM says ‘those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared’ as scandal spirals into widespread anger

Narendra Modi has vowed to set up “fast-track courts” to speed up the punishment of officials accused of leaking examination papers, as the Indian prime minister seeks to quell a youth-led “cockroach” protest movement that has rocked Delhi and posed one of the biggest challenges to his government.

In his first public remarks on the movement, Modi posted on X: “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth … Those who try to harm the future of our youth will not be spared.”

The offer of faster justice than usual from India’s clogged judicial system, which can take decades to deliver a verdict, was swiftly rejected by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), the satirical name the youth protest movement coined after India’s top judge called unemployed youths “cockroaches”.

Saurav Das, a CJP spokesperson, said: “It’s a Band-aid. That’s not giving us accountability. There have been zero convictions so far all these years, so this measure is of no use.” A core demand of the movement is the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, as well as reform of the education system.

An estimated 50,000 people protested in Delhi on Monday, after police denied them permission to march on parliament. Officers later mounted baton charges and fired teargas. By Wednesday, more than 1,000 people remained camped at the CJP’s protest site in central Delhi despite the gruelling heat and humidity. Many had travelled long distances to be there.

Renuka Chowdhury, an opposition MP with the Congress party, told the news channel India Today that no one could fathom why Modi would not sack Pradhan. “Honestly, is this one minister more valuable or more important than restoring harmony and order to the country?” he said.

Modi’s statement follows signs the government may be softening its stance. Ministers have insisted they are willing to talk to the CJP but have refused to discuss Pradhan’s resignation.

The protest site at Jantar Mantar has drawn crowds of supporters eager to show their solidarity. Unable to fit inside the enclosed area, many have spilled on to the surrounding roads. Some organise donations of food and water sent by wellwishers, while others distribute meals – including to the police on duty – fan those wilting from the heat or collect litter.

Young people across India have also rallied behind the CJP’s demands, with three consecutive days of demonstrations in Mumbai and solidarity protests in Chennai, Indore, Hyderabad and Patiala.

At a press conference on Wednesday, the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi escalated his criticism, demanding that in addition to Pradhan resigning, Modi should apologise for failing to provide a fair education system.

Gandhi said there had been 152 exam paper leaks across the country over the past decade without a single conviction.

“Somebody, or a group of people, are destroying our education system, India’s most valuable asset, destroying the lives of our students. What does the government do? Zero convictions,” he said.

The health minister, JP Nadda, accused Gandhi of exploiting the protests for political gain.

“Your concern is not to improve the education system, enhance the quality of education or ensure justice for students. Instead, you are trying to use students’ issues and their demands for political mileage. You are trying to derive political benefit from them, and that is unfortunate,” he said.

CJP leaders were deeply disappointed after Monday’s meeting with Nadda – the first in over 60 days – ended without a breakthrough. Its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, has since said that if ministers want to speak to them, they will have to come to the protest site and do so in public.

Many in India are asking why Pradhan will not resign. Anish Gawande, an opposition politician, said Modi viewed backing down as a sign of weakness, particularly now that he no longer commands the parliamentary majority he enjoyed during his first two terms.

“He is facing global headwinds that prevent him from executing any major reforms in agriculture, energy, the economy. The unemployment rate is climbing to levels not seen in three decades,” he said. “A show of weakness now will give an entry point for the opposition to move in and build a similar momentum around other issues […] Before you know it, things have spiralled out of control.”

I am used to hot days now. But the warm wind has really panicked me

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 10:00:41 GMT

I first noticed it a couple of weeks ago on the streets of Cardiff – and it felt alarmingly wrong

When the wind is warm, you know something is up. Naturally, I have been well aware of the awful reality of the climate crisis, but it has taken the warmth of the wind to really panic me. Not the endless 30C+ days, the desiccated garden, the tap slowing to a drip. No, it is the warm wind blowing on me. I can just about manage in punishing heat, even though it is particularly suffocating when the air is still. But I thought I had a tacit agreement with the British climate that at least when there was a breeze it would cool me down a bit. When a breeze warms me up, here in the UK anyway, it feels nothing less than un-British, and I wonder if we really are getting into the end of days.

I first noticed it a couple of weeks ago on the streets of Cardiff. I turned a corner on St Mary’s Street and there it was, a strong gust of properly warm wind, right in my face and down into my lungs. Reeling, gasping a little, I looked around for the idling bus that had surely generated this unpleasant blast of air. But this wind hadn’t emanated from a bus’s rear, for there was no bus in sight. It was the weather and it felt alarmingly wrong.

I have spent much time in south Wales and the weather has thrown a lot at me over the years. It’s one of the many things I love about it here: rain hammering down on a caravan roof; rain coming at you horizontally; wind to lift you off your feet; tempests whipping the sea into a frenzy; fog so thick that you can’t see the sea even when it is lapping around your ankles. And punctuating these various weather events are frequent spells of sunshine lighting up the colours so brightly that your eyeballs ache. But a wind that is warm? Never.

The last time I felt wind this warm it was coming off the Gulf of Mexico into Galveston. In Texas, it was tolerable. It came with the territory. But blowing hotly into Cardiff off the Bristol Channel? Nah, sorry. All wrong. We’re doomed.

Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnist

In a fractious, divided world, I think I know why Pride is the hottest show in town

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 09:00:40 GMT

The 2014 film was only a modest success – but now the musical’s message of gay rights and solidarity feels both outlandish and full of hope

Hands down the hottest ticket in London this summer is the musical Pride at the National Theatre, which is booked solid until the end of its run in September and will presumably transfer to the West End after that. There are lots of gay shows doing well at the moment: I saw Oh, Mary! for the second time this week when the show’s creator, Cole Escola, came over from New York to resume the title role, and Operation Mincemeat keeps going and going. But both those shows are tonally rather than politically gay. Pride, which is adapted from the 2014 film and had modest commercial success when it came out, is a different kettle of fish and I’m curious as to why it’s flown now.

I should say up front I haven’t seen the show (can’t get a ticket!). But this week, as I watched my timeline continue to fill up with effusive praise and lots of crying about the musical, I went back to the film. It’s a strange time to watch it, in a news cycle in which issues around sexuality in public life and old views about gay rights have surfaced to yank us back to earlier times. The death of the US senator Lindsey Graham triggered widespread speculation about what, exactly, Donald Trump held over him and gave rise to a lot of gay jokes pulled out of the deep freeze.

Pride is set during the 1984 miners’ strike, when an unlikely alliance sprang up between a group of lesbians and gay men in London and striking miners in a Welsh town. Stephen Beresford, who wrote the film and the stage production, tells the story of LGSM – Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners – a group set up by a young activist from County Antrim, Mark Ashton. I imagine there were hopes that the film would do a Billy Elliot, but neither British nor American audiences overly responded. Although the film was critically applauded, it didn’t break through.

Anyway, I don’t want to be too much of a buzzkill , because the whole point about Pride is that it doesn’t feel like homework and I would urge everyone who can’t get a ticket to the show to go back to the movie, which stars Andrew Scott (who must by law be in everything), a really good Dominic West, and Jessica Gunning, who was by far the best thing in Baby Reindeer. Ashton is played by a brilliant Ben Schnetzer and, compared with the entire output of, say, Russell T Davies, Beresford seems actually interested in the women in the story. I’m sorry, but I have to quote some key lines: “Give it to the lesbians, they love a banner”; “Police harassment, dear, I could set it to music”; “Don’t be daft, love. We’ve come all the way from Powys.”

That last line is uttered by Imelda Staunton, who will make you laugh and break your heart, and the main takeaway is solidarity, which viewed through a 2026 lens is perhaps the most outlandish thing about it. In this world of feverishly defended political differences between people on the same side, Pride tells a different story, in which vastly different groups organise around a common cause. Paddy Considine as the Welsh miner Dai Donovan was the first person to accept help from the “perverts”, as they were referred to in the popular press in those days, and says it best: “It’s more than money, it’s friendship.”

Perhaps that’s what’s done it, this time around. The Dorfman theatre at the National only holds 450 seats, which has given the show a way to build an audience without the pressure of filling a bigger theatre. It’s true, too, that gays will go to see a show we love several times, which definitely helps. But in this era in which all we hear is that we’re living in political end times, my sense is that this show offers something unusual for everyone. It is both shocking and moving to be reminded of how bad things once were, and what could still be achieved.

Meet the man whose groundbreaking book is being devoured by the left

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 09:00:39 GMT

Anton Jäger has been lauded for his exceptional ability to make sense of these strange political times – and he’s only 32. The writer and academic explains why we’re living in an age of hyperpolitics

‘I am acutely conscious,” said Andy Burnham outside 10 Downing Street on Monday, “that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street.” It was good to hear him say it because, beneath all the cabinet gossip and rune-reading, there is a feeling of terror about the immediate future and also about ourselves, the electorate. Is this who we are now? Wildly enthusiastic one minute, seething the next; as passionate about the change we want as we are convinced that those who promise it are incapable of enacting it?

It is perhaps not surprising that Anton Jäger’s recent book, Hyperpolitics: Extreme Politicization without Political Consequences, is being read by Labour watchers and leftwing thinkers. As the New York Times wrote, it’s “among the best and most dazzling efforts to model the political present in all its maddening strangeness”. Still, I think Jäger was surprised to have his honeymoon interrupted so I could interview him about it. Life comes at everyone quite fast in a hyperpolitical age.

Jäger, 32, raised in Brussels by parents who work in the arts (“bohemian class?” I ask, and he says carefully that they are boho “adjacent”), educated at the University of Essex, then Cambridge, is now a lecturer in the history of political thought and theory at University College, Oxford. He has an intense, angular face and a calm, almost self-effacing manner. His philosophical reference points are Deleuze and Guattari, Mouffe and Laclau, but asked to situate himself in the firmament of the European left, he says simply: “Even with all the baggage and connotations, I still think the easiest thing is to call myself a Marxist.”

His thinking runs as follows (don’t get hung up on the dates, though some, like 1989, are non-negotiable). The years 1914 to 1989 mark the age of mass politics, when politicisation was high and institutionalisation was also high – so people engaged with politics electorally and on the streets. They were joiners – of political parties, unions, congregations, working men’s clubs, reading groups; they participated in multiple interlacing institutions. Not by coincidence, this was also a time when political struggle resulted in concrete gains. Then, 1989 to the financial crash in 2008 (the years often called the “long 90s”) was the age of post-politics, when institutionalisation was low (we emphatically did not join clubs then, we went to clubs), and politicisation was through the floor. It was a time when technocrats took care of business while everyone else went to a rave, and we said history was over. From the crash through to about 2020 (sometimes earlier, this boundary is the most fluid) was the age of anti-politics – a resurgent Tea Party in the US, Beppe Grillo and anti-establishment protests in Italy, the Arab spring, the Occupy movement. Politicisation in this period came back with a vengeance, and even while institutionalisation hasn’t recovered, these movements still have institutional ambitions. Protest movements in Spain and Greece bore political parties, Podemos and Syriza; protest candidates in the US, France and the UK, had their eyes on retaking traditional parties from which the revolutionary intent had long been stripped away.

Hyperpolitics is what came next: intense politicisation, with neither institutional roots nor ambitions. “On the surface,” Jäger writes, “the Black Lives Matter protests would seem to have little in common with the mob that stormed the Capitol in January 2021. Morally, they are worlds apart … Organisationally, however, these movements exhibit a striking set of similarities: fleeting in duration, they maintain no membership rolls and struggle to impose any real discipline on their adherents.” As a consequence, everything explodes and nothing changes; movements surge suddenly forward and yet no territory is taken. He quotes political theorist Paolo Gerbaudo’s evocative phrase “bodies without organs”. Modern political movements, he writes, are “concentrated and muscular, yet without an internal metabolism”.

He found this pattern across the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development and he only stopped there, he says, because “I don’t have the linguistic and cultural reach to fully tell this story globally”. His descriptions are powerful. He writes of climate strikers and anti-lockdown demonstrators alike as “a myriad animated by brief, potent stimuli, stirred to action by charismatic influencers and digital demagogues”. And that, you have to admit, is exactly what it looks like.

These four eras – mass politics, post-politics, antipolitics and hyperpolitics – “are not just concepts,” Jäger says, “they have some empirical data behind them. ‘How institutionalised is society?’ is basically a question of, how does civil society look? How are membership organisations looking? What are the affiliations, what are the types of bonds that people have? That’s not very difficult to quantify. You can look at union membership, you can look at church attendance, you can look at less overtly political forms of belonging. The political axis is more difficult to measure, but not impossible – namely, how many people attend elections, how many people strike, how many people engage in political violence, how many people engage in political communication, write letters to editors or now post online?”

He argues that the height of mass politics was between the wars. To illustrate this in the book, he lists all the civic organisations during the Great Depression in the small Rhenish hamlet of Marienthal – they spanned all human activity, from work to thought to rabbit-breeding. I won’t list them all here but there were many. Considering the effect these organisations might have on the collective psyche, Jäger considers the history of his own family: “On the Flemish side, this meant that the Christian Democratic or the Catholic party was not just a party that said how you were to vote, or which union you joined, but also had a very strong say in what happened in the bedroom. It was a total doctrine, not something that purely applied to your political deportment.” There was little boundary between public and private, and no such thing as a political identity without a membership card. It was personally quite constraining, but it got shit done. (Sidebar, I’ve seen a nascent institutionalised-politics like this, in Manchester, in 2019; the local Momentum group was campaigning for Jeremy Corbyn, but it also had a running club, a knitting group and a book group. I was overcome by the sense of seeing a trade union movement reborn. Needless to say, Corbyn did not win that election. Institution-building can’t be done on the fly.)

The destruction of political organisations was “not monocausal”, Jäger says, though in the book he puts it squarely on the shoulders of the union busting by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan. People lost faith in organisations because the crunchy bit of their leverage – the bit where you get what you want by withdrawing your labour, the bit before all-out war – was taken away. Unions were defanged and workers impoverished, and many ultimately saw their industries collapse in the process.

Jäger says there were also cultural and generational shifts over decades – people in the 60s and 70s seeking a different relationship with collective institutions, for example, and looking instead for emancipation and equality – so it takes a while for the picture to cohere, and Communist parties remained tenacious through the 1980s in Italy, for instance. “In 1989, suddenly it’s as if there’s a day and night difference,” he says. With the fall of the Berlin Wall, the end of the cold war, he says: “Suddenly everyone deserves to party.”

It is a strange sensation to have the 90s narrated back to you by someone who was born in 1994, but it is mainly unsettling because it is so accurate. Tony Blair did describe globalisation as a process as inexorable as the weather, and that is also how neoliberals described the economy – a thing that happened to you. “This is the ambiguity of the post-politics of the 90s,” Jäger says. “Politics is no longer something that you see as effecting large-scale social change, and the forms of liberty that are available to you are now more private, more intimate, more individual. At the same time, the idea that you can collectively bundle together with other individuals and change society starts to appear very, very remote.”

There was also a lot of beauty to that time, which he describes through the photography of Wolfgang Tillmans and the novels of Annie Ernaux and Michel Houellebecq. We were obsessed with Houellebecq in the 90s, but we will have to talk about why, and the direction his novels took, and whether we will ever again live in a world whose best cultural artefact is the novel, another time. “The fact that Tillmans as a gay man is able to express and experience the rave culture of the 90s and 00s as a new form of collectivity that wasn’t available to him in the 70s and 80s, I don’t think we should deny the liberatory value of this. It very clearly is the case that there are individuals who did not feel at home in the families, or the communities or the neighbourhoods in which they grew up, in which they finally find a kind of new community that is much less demanding and is less exigent than what they had before. The ambiguity is, of course, that it also implies a profound disenchantment and cynicism around what politics can do.” That’s politics with a capital P – you might see a community animated about an issue, but with no faith in parliamentary channels.

There is a critical and rarely mentioned adjunct to the neoliberal destruction of institutions and the post and antipolitics that came afterwards, which is that it didn’t only come for the left. “Thatcher basically did a controlled demolition of popular Conservatism,” Jäger says, “and replaced much of this with PR spin, and also a lot of private funding, because the idea was: ‘We can get rid of our mass party because we’re in control of the media, we can win elections with that.’” The right today, he says, is just as inconsequential as the left, and for exactly the same reason, that it’s hyper but not formally organised. “The people who go on marches subscribe to the same podcast, might follow the same pages on Instagram, might be on the same Telegram channels, but they don’t have an organisational history they shared before they entered the march. This is different even to the BNP, where marchers had a shared history in football hooliganism, and the National Front. That shared subculture is no longer there.”

He says this is clear with Reform UK, “which is so heavily leader-dependent. The entire movement is at risk with this scandal of the crypto-billionaire, because there’s no party infrastructure. There is just Nigel and a smartphone and then a couple of private donors.” To me, this fails to take into account that the right is different to the left: they have more money. “Maybe I understated the availability of private funding,” he says mildly. “The fact that we can even talk of a trillionaire, such as Elon Musk, means there’s a complete secession of that individual from what we could even call society. That is a variable in explaining why hyperpolitics on the right thrives and why hyperpolitics on the left has found it much more difficult to achieve tangible results.” They are not more organised or more ideologically coherent or more strategic; they are just better funded – which puts quite a lot on the shoulders of capital itself as the overarching organising principle of global politics. Money might not be the only thing talking, but it’s the only thing getting what it wants.

The more immediately controversial proposition of the book, though, is that what we are watching in Trump’s US is not fascism, because the right only travels to that extreme in the face of a direct threat of organised socialism. “The left is doing itself too many favours by considering its opponents fascists,” he says. “You’re overestimating your strength. The contemporary far right is more a function of the crisis of liberalism than it is a function of the strength of the left.” What we’re looking at instead, with Trump, is “Bonapartism” says Jäger. He writes that Trump, and everyone else who has ever got ahead by championing the “left behind”, isn’t representing a strong mass movement or class, but, like Napoleon, relying on “the largely passive support of impoverished peasants … not a collective but ‘formed by the simple addition of isomorphous magnitudes, much as potatoes in a sack form a sack of potatoes’.” (That bit about potatoes is from Karl Marx’s The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte.) We skirmish a little about the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement as a standing army that looks extremely fascist, until Jäger concludes: “The spectrum from fascism to Bonapartism can flip into something more radical. At the same time, I’m still more struck by the differences than the similarities with these 20th-century phenomena.”

Neal Lawson, guru of Manchesterism and an Anton Jäger fan, lays these arguments over the predicament of our new prime minister. “It isn’t just lack of money Burnham has to contend with but the absence of secure political footings. Temporary hyper-political swarms have taken the place of substantial and secure alliances. He must find a way to surf these volatile waves or be another victim of them.” But we, the volatile waves, also have to figure out how to re-engage with institutions and build new ones, and is that possible? Jäger pauses, dispiritingly, like a mechanic who is about to give you bad news about your fanbelt. “This is an interesting and scary question. We do live in a society in which the incentives for leaving rather than entering organisations are much higher. Recent experience, whether joining a party or joining a union, often militates against the idea that there’s any sense in collective action, and the rational response is helplessness. And yet, repoliticisation is good. Hyperpolitics has increased people’s consciousness of the fact that politics matters.”

Hyperpolitics by Anton Jäger (Verso Books, £11.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Why would Trump agree to the Saudi nuclear deal?

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 09:00:39 GMT

The agreement offers the Saudis the same options Trump has sworn Iran will never have

The stark contrast between Donald Trump’s nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia and his nuclear demands for Iran would be comical if not so tragic. Trump has handed the Saudis the same nuclear options he swore Iran would never have.

To make matters worse, Trump seems to have offered the Saudis this sweetheart deal to make amends for his disastrous war of choice with Iran. Meanwhile, he continues to bomb Iran in a push to open the strait of Hormuz, which was not closed until Trump launched his counterproductive war.

As recently as this past April, Trump reiterated in discussing Iran: “There will be no enrichment of uranium.” That goal had become more urgent because, once Trump ripped up the nuclear accord negotiated by Barack Obama, Iran stepped up its enrichment to near the level needed for an atomic bomb. When Israel and the United States started bombing Iran in June 2025, Iran also barred independent UN inspectors.

So what does Trump offer the Saudis? The possibility, after a joint study, to enrich uranium (and reprocess spent atomic fuel) and to bar inspectors from certain sites that they might deem suspicious. The lack of inspectors would mean there is little to prevent the Saudi government from transforming a civilian nuclear program into a clandestine weapons operation, despite Saudi Arabia (like Iran) being a signatory of the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.

The Saudi crown prince has said that his country would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran did. Notably, Trump’s deal is much less stringent than the 2009 deal negotiated by George W Bush and Barack Obama with the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia’s neighboring ally-turned-competitor.

Trump describes himself as having mastered the “art of the deal”, but his agreement with the Saudis is likely to torpedo any more restrictive deal with Iran. Iran is already being asked to forsake a nuclear weapon while Israel has them. Any claim that Israel can be trusted to handle its weaponry responsibly is belied by its genocide in Gaza and its decimation of much of that occupied territory as well as southern Lebanon. Now Iran must consider that its Saudi adversary could also develop a bomb.

Why would Trump agree to such a deal? Money seems to have played a big part. The deal could provide tens of billions of dollars to the US nuclear industry if it were to sell reactors to the Saudis. Suddenly the principle that Trump said was worth fighting for can be jettisoned for the right price.

I suspect part of the reason is Trump’s effort to revive an alliance that his war has jeopardized. Trump has long had a soft spot for the Saudi crown prince, who possesses the kind of monarchial power that Trump covets. Like other Gulf Arab states, Saudi Arabia had looked to the United States as a security partner, even wanting to formalize the arrangement with a treaty.

But Trump’s war has made the partnership risky. Rather than the United States protecting its regional allies, the war provided an excuse for Iran to attack them, targeting the US military bases on their soil and sometimes their petroleum and other infrastructure.

About the only good thing that can be said about Trump’s giveaway to the Saudis is that it reflects a continued lessening of the genocidal Israel’s influence in Washington DC. An earlier version of a Saudi nuclear deal was premised on the Saudi government opening diplomatic relations with Israel. That requirement has now been abandoned. Riyadh has said that recognition is off the table without “a credible and irreversible path to a Palestinian state”. Netanyahu is doing all he can to prevent that.

As the nuclear rationale for war wears thin, Trump’s secretary of state, Marco Rubio, has begun to stress the importance of Iran allowing the strait of Hormuz to reopen. Trump has gone so far as to threaten war crimes – bombing Iran’s bridges and power plants – for every Iranian attack in the strait, even though war crimes by one side never justify war crimes by the other.

But the strait was open until Trump’s war encouraged the Iranians to retaliate asymmetrically by closing it. Now, Trump’s memorandum of understanding with Iran – another brilliant stroke by the master negotiator – implicitly allows Iran to charge fees after 60 days.

In other words, the main remaining justification for war has become a matter that was never an issue before Trump’s war, while Trump has effectively given away with his Saudi deal a main rationale for starting the war.

There of course is another factor behind the continued bombing. Trump seems to be seeking a face-saving concession from Iran before his Republicans face a midterm debacle. But that is hardly a reason for more bloodshed and destruction.

Revelation of the Saudi deal comes as the Trump administration is trying to persuade Congress to fund a deeply unpopular war that it had no say in launching. The defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, says it has cost $37.5bn so far. That is about what it would cost for, say, a year’s rental assistance for 2.3 million low-income people, or to enable about 7 million people to maintain their health insurance.

And to make matters worse, Hegseth wants a total of $67.1bn to keep the war going. Because Trump cannot articulate a persuasive rationale for his pointless war, Congress should say no. This war never should have started and now clearly should not continue.

Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University, and former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author of Righting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive Governments

How powerful is your passport? Explore the global rankings

The Guardian Thu, 23 Jul 2026 07:00:39 GMT

A symbol of global inequalities and shifting geopolitical fortunes, some passports offer their holders far more freedom to travel than others

Passports can resemble abridged memoirs, their stamps telling romantic stories of wanderlust, freedom and belonging.

But they are also a symbol of global inequalities and shifting geopolitical fortunes. Passports from some places allow their holders to travel abroad simply by booking a flight and packing a bag. Others, however, entail booking an appointment at the nearest consulate, presenting documents to prove identity and financial means, then waiting weeks for a decision.

How does the status of your passport compare globally? How has its power changed over time?

Search to find out …

A person with a passport from …

United Kingdom is in the 6th tier in the global passports ranking, based on the mobility score, which measures the number of destinations accessible visa-free or with a visa on arrival, an ETA, or a fast-track e-visa. Some passports share the same rank.

In the last 10 years, more countries have gained access to more destinations and, at first glance, it would seem that the world is opening up.

“People think that walls are increasing as the extreme right is coming [into government] in various places around the world,” says Armand Arton, who runs Passport Index, a website that tracks visa requirements. “But what the statistics are saying is that an increasing number of countries are signing visa-free agreements.”

You can chart a passport’s strength by counting the number of countries, states and territories its holder can enter visa-free, or with a visa on arrival, an electronic travel authorisation (ETA), or a fast-track e-visa. This is known as a mobility score.

Small island nations’ passport strength rose as they earned visa-free status from developing countries. Arton attributes the rise to these countries’ often small populations, which are not seen as a national security threat, and to a sense among some governments of a moral obligation to offer visa-free travel to people on the frontlines of the climate crisis.

China has moved up the rank by opening up and expanding bilateral agreements with regional neighbours. Since signing a bilateral visa-free agreement with Singapore in February 2024, there was a sharp increase in travel between the two countries.

When countries sign a visa-free agreement with the Schengen area, which comprises 29 European countries, the standing of their passports can shoot up the ranking almost overnight. That is why Georgia, Ukraine and Kosovo are among the biggest climbers in the passport table.

Vjosa Musliu is an associate professor at Vrije Universiteit Brussel who has written about the experience of travelling with a Kosovan passport, which has gained in mobility. She describes the joy of seeing her relatives and friends being able to travel.

“These were upper-middle class people with decent jobs who never travelled because of the cost of getting a visa, which is sometimes close to £300,” she says. “[People] who wanted to see grandmas and grandpas and not celebrate birthdays on FaceTime.” But visa-free travelling does not mean you automatically get free entry, she adds. “Technically you can travel for free, but there is still subjective interrogation that takes place at borders.”

Most passports have gained mobility in the last decade, but some have fallen in the tiered ranking. Vanuatu fell 14 positions when the EU and the UK removed it from their visa-exempt list, citing concerns over Vanuatu’s investor citizenship scheme. The US dropped five places to ninth tier this year, mostly due to countries applying reciprocity in their visa systems in response to Washington’s tightening of its visa requirements.

Then there are countries such as Afghanistan, Iraq, Syria, Pakistan and Somalia, for which the world is still mostly closed. Anyone with an Afghan passport can only travel visa-free to three countries, and will have to apply for a visa at a consulate before travelling to 113 countries.

Afghan passport holders are also barred from entering the US, where citizens of 19 countries face a full travel ban, and another 20 face partial restrictions.

Having a weak passport can sour even life’s greatest achievements. Omar Artan was to become the first referee from Somalia to officiate at a World Cup after being named on Fifa’s final list for the tournament, but he was denied entry to the US. It can also delay your plans. Visual artist Syed Hussain, who is from Pakistan, was granted a US residency in 2019 – but it took three attempts until he was finally granted the visa so that he could travel in 2024.

“You get the chance to go somewhere, and they hold you back for five years, and they don’t give you the reason why, they just give you a yellow paper and refuse the visa,” Hussain said. “It’s a 10-minute interview in which you cannot clarify your things, or bring your portfolio.”

Passport Index has introduced a “welcoming score”, which counts the number of countries whose passport holders are eligible to enter a destination visa-free, or with a visa on arrival, an ETA or an e-visa. Although some e-visas still require documents to be submitted and reviewed, they are generally considered less burdensome than traditional visas.

Setting up the welcoming scores against the mobility scores of countries paints a mixed picture. The US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand hold some of the world’s strongest passports, yet keep their own borders comparatively closed. At the other end of the spectrum are countries such as South Sudan, Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, whose citizens need visas to travel to most destinations but whose governments admit foreign visitors relatively easily.

The 29 European countries that belong to the Schengen agreement (plus four that apply the same rules), grant visa-free access to almost half of the countries in the world. But people who cannot travel visa-free must obtain a visa in advance from a consulate. This applies mostly to passport holders from south and south-east Asia, northern Africa, central Asia, the Middle East, and most of sub-Saharan Africa.

Beyond the Schengen area, passport mobility is likely to increase through new bilateral and regional agreements. Africa remains the least integrated region, with only 29% of travel within the continent taking place visa-free.

The balance will also shift as more countries replace traditional visas with digital ETAs and e-visas, “driven by advances in border security, traveller screening, and digital immigration management”, says Arton. This might spell the end of the paper visa.

But it also means, according to Arton, that travellers who previously enjoyed visa-free access will increasingly be required to obtain an electronic authorisation prior to departure. The EU, for example, is expected to introduce its Etias travel authorisation system by the end of the year for visitors who currently travel visa-free.

Passport data from Passport Index as of June, 2026. Visa requirements can change and may include additional conditions. Always check the relevant embassy, consulate or official government website before travelling.
