OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Photo Illustration by Rosie Clements for The New York Times

Supported by

By Emi Nietfeld

Ms. Nietfeld is a journalist and the author of the memoir “Acceptance.”

When I was a teenager, I dreamed of a better life. I grew up in an apartment where mice darted through waist-high piles of trash, thanks to my mom’s hoarding. For a year I was in foster care, and other times I was homeless, spending some summer nights in the back of my battered ’92 Corolla. Despite all this, I saw a path out and up: I would ace the SAT, pick the right major at a good college, then graduate into a lucrative career. It was far from a sure bet, but I wagered that this plan could change my destiny — and it did. I got a computer science degree from Harvard, then an engineering job at Google.

I wrote a memoir about my upward trajectory, and in the years since it was published I’ve been invited to speak at colleges around the country. At first, I saw myself as a slightly older role model to students. But while speaking to rising graduates this year, I felt more like the narrator of a historical novel. I started to wonder: Is my perspective relevant at all?

When I graduated from college in 2015, my classmates and I were steeped in millennial values. Advisers urged us to follow our dreams, to do what we loved, and, for women, to lean in. A poster on my dorm room wall featured a quote from Sheryl Sandberg, the personification of 2010s corporate feminism: “What would you do if you weren’t afraid?” I proudly met the world’s youngest self-made female billionaire, Elizabeth Holmes. Work offered us not just a salary, but a purpose. It was salvation and selfhood and transcendence all at once.

Identifying with your work is no longer the vibe. I started at Google gung ho and left so jaded by sexual harassment that I promised myself I’d never love a job again. The fall of Ms. Holmes and other executives accused of fraud created a societywide disenchantment with supposedly genius company founders. Then came Covid-19, which forced a reappraisal of how much space the office should occupy in our lives. A half-decade later, state minimum wage laws top out under $18 an hour while the stock market mints new millionaires in the United States at the rate of 1,200 a day.

Gen Z-ers are often accused of shrugging off work — in fact, they say so themselves — and who can blame them? They’ve watched millennial workers burn out, wages stagnate, degrees turn worthless and institutions crumble. Now, they’re entering what’s widely called the worst job market in years. Almost half of recent college graduates are unemployed or underemployed. The cost of living has soared; buying a house feels impossible. Who knows where we’ll live anyway once the Earth is uninhabitable. One viral meme captured the prevailing sentiment that “basically nobody under 40 right now expects good things to happen ever again.”

I wanted to understand how the outlook of young people has changed, so I reached out to colleges I’ve visited to talk to graduating students about their hopes and fears for their looming adulthood. I found that like job seekers of all ages, they feel terrified and discouraged. But one thing stood out: Many students told me that ambition as I knew it no longer makes sense.

It’s not just that they believe upward mobility like mine is now impossible. They no longer believe work in the traditional sense leads to any reliable payoff. The casino economy they’re entering doles out success in the form of windfalls, and makes those wins vanish just as suddenly. Ambition requires a belief that you have meaningful control over your future. With so much uncertainty today, it can feel pointless to prepare for tomorrow.

The most driven young people are still striving. But their ambition looks significantly different from mine in college, when I sat in an auditorium listening to Ms. Sandberg recount how she became a Facebook executive. Gen Z values money and free time over job titles. In a recent global survey, Gen Z respondents who were not pursuing leadership roles pointed to burnout and “too much responsibility” as their main reasons. In other polls, three in four Gen Z-ers wanted to become entrepreneurs, and more than half said they would be influencers if they could. They’re trying to “get the bag” and make a fortune, but they’re not depending on getting promoted by their boss to do it.

Alejandra Perez is one student who sees entrepreneurship as her future. Ms. Perez, 21, has an active LinkedIn, a smooth blowout and a fresh bachelor’s degree in marketing and business administration from St. Mary’s College of California. Her family runs a beekeeping business that she helps out with, and she plans to launch her own company selling honey products. She considers owning her own business to be the key to unlimited opportunity. She thinks classmates who choose to climb a corporate ladder are forfeiting their true potential, an opinion shared by many of the students I spoke to; none named a dream company they aspired to work at.

Ms. Perez’s material goals are relatively modest: She wants to be able to buy a home in a safe neighborhood, invest in stocks and afford trendy sneakers and fancy desserts. Despite this, when it comes to her earning potential, she said, “I don’t have a limit.” She envisions building her business up to a seven-figure income.

These sky-high expectations are in line with those of other members of her generation. In a recent poll, Gen Z-ers on average said that in order to feel financially successful they would need to earn nearly $600,000 a year — or roughly what the top 2 percent of Americans make. Most of the students I spoke to told me they would need $200,000 to $300,000 a year just to feel stable. To be rich, or afford kids, many said they would need millions in the bank. A 2010 Pew survey found that for millennials entering adulthood, marriage and children were far more important than owning a home, earning a lot of money or having free time. While the desire to create a happy family certainly hasn’t disappeared for Gen Z, that value is surpassed in polling data by “financial independence” — having so much wealth you never need to work again.

In some ways, Ms. Perez’s ambitions reminded me of those of a 2010s-era girl boss. But there is a crucial difference: She is not willing to sacrifice her personal life for a company title. Ms. Perez’s fiancé graduated last year and now works as an admissions officer at St. Mary’s. They are marrying next year and hope to have three kids, whom Ms. Perez, a Catholic, wants to raise herself while running her business from home. One of her role models is Lila Rose, a podcaster and anti-abortion activist who is both a high earner and a mother who is present for most of her kids’ waking hours. Young conservative female influencers like Ms. Rose, Brett Cooper and Isabel Brown bring their children on work trips and hold their newborns in video interviews, conspicuously displaying a lifestyle that balances faith, family and financial comfort. It’s a version of having it all for the influencer generation — and a response to economic scarcity by doubling down on personal choices.

Ms. Perez looks at her peers with alarm, and not because she worries about unemployment rates. “It’s like there’s no motivation,” she said. Others I spoke to levied similar judgments. Adreanna Marin, a 39-year-old aspiring social worker at California State University, San Marcos, who first started college 20 years ago, told me, “It almost seems like ambition is no longer existent, honestly, among college students.” Many students blamed smartphones, the boogeyman of our age. “We are the future, and we can change it,” Jaasiel Hernandez, 20, an engineering student at Porterville College in California, said. “But it’s easier to sit down and scroll.” His comment echoed a common fear: If you live on autopilot, you’ll turn 30 in your parents’ basement, unemployed, in debt and glued to your feed.

Researchers believe ambition is shaped by both personality and circumstances. A landmark 2012 study led by Timothy Judge, a psychologist who studies attitudes toward jobs and success, analyzed the trajectories of more than 700 people over 70 years and found that the most driven people grew up middle class: not too rich to be complacent, not too poor to dream big. As the middle class shrinks, it seems as if ambition may be shrinking, too. Mary Volmer, a chaplain and lecturer at St. Mary’s, told me that students no longer ask themselves, “What can I achieve?” but “What do I need to survive?”

Mecca Durhal, 24, is one graduate I spoke to who thinks primarily about survival. Mx. Durhal has no 10-year plan, five-year plan or even next-year plan. The child of a software engineer, they grew up working class to middle class in Detroit and graduated in May from the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. They took liberal arts classes that excited them most intellectually — sociolinguistics, internet culture, Egyptology — and earned a bachelor’s in general studies. What comes next? “I super don’t know,” Mx. Durhal said.

The feeling that higher education’s fundamental promise has been violated isn’t limited to humanities majors. Nathan Majeed, who recently graduated with a computer science degree from St. Mary’s, said he had once expected a streamlined path: “Go to college, put in four years of work, then you get out. The job is basically guaranteed — it falls into your lap.” That’s no longer the situation. Mr. Majeed applied to almost 200 I. T. jobs without any luck, then finally found a role through a former boss.

Before starting college, Mx. Durhal hoped to become a writer or a Japanese translator. But in the years they’ve been in school, they’ve watched A. I. platforms become commonplace and creative jobs evaporate. Now they have no expectations of working a job that they like. They are applying online to administrative assistant roles, trying to dodge A. I. résumé filters and hoping for a yearly income of $40,000. That comes out to $3,300 monthly, before taxes — though they are currently paying $1,700 a month to share a townhouse with three friends. They fear they will be paying off student loans until they die. When people ask what their goals are, they reply, “The economy and society that we live in is not structured right now for me to have good answers.”

Gen Z’s relationship to labor is more transactional than sentimental. Eight out of 10 students who graduated from high school in 2022 don’t expect work to be an important part of their life, nor for their job to be particularly interesting. This lack of present, or future, reward is pushing some young people to reject the grind entirely. In Mx. Durhal’s worldview, delayed gratification just isn’t worth the wait. “I think looking only ahead to the future is actually detrimental to you,” they said. Mr. Majeed told me a different version of the same thing. “Our generation recognizes a bad deal when they see it,” he said. “If I have to go through pain, I’d rather it be on my own terms than the terms you made.”

Nowhere is this shift more apparent than in Gen Z’s emphasis on “mental health,” defined more by self-care than by psychiatric disorders. While millennial work culture might be best typified by the character of Andy in “The Devil Wears Prada,” who placates her abusive boss in order to climb to her dream job, Gen Z idolizes Alysa Liu, the raccoon-haired Olympic figure skater who quit the sport in 2022 because she no longer enjoyed it, then returned of her own accord and won gold. Ms. Liu is the latest in a string of athletes lauded by youth for saying no, from the tennis player Naomi Osaka, who at one point refused to speak to the press, to the gymnast Simone Biles, who withdrew from several Olympic events. For many, the lesson is that there is a limit to the personal costs of achievement.

Mx. Durhal’s hopes are more humble than winning an Olympic medal — they want to be able to make an occasional plane trip to visit friends in other states. As for owning a home, that might as well be an alternate reality. “I don’t think that’s feasible or realistic for me to want, so I’m not wanting it,” they said. In essence, Mx. Durhal has made peace with falling out of the middle class. One study found that nearly half of 18- to 29-year-olds now live with their parents — one of the highest rates since the Great Depression. Other students I spoke to acknowledge that doing work they care about will mean renting forever — if they can afford even that.

I admire these students’ Zen-like ability to enjoy today in spite of tomorrow. But their powerlessness saddens me. In 2024, an Emory University professor, Stephen Nowicki, observed that his college seminar students felt less control over their lives than the average prisoner felt in 1966. The belief that you shape your own destiny strongly tracks with health, income and happiness. People who feel they have agency tend to eat better, apply for more jobs and recover more easily from setbacks. It’s true that in times of uncertainty, despair is a rational response. But when young people stop believing that long-term effort will improve their lives, something larger is lost: the capacity to imagine a meaningful future.

Ms. Perez and Mx. Durhal have a lot in common. Neither cares about prestige or job titles. Both want the income and flexibility to live according to their personal values. Dr. Judge, a professor at Ohio State University who led the foundational ambition study, told me that compared with previous generations, his current students think harder about what they want out of life. “Now’s the time to question it — early in your career, when you’re in the formative stage,” Dr. Judge said. “I think it’s a good thing.”

There’s a lot for us still to learn from the way Gen Z approaches work. Years of research have shown that extrinsic motivators like money and fame make people miserable while intrinsic motivators like enjoyment or self-mastery fuel satisfaction. In Dr. Judge’s study, the most ambitious people died slightly younger than those with less drive. He thinks it’s because those who focused on accomplishment experienced more stress and neglected their health and relationships.

While talking to students, I found myself questioning my own choice to worship at the altar of work. I wrote much of this article on weekends, sometimes while my toddler begged for me; I have chronic pain triggered by sitting too long; I don’t know how to turn off my drive. Before talking to these students, I never really considered what “success at any cost” actually cost me.

At the same time, ambition isn’t just about personal accomplishments. It’s also about having faith in our ability to shape the future. Speaking to Mx. Durhal and other young adults for whom tomorrow seems uncertain, I see a generation that’s learning not to hope too hard. Humans are future-oriented creatures. Not being able to look ahead deprives us of what matters most. Data collected in an ongoing study on people’s well-being showed that young adults across the world score low not just on happiness but on eudaemonistic well-being, including meaning, purpose and fulfilling relationships.

As an adolescent, I took solace in the saying “Even if I knew that tomorrow the world would go to pieces, I would still plant my apple tree.” This aphorism, often attributed to Martin Luther, wasn’t about the joy of digging holes. It represented defiant optimism in the face of uncertainty. In the hardest moments of my youth, my goals gave me dignity and agency. When the present felt unbearable, my aspirations allowed me to transcend my surroundings. I think about sitting in the back seat of my rusty car, clutching an SAT book. I still bear the scars of my work ethic; I wish I’d known, like today’s youth, how to give myself more grace. But I also wish they understood how the dream itself illuminated the path a few feet ahead of me, until I stood on solid ground.

I agree the saddest part of your research is the lack of self-actualisation/agency: that the actions one takes today might, just might, take you forward. It’s all about putting yourself out there (I’m interested in how much fear of failure entered into your conversations?). My work life started at 14 with a retail job (I had no idea you had to be 16 and the manager liked me so she lied on my application and hired me; I worked for 2 years there.). I worked retail all through high school and college. At 22, my impossible career goal was working in the music business, which I had no clue how to get there nor connections to. But I needed a job and took a temp admin asst job first. Then I picked up the phone, called some music companies and pushed some buttons because I needed an extension: I left a voicemail. They called me back. They transferred me to someone else, who called me back. I worked for free 30 hrs a week while I worked every night and weekend for $. That got me recommendations and connections and I was in. My 20s were working for record companies and I had a blast. Then Napster entered the music scene so I pivoted and went to Silicon Valley for a career in software. So I wonder about Gen Z’s comfort with risk, fear of rejection/failure and the desire to learn and grow for personal growth’s sake; I always knew each role was not self-defining but a continual sharpening of my mind, skills and future.

@HNSinc I got really into the research on “locus of control”: how much do you believe your actions shape your outcome. Yes, despair is a rational response to some of the conditions. But, also, locus of control tends to get fixed at a young age and doesn’t change much. I do worry that learned helplessness is happening here. There’s a big risk in not recognizing the agency you do have.

Stocks Tumble as A. I. Spending and Oil Prices Weigh on Market

The New York Times July 23, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The S&P 500 tumbled more than 1 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite sank more than 2 percent.

How stocks are trading in the United States

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

By Aruni Soni

Stocks were hit Thursday by soaring oil prices, rising borrowing costs and worrisome earnings reports from two large technology companies.

The S&P 500, a benchmark for the U. S. stock market, tumbled around 1.2 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite sank more than 2 percent. Both indexes posted their largest one-day declines of the month.

Earning reports from tech giants Tesla and Alphabet in the second quarter fanned broader concerns in the market about runaway spending on artificial intelligence.

Alphabet said that it expects its spending to total between $195 billion and $205 billion in 2026, up around $15 billion from its forecast earlier this year. Its stock slid nearly 7 percent. Tesla’s profits of $1.1 billion fell short of investors’ estimates of $1.3 billion, sending its stock spiraling down around 14.5 percent.

Shares of other large tech companies like Intel, AMD and Amazon were also sharply lower on Thursday.

How the tech-heavy index in the United States is trading

Note: Data delayed at least 15 minutes.

Source: FactSet.

The New York Times

Investors also grappled Thursday with rising oil prices, as strikes on tankers in the Red Sea by the Iranian-backed Houthi militia group added to fears about the flow of oil out of the Middle East. That uncertainty pushed the global price of oil past $100 a barrel, the highest since May.

Shipping traffic has slowed to a trickle since the Houthi threat. Only 15 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, according to Kpler, a maritime data firm. That was roughly in line with recent days, and well below prewar traffic levels of around 130 ships per day.

The conflict is widening at a vulnerable time for energy markets. Oil stockpiles are smaller than they were when U. S.-Israeli strikes on Iran began at the end of February, and Ukrainian attacks have severely damaged Russian refineries, tightening supplies of transportation fuels like diesel.

Gas prices in the United States rose 3 cents on Thursday, to $4.09 a gallon, according to the AAA motor club. The national average price at the pump has risen 37 percent since the war began.

Gas prices usually trail crude oil increases or drops by a few days. Many of the world’s refineries are offline or producing less after sustaining damage in the Persian Gulf and Russia, straining fuel markets.

Another signal of market worry is the rising yield on the 10-year Treasury, which helps set borrowing rates for companies and consumers. On Thursday, the yield reached 4.7 percent, its highest level in a year.

As oil prices climb more steeply, the market is anticipating higher inflation, analysts at Deutsche Bank noted, pricing in “a more hawkish path for central banks.”

The European Central Bank held interest rates steady on Thursday, after raising them at its meeting in June. Investors’ attention is now turning to the Federal Reserve, which meets next week. Futures markets are implying a 36 percent chance of a rate increase when officials meet.

Jenny Gross, Shirin Hakim and Pranav Baskar contributed reporting.

Aruni Soni is a business reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Four Young Mathematicians Receive Prestigious Fields Medals

The New York Times July 23, 2026

2026 Fields Medalists

Advertisement

Supported by

The awards are bestowed only once every four years to mathematicians under the age of 40.

By Kenneth Chang

Four mathematicians whose work covers areas like algebraic geometry and partial differential equations are the latest recipients of the Fields Medals, an award that is given out every four years to the brightest young researchers in the field.

This year’s recipients, announced on Thursday during the International Congress of Mathematics in Philadelphia, solved cutting-edge problems, including one that seemed like a simple puzzle of geometry and another that derived a fundamental equation that describes the motion of gases.

The medalists include two people who were born in China — Yu Deng, 37, a professor at the University of Chicago, and Hong Wang, 35, a professor at New York University and the Institute for Advanced Scientific Studies in France. This is the first time the cadre of Fields winners includes more than one Asian mathematician. Dr. Wang is also just the third woman to receive a Fields.

The other two medalists are Jacob Tsimerman, 38, a professor at the University of Toronto, and John Pardon, 37, a professor at Stony Brook University on Long Island.

The honor is accompanied by 15,000 Canadian dollars, or about $10,600, and a gold coin with the face of Archimedes, an ancient Greek mathematician.

The congress, which is the world’s largest and most prestigious gathering of mathematicians, comes as the field faces upheaval from artificial intelligence, which is quickly gaining skills that rival those of human mathematicians.

On Sunday, a mathematician reported that he and friends had disproved a conjecture that had first been proposed in 1939. Using the Fable A. I. model from Anthropic, they found a counterexample while watching the World Cup final.

The counterexample was easily checked, leaving no doubt that the result was valid.

The congress will include talks about how A. I. and other tools like software that checks proofs are changing mathematics.

One of the Fields winners, Dr. Tsimerman, is even changing the focus of his research to studying the mathematical foundations of A. I. systems to better understand how they work and help avoid unintended consequences.

John Charles Fields, a Canadian mathematician, conceived of the medals in the 1920s, and the first medals were awarded in 1936. They are unusual among top academic honors in that they go to people who are still early in their careers, showcasing not only their accomplishments but also their promise.

To be eligible, a mathematician must be under the age of 40 on Jan. 1 of the year of the award. Because the medals are bestowed only once every four years, the Fields add prestige through rarity — which makes them somewhat akin to Olympic medals.

Another mathematics award, the Abel Prize, is modeled after the Nobel Prize and recognizes lifetime achievements.

The International Mathematical Union, which administers the Fields Medals, informed the recipients several months ago, but they were told to keep it secret until the official announcement on Thursday at the International Congress of Mathematicians, the world’s largest gathering of mathematicians.

The news leaked last week after hackers discovered the names, which had been poorly hidden on the website for the meeting.

“Some of my friends congratulated me, saying that they guessed maybe this is true and then they want to congratulate me,” Dr. Wang said. “But I didn’t give them any confirmation.”

Kenneth Chang, a science reporter at The Times, covers NASA and the solar system, and research closer to Earth.

ICE Targets ‘Detention Desert’ With New Facility in North Carolina

The New York Times July 23, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Even as ICE has retreated from its plan to buy warehouses, the new complex near the Virginia border signals that the agency remains determined to increase its detention capacity.

By Eduardo Medina and Hamed Aleaziz

Eduardo Medina reported from Hertford County, N. C.

For weeks, residents near the long-dormant Rivers Correctional Institution in Winton, N. C., have noticed trucks inside the prison’s gates, people walking around the entrance and fences being erected.

Internal documents obtained by The New York Times show that U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to open a detention center at the complex in northeastern North Carolina by the end of the year. The facility is owned by GEO Group, one of the largest private prison operators in the country. Contract negotiations are ongoing, but the documents show that the facility will have about 1,400 beds, making it among the largest detention centers on the East Coast.

The opening of the facility — the first of its kind in North Carolina — signals that even as ICE has been retreating from its plan to buy up warehouses around the country, it remains determined to increase its capacity for detaining people as part of the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

Documents obtained by The Times in June show that ICE plans to offload seven warehouses that it bought for more than $700 million, scaling back a signature initiative under the previous homeland security secretary, Kristi Noem. The Department of Homeland Security sent a letter to Pennsylvania officials this month saying that it no longer planned to use a warehouse in Berks County.

But it continues to partner with private companies like GEO Group to repurpose existing prison complexes in places like North Carolina, Colorado and Arizona, all of which have large immigrant populations.

The agency has to find bed space in places that are perceived as “more friendly” toward such facilities and do not prohibit them, said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former ICE official who has served in Republican and Democratic administrations.

At the same time, North Carolina and its surrounding states are a so-called detention desert. Most detainees in the region are often taken to facilities farther south — as happened during the immigration crackdown in Charlotte last year — which costs more time, money and resources. Immigration lawyers and advocates say that a new detention center near the Virginia border could greatly increase agents’ capacity to detain more people across neighboring states.

North Carolina, which has a powerful Republican-controlled legislature, also recently passed laws that require sheriffs and state law enforcement agencies to cooperate with ICE, which is likely to increase the need for capacity.

The Winton facility is poised to make North Carolina a major hub for ICE detentions along the East Coast, said Stefanía Arteaga, the co-founder of Carolina Migrant Network, an immigrant rights group.

The internal documents show that the ICE field office in Washington plans to manage the detention center. A state official, who requested anonymity to discuss private planning, said the facility could be open as soon as late September.

The contract negotiations have not been made public by GEO Group, which did not respond to requests seeking comment. A spokesperson for ICE said in a statement that the agency had “no new detention centers to announce at this time.”

“It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U. S. and is actively working to expand detention space,” the statement said.

Since President Trump took office in January 2025, federal immigration agents have arrested more than 6,300 people in North Carolina, which is double the number of arrests made during the previous two years combined, according to the Deportation Data Project, an academic group.

In Hertford County, N. C., whose county seat is Winton, some local officials have expressed concerns about being kept in the dark over the federal government’s plans, as they try to manage all the speculation. The county is heavily Democratic.

“This is the most divisive issue that we’ve had in this area,” said Mayor Weyling J. White of Ahoskie, about 10 miles from Winton, noting that he had major reservations about having an ICE-operated facility nearby. “What kind of quality of life do those jobs bring?”

The county, which has a population of less than 20,000, is predominantly Black with pockets of Haitian and Mexican communities. Its poverty rate is about 23 percent, nearly double the statewide rate.

It also sits in a competitive congressional district, currently held by Representative Don Davis, a Democrat. The district was redrawn last year to favor the Republican candidate, Laurie Buckhout, a retired Army colonel. Neither candidate responded to requests for comment on Thursday. Gov. Josh Stein, a Democrat, also did not respond to a request for comment about the facility.

Well-paying jobs are scarce in the county, so some see the new ICE detention center as an economic lifeline. Others worry about becoming another flashpoint in the immigration crackdown and serving as an outpost for a deeply polarizing federal agency.

The former Rivers Correctional Institution, which closed in 2021 as the Biden administration moved to end federal contracts with for-profit prisons, also has a history of poor conditions.

A federal report of private prisons in 2016 found that Rivers had the highest rates of inmate-on-inmate sexual misconduct, violence, contraband finds (excluding cellphones) and positive drug tests. More recently, prisons across the state have struggled to find employees, and it is unclear how Rivers would fare if it reopened.

“Part of my worry is that we’re not prepared for what’s going to happen when that place opens,” said Jennifer Smyth, who teaches English to nonnative speakers in Hertford County. Even if the county doesn’t see more ICE arrests, she says she worries about increased activity in other parts of the state.

Residents say the financial struggles and need for job creation are evident: Downtown Winton has several abandoned buildings, and the surrounding infrastructure is easily prone to flooding.

But a steel manufacturer is expected to bring more than 700 high-paying jobs to Hertford County by 2030. On GEO Group’s website, there is one job posting for a facility maintenance manager in Rivers; the pay minimum is $72,800.

Leroy Douglas, a Hertford County commissioner who politically identifies as an independent, said the two recent fatal shootings by ICE agents in Texas and Maine had made some residents more resistant to having an immigration detention facility in their backyard. But plenty of others, he added, approve of the plan, especially those who lost their jobs when the Rivers prison closed in 2021.

It is unclear how many locals would be employed there. In 2021, the prison employed about 300 people.

While he doesn’t agree with a lot of ICE’s aggressive tactics, Mr. Douglas said he did not believe that agents would be “running rampant around Hertford County, because that’s not what this is about.”

“If they open up, I really see no negative change in our actual community,” said Mr. Douglas, whose wife worked as a correctional officer at GEO Group decades ago before moving into administrative roles at the company. “I actually see a positive one because there would be a few more jobs.”

Mr. Douglas says he has had no communication with ICE or GEO Group leaders. Other county commissioners did not respond to requests for comment.

In Facebook posts speculating about the prison reopening, comment sections have turned into broader debates about the morality of ICE and border security.

Local activists have begun to mobilize against the facility, organizing protests and flooding county officials with questions. Bobby Ray Riddick, who retired years ago and used to work at a chicken processing plant, is one of them, with 10,000 followers on Facebook.

“This is going to be a ride that I don’t think we’re ready for,” Mr. Riddick said.

Eduardo Medina is a Times reporter covering the South. An Alabama native, he is now based in Durham, N. C.

Hamed Aleaziz covers the Department of Homeland Security and immigration policy for The Times.

The Tate Brothers, in Federal Custody, Watch Their Powerful Backers Go Quiet

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

After Andrew and Tristan Tate, prominent leaders of the so-called manosphere, were arrested in Miami, many of their onetime allies on the American right pulled back support.

By Megan TwoheyIsabella KwaiMatei Barbulescu and Alan Feuer

On Sunday morning, hours after the manosphere influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate were arrested by federal agents in Miami, one of their representatives reached out to Alina Habba.

Not long ago, Ms. Habba, a lawyer, was a vocal supporter of the Tate brothers as they faced allegations of human trafficking and other serious crimes in Romania and Britain. In a podcast appearance in January 2025, shortly after being named a counselor to President Trump, she told Andrew Tate, “I got your back over here.”

Now the brothers were in a federal detention center after Britain requested their extradition for a slew of new criminal charges there. Their representative wanted to know: Was Ms. Habba free to talk?

She did not respond, according to two people familiar with the outreach. It was a sign of the brothers’ eroding support among their onetime allies on the American right.

In recent years, the Tates had leveraged their enormous following of young men to cultivate support among Mr. Trump’s advisers, family members and other prominent conservatives. Those efforts paid off last year when, feeling pressure from members of the new Trump administration, Romanian prosecutors lifted a travel ban on the brothers, freeing them to leave the country and jet-set around the world.

But they are now facing a new level of legal jeopardy. Britain has issued 38 charges against them, including rape and sex trafficking; Andrew Tate was also charged with extreme pornography and indecent images of children. The brothers have denied all of the criminal accusations and called the charges politically motivated.

The extradition request has forced the Trump administration to participate in the process: Federal prosecutors are representing the British government’s case in a Miami court.

Mr. Trump does not plan to intervene in the case, said the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, on Thursday. And many of the Tates’ allies in the president’s orbit, who were once happy to be associated with their brand of hyper-masculinity, now appear to be backing away.

Ms. Habba, who is no longer in the administration but still speaks with Mr. Trump, wants nothing to do with the Tates, according to people familiar with her thinking.

Paul Ingrassia, the acting general counsel of the General Services Administration, who previously served on the Tates’ legal team and has lavished praise on Andrew, wrote a post on X shortly after the arrests criticizing “politically driven prosecutions.” In a call with The New York Times on Thursday, Mr. Ingrassia said the post was simply articulating his beliefs about the Constitution.

Asked if he still supported the Tates, he said, “I have no ongoing connection to them now.”

Donald Trump Jr., who once called Andrew Tate a friend and publicly defended him against previous criminal allegations, has said nothing about the arrests. Neither has his younger brother Barron Trump, who had also been friendly with Andrew. Candace Owens, a conservative commentator who backed both brothers on her popular show, has also stayed silent.

Privately, people close to Donald Jr. have played down his relationship with the Tates; one person said he had not spoken with anyone in the administration about their arrests.

Asked by The Times about his retweeting of Tristan Tate on Saturday, Roger Stone, a prominent Republican operative, said he did so before the news of their arrests. And Paolo Zampolli, a special envoy for Mr. Trump who had hosted the Tates at a party in Washington two days before the arrests, said he hadn’t realized the extent of the allegations against them.

“I didn’t know they were arrest material,” Mr. Zampolli said in an interview.

Not everyone is pulling back from the brothers. Representative Abe Hamadeh, Republican of Arizona, spoke out against their extradition, writing on social media that “political lawfare is dangerous.”

The conservative media star Tucker Carlson, who has conducted sympathetic interviews of the Tates, told The Times, without evidence, that he believed their arrests were related to their outspoken criticism of Israel.

“After decades of ignoring grooming gangs and covering for Jeffrey Epstein, the British and American governments seemed to have lost interest in prosecuting sex crimes,” Mr. Carlson said. “Then the Tate brothers criticized Israel, and I was reminded that under certain circumstances they’re willing to act.”

Joseph McBride, a longtime lawyer for the Tates, disputed that their support had eroded. He said he was not surprised that any Trump official who had previously backed the brothers was now taking a more neutral stance given the administration’s role in the legal case.

Mr. McBride said the Tates were focused on fighting the extradition request in court rather than seeking help from Mr. Trump’s circle. He said he was unaware that a representative for the Tates had contacted Ms. Habba.

“There’s no reason at this point for Trump to parachute in from Air Force One to the courtroom, because we think we’ll win in court,” Mr. McBride said.

In recent years, there has been only one instance in which the United States has refused an extradition request from Britain.

The Tates, who have American and British citizenship, made their fortunes by running an online pornography business, first in Britain and then Romania, and by selling online courses to young men. One offering was called P. H. D., for “Pimping Hoes Degree.”

Romania began its investigation into the brothers in 2022. Two years later, prosecutors in Britain charged the brothers with rape, sexual assault and human trafficking. The two countries agreed that Britain would wait to extradite the Tates until the Romanian criminal investigation was done, but that case has suffered major setbacks.

Since their release from Romania in February 2025, the Tates had been living large, spending time in the United Arab Emirates, Kazakhstan, Hong Kong and Russia. During a January visit to Miami, they made headlines when a video circulated of them partying at a club with Nicholas J. Fuentes and other far-right influencers while the song “Heil Hitler” by the rapper formerly known as Kanye West blasted from speakers.

They did not go to Britain, where they faced not only the 2024 criminal charges but continuing investigations into other accusations.

In March, a police watchdog group said it was reviewing potential misconduct by the officers who had originally investigated rape and sexual assault allegations against Andrew Tate from 2015. Shortly after, the British police reopened that investigation.

Last year, after the Tates visited Florida, the state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, opened an investigation of the brothers. His office also sent an email to Matthew Jury, a lawyer who represents several Tate accusers in Britain, promising to assist if Britain ordered their extradition, as first reported by The Times of London.

Mr. Jury’s law firm passed the message onto the home secretary through an intermediary but did not receive a response, according to a person familiar with the communication. As recently as June, the firm wrote letters to Prime Minister Keir Starmer criticizing the government’s inaction over extradition, according to The Telegraph.

That month, prosecutors in Britain, including one who specializes in cases involving child sexual images, successfully fought an effort by the brothers asking the court to disclose the names of the women in the original criminal charges.

The Tates were arrested on Saturday evening as they arrived at a bare-knuckle-boxing event that Andrew was supposed to co-host. British prosecutors said the charges stemmed from incidents that happened between July 2010 and August 2017 but did not disclose names or other identifying details.

In the days before the arrests, the brothers had been posting on social media from Washington, where they were photographed with Representative Wesley Hunt, Republican of Texas, and partied with Mr. Zampolli.

Mr. McBride said in a statement on Saturday that the extradition request was approved by a “low-level functionary at the Justice Department who never got approval from leadership.” But higher-ups in the agency did sign off on the arrests, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss it.

The Tates will remain behind bars in Florida as a federal judge considers whether Britain has met the legal threshold for extradition, a process that could take months. If the judge signs off on the extradition request, it will then go to Secretary of State Marco Rubio for final approval.

Asked about the request while traveling in Manila on Wednesday, Mr. Rubio said that while the matter is considered by the judge, “there’s no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever.”

Lauren Southern, a former conservative influencer who has accused Andrew Tate of raping her in Romania and provided testimony to Romanian authorities, was among those who celebrated news of the extradition request.

“It’s been a really wonderful weekend for those of us who are rooting for justice,” she told The Times. “Now there’s a reckoning and suddenly everyone wants to pretend they had nothing to do with building this beast.”

It is unclear where the Romanian criminal case against the brothers is headed and how it may be affected by the extradition request. The country’s foreign minister said she had not been informed about it ahead of time. A spokeswoman for Romanian prosecutors did not comment.

The Trump administration’s willingness to honor the request is fueling rifts on the American right, as Mr. Carlson, Mr. Fuentes and others seek to frame it within broader political talking points. More traditional conservatives, like Ben Shapiro, are accusing the Tates’ allies of embracing misogyny and criminal behavior.

“The conservative movement should cast them aside now, just as it should have years ago,” Mr. Shapiro told The Times.

Reporting was contributed by Michael Crowley, Shawn McCreesh, David Ovalle and Ed Wong.

Megan Twohey is an investigative reporter at The Times. Her work has prompted changes to the law, criminal convictions and cultural shifts.

Isabella Kwai is a Times reporter based in London, covering breaking news and other trends.

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Saying ‘Google It’ Makes You Sound Old. ‘Search It Up’ Instead.

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Supported by

On Language

As online research evolves, so has the language we use to describe it.

By Sophie Haigney

I have Googled thousands of things in my life. Probably hundreds of thousands. In fact, I am willing to bet I am a power Googler, engaged in a kind of continuous conversation with the search engine about all manner of questions and concerns and interests: “what happened to pippa middleton,” “weird rash on chin not itching,” “quarterly tax new york state address,” “if I have googled five things a day for 15 years how much have I googled” and so forth. My Google search bar feels sometimes like an extension of my mind, the place my idle thoughts get typed in, only to generate hundreds of thousands of new pathways for me to explore. “To Google” might be one of my most-used verbs.

But the kids these days — Gen Z and Alpha — aren’t talking about Googling things. They may still be using Google, but they’re not “Googling it.” Instead they’re saying “search it up,” as in: Who is that Norwegian soccer player with the long blond hair? Search it up. The “it” is dropped if you have a direct object, as when you “search up Erling Haaland.”

The shift toward using this phrasal verb has been profound in the youngest generations. A few years ago, a podcast called “A Way With Words” interviewed a 13-year-old who described how all her friends were using the term; one of the hosts posited that “search up” was being used by “zillions of people.” (There is even a PBS KIDS mini-series, which started in 2020, called “Search It Up!”) The other day, I spoke to an 11-year-old named Carson, who told me she uses the phrase exclusively. “I don’t think I’ve ever heard one of my friends say, ‘I Googled it,’” she said.

The phrase “search up” was added to the Cambridge Advanced Learner’s Dictionary and Thesaurus only in 2024, but it did appear in pre-internet times, with a first mention in the Oxford English Dictionary in 1529. One example sentence from 1780: “He searched up all the Hebrew copies he was able, and burnt them.” Many of the older terms describing the act of research had a foot in the physical world: “look up,” “browse” and “peruse” all conjure a literal sense of moving through sources in search of information.

“Search” started describing internet exploration near the end of the last century. The word had moved from signifying literal seeking-and-finding to something more abstract: whatever happens when we put words into an interface that, after launching automated web crawlers, spits out a page of results in a fraction of a second. “Search,” in the old sense of the word, has little to do with a process like this; it’s no wonder we sought out a new term for it.

So we came to Googling, which Merriam-Webster and the Oxford English Dictionary added to their pages as a verb in 2006. (It had already been named the “most useful word of the year” by the American Dialect Society in 2002, in a year-end collection that also included “weapons of mass destruction” and “blog.”) The first person known to use the proper noun as a verb was the Google co-founder Larry Page himself, in a 1998 signoff on a listserv: “Have fun and keep googling!” In later years, though, the company discouraged the use of “Google” as a verb for trademark reasons, worrying that it would be a victim of “genericide.” Too bad for them: We kept “Googling it.”

So why are young people abandoning the word now? Part of this shift follows a typical pattern from a branded term to a generic one. The Georgetown linguistics professor Deborah Tannen told me this change reminded her of how “Kleenex” used to be a stand-in for tissue, “Frigidaire” for refrigerator or “Levi’s” for all blue jeans. Over time, either because competitors unseated these innovators or because the novelty wore off, people switched back to the common words. “It strikes me that at the time when we started saying ‘Google it,’ Google was ‘it,’” Tannen said; other search engines like Ask Jeeves became the butts of jokes.

And in the age of Claude and ChatGPT, the old-school search engine is both less novel and less impressive. Carson, the 11-year-old, is part of a generation for whom Google is just a fact of life. “When the adults were kids, they didn’t really have Google,” she told me, “but now that we’re kids it’s more normal.” Even if young people like her choose to type their question into Google, they would be much more likely to read the Gemini summaries that Google’s own large language model spits out than to sift through the list of linked results. This shift has affected web traffic globally and has turned “search” into an action that is less and less about browsing and weighing different options from a compendium of human knowledge indexed for our own use.

Today “searching it up” via L. L. M. seems more like speaking with an oracle. (Another new phrase, “Ask ChatGPT,” emphasizes this weird deference to this nonhuman entity: We’re not searching at all but asking.) Whereas Google produced a mountain of possible answers, when you type a query into an L. L. M., you just get a single cohesive answer: a pastiche of all the results it has already trawled and compressed into a smooth-voiced mash-up.

Google’s functional monopoly on search had plenty of negative effects on the internet, so it’s hard to mourn its decline wholeheartedly. But as a mode of looking things up, I love Googling. It feels like wandering in an infinite library. Searching something up with a chatbot leads immediately to a conclusion: The journey happens without you, and the answer simply arrives. The search is over, almost as soon as it began.

Sophie Haigney is working on a book about our obsession with collecting objects, from priceless fossils to plastic Power Rangers.

U. S. to Withdraw Subpoenas Issued to New York Times Journalists

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Trump Administration

A federal judge raised questions about the government’s handling of the subpoenas, which The Times said were an attempt to intimidate the free press.

By Michael M. Grynbaum and Jonah E. Bromwich

The Justice Department said on Thursday that it would withdraw the subpoenas that sought phone records and grand jury testimony from New York Times journalists who had reported on the security capabilities of President Trump’s new Qatari-built Air Force One jet.

“The government is prepared to unilaterally withdraw the subpoenas at this time,” Sean Buckley, one of the highest-ranking officials in the U. S. attorney’s office in Manhattan, said at a hearing in U. S. District Court.

The government’s move came after Judge Arun Subramanian grilled Justice Department lawyers for nearly an hour over their handling of the subpoenas, which The Times had sought to quash. The newspaper called the subpoenas an effort to intimidate its reporters.

Judge Subramanian said the Justice Department was not prevented from subpoenaing the Times reporters again if the government followed appropriate procedures.

The case had emerged as a flashpoint in the Trump administration’s efforts to escalate pressure on independent news organizations.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

Michael M. Grynbaum writes about the intersection of media, politics and culture. He has been a media correspondent at The Times since 2016.

Key Republican Senator Says He Will Support Trump’s Pick for C. D. C. Director

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Senator Bill Cassidy, who is believed to hold the deciding vote in the Senate health committee for Dr. Erica Schwartz’s confirmation, had declined for days to say whether he would back her.

By Sheryl Gay Stolberg

President Trump’s nominee to lead the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention won the support of a crucial Republican on Thursday after a page on the agency’s website about vaccines and autism was modified to address his objections.

The page still asserts that vaccines may be linked to autism — a claim for which there is no scientific evidence and which infuriated Senator Bill Cassidy, Republican of Louisiana and the chairman of the Senate health committee, who is a physician. But the revised page now includes a fresh statement at the bottom saying scientists “have not identified the root causes” of the disorder.

The nominee, Dr. Erica Schwartz, voiced strong support for the safety and efficacy of vaccines in testimony before the panel last week. But she faced an intense grilling from Mr. Cassidy about whether she would stand up to Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whose ardent vaccine skepticism is of deep concern to the senator.

Until Thursday morning, Mr. Cassidy had declined to say whether he would vote to confirm Dr. Schwartz. In finally announcing his support for her, the senator referred to the changes to the C. D. C. website.

“As a sign of good faith, H. H. S. has now modified the C. D. C.’s autism and vaccines web page,” Mr. Cassidy said, referring to the federal Department of Health and Human Services. “There’s more to do to repair damage that has been done to the U. S. public health response, but this is a start.”

The committee, which met for a brief two minutes in public session on Thursday, was supposed to vote on Dr. Schwartz’s nomination then. But the vote was delayed until next week because of the absence of at least one other Republican, Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who was tending to a family emergency.

Mr. Cassidy, who has less than six months left in the Senate, had little incentive to please President Trump; he recently lost his primary to two other Republicans, one of whom was backed by Mr. Trump and allies of Mr. Kennedy. He also has tangled bitterly with Mr. Kennedy, particularly over the secretary’s insistence that vaccines may be linked to autism.

But Mr. Cassidy said he had decided to support Dr. Schwartz, a deputy surgeon general in the first Trump administration, after speaking with her following the hearing, reviewing the transcript and talking to people who have worked with her.

“C. D. C. needs someone who understands that the way to prevent vaccine-preventable diseases is to reassure the public that vaccines are safe and effective,” Mr. Cassidy said on Thursday. Of Dr. Schwartz, he added, “I’m confident that she knows what she is doing and will stand against those who do not.”

With Mr. Cassidy’s announcement, and the decision to wait for all Republicans to be present for the vote, it appears likely that Dr. Schwartz’s nomination will be approved and forwarded to the full Senate, probably on a party-line vote.

The panel’s ranking member, Senator Bernie Sanders, independent of Vermont, said he was impressed with Dr. Schwartz, who is a lawyer as well as a physician. Mr. Sanders also said he shared Mr. Cassidy’s concerns about “major public health crises” and “conspiracy theorists telling parents all over this country that vaccines don’t work or vaccines are dangerous.”

But he said he would vote against her, because he is not convinced that Dr. Schwartz would be able to stand up to Mr. Kennedy, who runs the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the C. D. C.

“I am afraid that right now within H. H. S. we have a secretary who will not tolerate dissent,” Mr. Sanders said.

Last year, Mr. Kennedy ordered the C. D. C. to change its website on vaccines and autism by abandoning its longstanding position that the two are not linked. The updated web page kept the old headline — “Autism and Vaccines” — and added an asterisk saying the headline remained intact only because of a promise to Mr. Cassidy.

The page still says the statement that vaccines do not cause autism “is not an evidence-based claim.” But the reference to Mr. Cassidy has been removed and the asterisk is now followed by a new statement.

“Scientists have not identified the root causes of autism,” the page now says, adding that Mr. Kennedy’s department “continues to support rigorous scientific research and will update this page as reliable new evidence becomes available.”

The C. D. C. has been without a permanent leader for all but one month of Mr. Trump’s second administration, as the president has struggled to find someone acceptable to the Senate. He withdrew the name of his first nominee, Dr. David Weldon, a former Florida congressman, after Dr. Weldon could not garner enough Republican support.

His second nominee, Susan Monarez, was confirmed but the White House fired her at Mr. Kennedy’s urging just 29 days later.

The agency has been run for nearly a year on an acting basis, most recently by Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the director of the National Institutes of Health.

Sheryl Gay Stolberg is a correspondent based in Washington for The Times, covering Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and President Trump’s health agenda.

House Rebukes Trump on Iran as Senate Blocks Debate

The New York Times July 23, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

For the second time, a few House Republicans joined Democrats to back a measure calling on the president to seek authorization for the war.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

The House on Thursday voted a second time to direct President Trump to end the war in Iran or seek explicit authorization to continue it, dealing him another bipartisan rebuke as he again ramps up military operations in the Middle East without approval from Congress.

Four Republicans joined Democrats in backing the measure, which does not have the force of law but is the latest evidence of disapproval on Capitol Hill with Mr. Trump’s handling of the conflict. Not long afterward, Republicans blocked a similar measure from consideration in the Senate, after key G. O. P. skeptics of the war either changed their stance or did not vote.

The House action came after the United States concluded its 12th consecutive night of strikes in Iran, following the collapse of a cease-fire that many Republicans had hoped would yield a diplomatic breakthrough to wind down the war well before they must face voters in November’s midterm elections.

The measure passed on a vote of 214 to 208. The Republicans who joined Democrats in favor were Representatives Tom Barrett of Michigan, Warren Davidson of Ohio, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania and Thomas Massie of Kentucky. That was the same quartet that helped Democrats push through a similar war powers resolution last month.

“My position hasn’t changed,” Mr. Barrett, who is among the most politically vulnerable Republicans in the House, said in a statement after the vote. “Only Congress has the authority to authorize military action in Iran. I remain ready to work with anyone to eliminate hostile threats to our nation without getting us into another endless war.”

The resolution, sponsored by Representative Pramila Jayapal, Democrat of Washington, was among the final matters the House voted on before leaving Washington for a five-week summer recess. Many Democrats predicted that members of Congress would hear from voters during the break about how frustrated they are with the course of the war.

A Washington Post-Ipsos poll released last week found that only 29 percent of Americans support the war in Iran. A POLITICO poll found that Trump supporters who identified as “MAGA” voters said there were conditions to their continued support, with 37 percent saying they would only continue backing the conflict so long as prices for Americans did not rise. Global oil prices hit $100 a barrel on Thursday for the first time since May.

Representative Jason Crow, Democrat of Colorado, said that the waning public support would likely push more Republican lawmakers to speak out more forcefully against the Trump administration’s unilateral approach to the war.

“When we come back in September, I bet we have more people joining with us saying, ‘All right, let’s wrap this up,’ ” he said on Thursday.

The House vote underscored the growing divide between Republicans on Capitol Hill and the White House as the war in Iran drags on.

A growing group of Republican lawmakers has become more vocal about questioning the lack of congressional authorization or consultation, and also the administration’s failure to lay out a clear endgame. But Mr. Trump has shown no willingness to involve the legislative branch and little sign of winding down the campaign. Instead, he has escalated his bellicose language and asserted that he has unchecked power to continue the military operation.

Mr. Trump brushed aside Congress’s earlier rebukes last month, when the House and Senate both passed a similar measure, the first time since the conflict began in February that lawmakers voted to disapprove of it.

House Republican leaders are now pressing forward with a budget plan that would pay for the war, putting their members in the politically unappealing position of voting to finance an unpopular conflict that the Republican-led Congress has not authorized, and over which it has exercised little oversight.

In the face of Mr. Trump’s disregard for the congressional action, Representative Gregory W. Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, said that he had begun the process to file a lawsuit against the administration for ignoring the resolutions.

“We have a situation where we’ve passed, now twice, war powers resolutions,” Mr. Meeks said in an interview on Thursday. “The president should not be able to get around this.”

In the Senate on Thursday, a similar resolution stalled after only one Republican, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, backed it.

Senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican who previously voted to direct Mr. Trump to end hostilities or seek authorization to continue them, changed his stance. Senators Rand Paul of Kentucky and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, two other Republicans who had backed similar efforts, did not vote.

It was the 12th time Democrats had forced such a vote, and they vowed to continue doing so as they implored Republicans to stop deferring to Mr. Trump and join the effort to wind down the war.

“As the war escalates even further, as more American service members are killed, as more civilians are killed, as oil and gas prices and other prices go up, this is an opportunity for this Congress to finally take responsibility,” Senator Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland Democrat who sponsored the measure, said before the vote. “We know the president has no respect for the law, but we have an obligation to our constituents. We should not duck that responsibility.”

Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, was the only member of his party to oppose it, in line with his past votes on the issue.

Mr. Cassidy said he had switched his position after multiple briefings by administration officials, though he still had concerns about the conflict.

“Now, do I approve how the war is being carried out? Not necessarily,” he said on Thursday. But he said he was not comfortable calling for an immediate withdrawal.

Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican who opposed Thursday’s measure as he has previous such efforts, said that he might change his stance should the conflict continue to drag on. But he noted that presidents of both parties have at various times dodged the statute requiring consultation with Congress on military engagements.

“My rationalization for not really applying the War Powers Act earlier is all the games that have been played,” Mr. Tillis said. Given Mr. Trump’s formal notification to Congress on July 10 that hostilities with Iran had resumed, he said the president should have until Sept. 10 — the end of a 60-day window laid out in the war powers law — to act without authorization from Congress. (The 1973 law actually forbids the president from ordering American forces into a conflict without congressional approval unless the United States is under attack, but it provides a 60-day clock to terminate such an operation if he has not secured authorization.)

“The clock is ticking,” Mr. Tillis said.

But close allies of the president noted that he had repeatedly ignored what Congress had to say on the matter.

“Do you think he cares?” Senator Tommy Tuberville, Republican of Alabama, said on Thursday with a chuckle. “No.”

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

Modi Caught Off Guard as India’s Economic Failings Inflame Young People

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Global Economy

Advertisement

Supported by

Prime Minister Narendra Modi was busy trying to put out other fires when a student movement suddenly exploded. There are no easy solutions to the problems behind it.

By Alex Travelli

Reporting from New Delhi

Narendra Modi, the powerful and acutely image-conscious prime minister of India, is suddenly facing a political problem he had not anticipated on entering his 13th year in office.

Mr. Modi has had his eye trained on economic anxieties for much of the year, which were sharpened by the external effects of the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran. His government had to manage shortages of imported oil and gas, distributing the costs among businesses and ordinary citizens.

But it was another sort of economic pressure that has now caught up with him and helped drive thousands of students to protest in the capital: The crumbling and sometimes crooked machinery of India’s underfunded education system, along with a painful lack of jobs for the millions of graduates it produces.

After 25 days of protest, and nearly three days since police used batons and tear gas to disperse protesters, Mr. Modi was still struggling for a meaningful response. On Thursday, he posted on social media that “Nothing is more important than the welfare and future of our youth!” He has promised fast-track tribunals to punish the individuals who spoiled the exam but nothing else.

This sounded both late and lame to the protesters who were on the street, infuriating many of them further. The movement’s demands are widening rapidly from their initial complaints focused on over accountability for the scrapping of a college-entrance exam to, among other things, compensation for the protesters injured in clashes on Monday.

Many of the protesters are students, and many others have jobs, but they share a sense of desperation and rage about education and employment prospects. Smaller protests have emerged in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Ahmedabad and other cities, raising demands that Mr. Modi will find difficult if not impossible to answer in the short term.

Arsh Gupta, a 20-year-old college student, said “there are a lot of feelings” that brought him to the central protest site on Thursday. The original testing failure “is not a small thing at all,” he said, but he was driven more by other issues, most of all “the feeling that we’re living under a dictatorship.”

At the forefront of the protests is the Cockroach Janta Party, not an actual political party but a movement that takes its name from an insult made by the chief justice of India’s Supreme Court. It is taking aim at these much longer-term crises. The education system is in disarray, the C. J. P.’s spokesmen said, demanding that corrupt and bungling officials must face accountability.

India’s economy may be growing at a healthy rate, but it offers the protesters little hope. While the gross rate of unemployment looks low, recorded as between 4 and 7 percent, most workers fall outside the formal sector and never get counted. Young adults, especially those who have earned degrees and want to put them to use, are the most frustrated. Nearly 40 percent are unemployed, according to the State of Working India 2026 report published by Azim Premji University.

The protesters’ anger intensified after Monday’s show of force by the police, and appears to have turned against the whole of India’s government.

None of this was on Mr. Modi’s menu for 2026.

The Iran war presented a tough series of challenges but also an opportunity to make a fresh break. Economic difficulties had been piling up for months while Mr. Modi’s party was also fighting to win power in a series of state elections.

After winning control of state governments culminating with West Bengal in May, Mr. Modi turned to keeping down inflation and reining in the public’s expectations.

Mr. Modi started warning Indians that painful times were coming. Food prices were rising, and the rupee was nose-diving.

Around the same time, it emerged that the questions to a national medical college entrance exam had been leaked, so the results for millions of students were canceled. The C. J. P. took up the test-takers’ cause almost instantly.

The protest’s leadership is, however, dispersed and nonprofessional. That makes it unlike the farmers who staged a siege-like protest around Delhi for more than a year from 2020 to 2021, or even a current protest on behalf of Jammu and Kashmir, whose elected leader is trying to restore its statehood.

These mostly middle-class protesters cannot easily be made to look marginal.

Nor can the issues they raise be answered overnight. The causes of India’s jobs crisis have been brewing for a long time. A great deal of students’ time and their families’ money has been invested in courses that routinely fail to equip them for the workplace.

Amit Basole, an economist and lead author of the State of Working India report, noted that young graduates in India have always been disproportionately unemployed. But their number has grown terrifically in recent years, along with the debt their families owe for their educations.

“It’s a systematic failure. If the government’s not responsible, then who is?” asked Pranavi Tripathi, a 22-year-old business graduate protesting in Delhi on Thursday.

Alex Travelli is a correspondent based in New Delhi, writing about business and economic developments in India and the rest of South Asia.
