The Conversation

By Frank Bruni and Bret Stephens

Mr. Bruni is a contributing Opinion writer; Mr. Stephens is an Opinion columnist.

Frank Bruni: Bret, our unctuous and unctuously coiffed defense secretary just strutted over to Congress and requested something like five gazillion dollars so that we can win a war that President Trump repeatedly assured us we’d already won. Please tell me that even a hawk like you doesn’t want to give Pete Hegseth that kind of blank check.

Bret Stephens: First of all, I love the word unctuous; it reminds me of Mr. Collins in “Pride and Prejudice.” When it comes to Hegseth, other words that come to mind are oleaginous, turgescent, bombastic and insufferable. Second, in terms of funding, I’d give him even more than he asked for.

Frank: You must be kidding. You’re setting up a punchline, right? Hit me with it.

Bret: Totally serious. The Iran war has exposed serious shortages in our weapon stockpiles, especially the kinds of precision munitions like Tomahawk cruise missiles and Patriot interceptor missiles that we will need in large quantities in the event of a war over Taiwan or some other emergency. This should actually be a bipartisan issue: Jake Sullivan, President Biden’s national security adviser, has also warned about these kinds of critical shortages. And we also need to invest in critical infrastructure that can protect our troops in the age of cheap drones. The Times published an alarming and highly detailed editorial series in December making these very points.

Frank: One big problem with your position is that it doesn’t take into account which government officials are getting this titanic pile of money and whether they can be trusted with it. Members of the Trump administration can’t. We’ve seen that, on the military front, in ways both specific and general. Specific: Many experts believe that those “Trump class” warships that he demanded are as much about his ego as about the nature of future warfare. General: We’re locked in this Iran debacle not because of our arsenal but because of our asinine leaders, whose planning was so amateurish — so frat-house — that it didn’t even take into account the possible closing of the Strait of Hormuz. Yeah, let’s shower these incompetents with tens of billions more.

Bret: The problem you’re putting your finger on is real: How can anyone trust this crew with anything? Except that investments in military spending are long-term and future presidents will have to rely on some of the decisions of this one to defend us and our allies at some later date. For instance, I don’t think it should be controversial, in the era of Russian or Iranian ballistic missile salvos, for the U. S. to invest heavily in ballistic missile defense, or in fielding unmanned weapons at scale, or in replacing our aging fleet of B-52 and B-1 bombers with the stealthy B-21 that is already in test flights. Leaving the Trump battleships aside, which will almost certainly never be built, the public needs to understand that military affairs are undergoing a revolution and we need to master it.

As for Iran, I’m hoping Trump destroys Iran’s one remaining undamaged nuclear site and, in defense of international law, forces Iran to open the strait. I’m less worried about his hawkishness than I am about his TACO tendency.

Frank: Your hope, when it comes to Trump and Iran, is impressively and poignantly durable.

Bret: You’re being very polite in not calling me certifiably deluded.

Frank: My mother raised me right. And I know, from having broken bread with your charming mother, that she did the same with you.

Let’s pivot from all this weapons talk. How is it that we have limitless resources for a disastrously executed military engagement and such finite amounts for other matters of public safety? It will be a while before we have full clarity on whether and how this cyclospora outbreak could have been prevented, but there’s no doubt that Trump’s cuts — and such madness as putting Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in charge of Americans’ physical well-being — are already seriously hurting Americans while leaving us vulnerable to more and worse. This administration doesn’t care much for inspections and medical expertise. Mustn’t coddle the elites and mustn’t get in the way of corporate profit. Is an America made great again one in which we interrupt our watching bombs fall with trips back and forth to the toilet? More munitions, more adult diapers: the Trump legacy, at least metaphorically.

Bret: I think that what you are saying is a bit of a myth. We were spending close to 5 percent of our gross domestic product on defense in 2010, when Barack Obama was president. Last year we spent just over 3 percent. That’s historically low. Most of the federal budget goes to programs like Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid, veterans benefits and debt service, not defense. And in terms of cyclospora, aside from giving me a new word for everything that comes out of JD Vance’s mouth, I think it’s sorta unfair to blame any official, even Bobby Kennedy Jr., for the kind of outbreak that could happen in virtually any administration, Republican or Democratic.

Frank: I’m so glad you brought up Vance. It gives us a point of agreement, which I shall turn into a point of tension in just a bit. But first: Thank you for your recent column about him, in which you wrote: “The prospect of this callow and sinister opportunist taking the place of the erratic buffoon now governing us may be the single scariest thought in world politics today.” I could hug you. I could kiss you. I’ll chastely stop there.

Bret: Let me go on the record right here: Even as I would gladly vote for Marco Rubio over nearly any Democrat, I will vote for any Democrat in 2028 over Vance.

Frank: Uh-oh. There goes the promised point of tension. I was planning — given all the chatter about her lately — to ask you if you’d vote for Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez over Vance?

Bret: Yes. At least she’s evolving in a mildly saner direction. And she’s probably now found Taiwan on the map.

Frank: Gavin Newsom? You’ve lavished many withering paragraphs on him.

Bret: Gulping hard, but yes. Newsom is bottomlessly vain, frequently wrong and slicker than an oil spill: in other words, a typical politician who, to his credit, sometimes learns from his mistakes. Vance is purely opportunistic and infinitely malleable, a Looney Tunes conspiracy theorist who gives me the creeps.

Frank: Bernie Sanders, running on a ticket with Abdul El-Sayed?

Bret: Can you suggest another veep? But as far as Bernie is concerned, a spell of socialism, straight up no chaser, would have the silver lining of giving future generations permanent intellectual immunity against that temptation.

Frank: I find Vance fascinating. That’s not a compliment. Trump comes by his awfulness honestly, organically; he really can’t be anything other than his congenitally wretched self. Vance is all oxymoronically cloddish guile. It’s so telling that this second memoir of his, “Communion,” styles him as deeply religious. As a man of scruples. I call that camouflage. I file it under the doth-protest-too-much principle, though maybe it’s actual self-delusion. Thoughts?

Bret: Years ago, a friend of mine from high school began taking his Catholicism seriously; it made him a kinder, humbler, more self-aware and consistently decent person. Vance’s conversion seems to have accomplished the exact opposite. His model for a pope isn’t Leo XIV but Pius XII. He’s all Borgia, zero Wojtyla. He is using his conversion as a springboard to power, not as a shield against power’s temptations.

Frank: It offends me deeply when Vance or anyone else does that — and many, many people do that. It’s such an injustice to those among us, like your high school friend, who are genuinely faithful and well intentioned. I don’t want to feel cynical about religion. The Christopher Hitchens camp never appealed to me. It doesn’t adequately take into account how much good happens because of the do-gooders’ spiritual prompts.

Bret: Agree. Isaiah Berlin was right when he said that “dry atheists seem to me blind and deaf to some forms of profound human experience.”

Frank: But there’s a big chunk of the MAGAverse for whom the pantomime of religion permits as many of the seven deadly sins as they wish to rack up. (And they’re racking like crazy these days, with greed and gluttony getting especially vigorous workouts.) Mouth enough dogma, sprinkle your conversation with enough references to Christ, maybe drape a cross around your neck, and all manner of cruelty and corruption is forgiven. Seems to be Hegseth’s calculation.

Bret: That’s been an issue with Republicans for a long time, and with any political movement that sets itself up as the camp of virtue: They oppose all vices except the ones to which they happen to be drawn. In fact, if there’s one saving grace to Trump, it’s that he never really presented himself as anyone’s idea of a saint. And he tore the mask off some of the hypocritical primness that used to define the party. Notice that I’m saying something modestly nice about Trump, who, as you rightly noted, has an ineradicable authenticity that Vance can never have.

Frank: Even Trump and Vance can’t ruin many of this country’s greatest sources of pleasure and pride. Like … ranch dressing!

There was much written during the World Cup about foreign visitors’ infatuation with various quirks of American cuisine and culture, and in The Wall Street Journal, Ben Cohen noted their affinity for ranch dressing, which coincided with the Hidden Valley Ranch brand’s efforts to expand ranch’s reach. Here’s a paragraph on that, referring to Nick Higgins, the brand’s general manager:

Inside the Hidden Valley headquarters in Oakland, Calif., Higgins and his colleagues study all kinds of food and ask themselves a simple question: Will it ranch? The answer is yes. Of course it will ranch. Veggies, salads, pizza, wings, fries, caviar, pickles, cottage cheese, ice cream — they’re all eminently ranchable. And now that anything can be ranched, everything is getting ranched.

That’s American ingenuity, Bret!

Bret: And one more Journal story of note: As the tournament drew to a close, the paper’s Joshua Robinson and Jonathan Clegg reported on another way visitors fell for the States, no matter their feelings about our politics:

They fell in love with the hash browns at Waffle House. They discovered the brisket sandwich of Buc-ee’s. They lamented the lack of public transportation options, then marveled at Waymo. All of it was eye-opening. The scale of our shopping malls, the size of our highways and the cornucopia that is the Costco frozen-food aisle.

Always nice to be reminded — Vance et al. to the dismaying contrary notwithstanding — that there’s really something precious to this land of ours.

F. D. A. Announces New Cyclosporiasis Outbreak with 72 Cases

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

Health officials did not identify the location of the outbreak, or what they believed was causing it.

By Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

The Food and Drug Administration has identified a new outbreak of cyclosporiasis that has sickened at least 72 people, according to an update posted to the agency’s website late Wednesday.

The additional outbreak comes in the midst of the nation’s worst year on record for the intestinal illness, which is caused by a parasite transmitted through food or water contaminated with human feces.

The agency has not yet provided information about the source of the new outbreak or its location. The F. D. A. is currently investigating five other clusters of cyclosporiasis cases, including an ongoing outbreak of at least 1,644 illnesses in Michigan, Ohio, West Virginia, Indiana and Kentucky that has been linked to shredded iceberg lettuce sold by Taylor Farms and grown in central Mexico. Last Friday, Taylor Farms announced that it was recalling shredded iceberg lettuce products from 27 states, but did not disclose where these products had been sold or how consumers could spot them.

The announcement of a new outbreak means that the F. D. A. has identified a cluster of cases that appear to be connected to a common source — such as the same type of produce or the same event or restaurant, said Frank Yiannas, a food safety expert and former top official at the F. D. A.

The fact that the F. D. A. has listed the 72 cases as a separate outbreak does not necessarily mean that these new cases are entirely unrelated to the larger outbreak centered in Michigan, said Felicia Wu, a professor of food safety, toxicology and risk assessment at Michigan State University.

The agency may have listed the outbreak separately from the one centered in Michigan because they believe it is linked to a different food, or is affecting people in a different part of the country, but it may turn out that the strain of cyclospora is the same as the parasite affecting thousands of people in the Midwest.

While investigators can use genomics to quickly and definitively link food-borne illnesses caused by bacteria, it’s difficult to study the DNA from parasites. So it’s possible investigators don’t yet know whether the different outbreaks are connected. We’re in a “wait-and-see situation,” Dr. Wu said.

On Tuesday, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced that there were more than 11,000 cases of cyclosporiasis nationwide that were either confirmed or under investigation. Since 2016, the C. D. C. has reported an average of about 2,800 cases per year nationwide.

Because the parasite thrives in warmer temperatures, it’s normal to see an uptick in cyclosporiasis cases between May 1 and Aug. 31. But experts say that this year’s surge exceeds the typical summer increase.

“This year is a terrible year” for cyclospora, Mr. Yiannas said — adding that the number of cases we’ve seen so far is “unheard of.”

The F. D. A. is currently investigating an unusually large number of food-borne outbreaks — not just those caused by cyclospora, but also salmonella, listeria, E. coli and clostridium botulinum. The agency has 16 active outbreak investigations listed on its website, which may be a record for the number of ongoing investigations at the same time, said Susan Mayne, who led the agency’s Center for Food Safety and Nutrition from 2015 to 2023.

The large number of outbreaks comes after significant staffing losses at the C. D. C. and F. D. A., as well as at state and local public health departments, which are on the front lines of investigating food-borne illnesses. “The C. D. C.-F. D. A. teams working on food-borne illness outbreaks, along with state partners, are trying to do more and more with less and less,” Dr. Mayne said.

The F. D. A. and C. D. C. did not respond to requests for comment.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

U. S.-Saudi Deal Prompts Fears of a Global Nuclear Arms Race

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

In Europe, Asia and the Middle East, countries seek nuclear capabilities to hedge against aggressive neighbors and a receding Washington, potentially creating a more freewheeling era.

By Mark Landler

Reporting from Paris

When President Dwight D. Eisenhower went to the United Nations in 1953 to offer countries nuclear technology and know-how in return for a promise to use them peacefully, the policy went by a memorable shorthand, “Atoms for Peace.” Seven decades later, it could go by a less idealistic name: nuclear hedging.

President Trump’s civil nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, announced this week, reflects a volatile world in which America’s allies are seeking nuclear capabilities to hedge against predatory neighbors, harmful energy disruptions and the shrinking security umbrella of the United States. It also reflects a White House, hungry for lucrative deals for American companies, that is willing to loosen nonproliferation standards for a favored partner in a dangerous region.

Saudi Arabia’s deal could eventually allow it to enrich fuel for nuclear reactors and limit the sites that international inspectors could visit to ensure its peaceful intent. Both of those concessions, unheard-of in recent American civil nuclear agreements, will feed fears that the Saudis could pivot to a nuclear weapons program.

Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the de facto Saudi leader, has made no secret of that possibility. If Iran obtains a nuclear bomb, he has warned, the Saudis will follow suit.

Mr. Trump sought to allay such concerns on Thursday, declaring that the agreement was limited to civil uses of nuclear technology. But given the checkered history of such deals, and the lack of specifics about this one, his comments were unlikely to quell concerns about a new global arms race.

“We’re back in an era of nuclear hedging,” said Vipin Narang, a professor of nuclear security and political science at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “You’ve got a lot of nervous countries facing a deteriorating security situation who are unsure they can rely on their formal or informal protectors.”

“We’re going to see a cascade of states looking for the capacity to pursue a military program” that could yield a weapon, said Professor Narang, who worked on nuclear policy in the Pentagon during the Biden administration.

Gary Samore, a professor of politics at Brandeis University who advised on arms control negotiations in the Obama and Clinton administrations, said those countries were sometimes referred to as “friendly proliferators.”

Not all, or even any, of them will ultimately pursue a bomb, the experts said. The last country to enter the club of nuclear-armed states was North Korea in 2006. But it does suggest a risky new period, in which the global nuclear market could become more freewheeling and less rulebound. Nuclear buyers, rattled by the shift in the global posture of the United States, are likely to make greater demands, while rival sellers, like Russia and China, could seize on the Saudi precedent to grant them.

“It’s very connected to the damage Trump has done to credibility of the U. S. as a guarantor of security,” Mr. Samore said.

In countries such as Germany and Poland, South Korea and Japan, governments without nuclear weapons are debating the need to pursue them. South Korea, menaced by the nuclear-armed North, has initiated a plan to develop a fleet of nuclear-powered submarines, with the support of the United States.

The Japanese defense minister, Shinjiro Koizumi, said this week that his country needed to confront the role of nuclear weapons in its defense, despite a longstanding aversion rooted in the wartime destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, has said that his country should pursue a nuclear program, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany has joined a high-level nuclear steering group with France and other European countries.

France, which along with Britain is one of Western Europe’s two nuclear powers, has vowed to expand its arsenal and offer a form of extended deterrence to its neighbors to compensate for Mr. Trump’s pulling back. In a show of cooperation, Paris recently sent a nuclear-capable fighter plane to a German air base.

“The next half-century will be an age of nuclear weapons,” President Emmanuel Macron of France said in March. He was announcing the shift in his country’s nuclear doctrine to one of “forward deterrence” — the use of France’s nuclear weapons to prevent attacks on territories beyond its own borders.

During that speech, Mr. Macron spoke of a world filled with nuclear flash points: India, Pakistan, North Korea and China. But experts said that France’s offer of deterrence to European neighbors could mitigate the interest of allies in acquiring nuclear capabilities. While a French nuclear umbrella would not be a replacement for the one provided by the United States, it could still act as a deterrent.

“The best nonproliferation tool the U. S. ever had is its military alliances,” said Matthew Fuhrmann, a professor of security studies at the University of Texas. “If the U. S. did not extend nuclear protection to as many countries as it did, we’d be in a world with more nuclear weapons states.”

France’s stepped-up role, he said, would reduce the risk of other European countries seeking a weapon. “But I don’t think it lowers their desire to hedge,” he added, noting that merely having a civil nuclear program gives countries leverage with nuclear powers like the United States.

There is an irony to France’s playing a moderating role, given that historically, the country has been one of the most prolific sellers of nuclear technology. France helped to build nuclear programs in Israel, Iraq and Pakistan.

The pace of civil nuclear agreements had fallen off in recent years, Professor Fuhrmann said, in part because the global demand for nuclear energy plummeted after the Fukushima nuclear accident in Japan in 2011. But worries about energy security surged after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and jumped again after the American-Israeli war against Iran prompted Tehran to halt marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.

In striking a deal with the United States, Saudi Arabia is following in the footsteps of the United Arab Emirates, which signed a civil nuclear agreement with the Obama administration in 2009. That deal did not allow the Emirates to enrich nuclear fuel, cutting off its pathway to producing a weapon, and provided for stringent inspections. Experts labeled it the “gold standard” for nonproliferation.

In addition to easing those restrictions, Mr. Trump initially dropped a condition pressed by his predecessor, President Joseph R. Biden Jr., that Saudi Arabia normalize relations with Israel.

On Thursday, Mr. Trump reversed course and said that he was, in fact, making that a requirement of the deal. The Saudi government did not immediately comment but has repeatedly made clear that it would not recognize Israel without also establishing a pathway toward a Palestinian state.

The deal’s original concessions, analysts said, reflected Mr. Trump’s recognition that the U. S.-Israeli war against Iran had destabilized Saudi Arabia and the entire region.

“This deal is a tangible confirmation of the erosion of trust and confidence in Washington as a result of the Iran war,” said Suzanne Maloney, an expert on Iran who is vice president and director of the Foreign Policy program at the Brookings Institution, a research organization in Washington.

“Gulf leaders have no realistic alternative to the U. S. security umbrella,” she added, “but they also are seeing firsthand evidence of its limitations and liabilities. So they are determined to expand their autonomy and capabilities.”

The war against Iran is another disincentive for countries to pursue a weapons program. With its nuclear facilities lying under rubble, whatever ambitions Iran has to produce a bomb have been set back. But even that could cut both ways, since other aspiring nuclear powers could conclude that the best way to avoid such pre-emptive strikes is to achieve nuclear status as quickly as possible.

Conceding benefits to Saudi Arabia will probably not put Riyadh on the pathway to a bomb anytime soon, the experts said. The kingdom is starting from scratch in the nuclear race, and it would take years to develop a homegrown capacity to manufacture weapons-grade uranium.

But other countries, with more advanced capabilities, may demand the same terms. They might succeed if the United States no longer holds the line on giving nonnuclear states sensitive enrichment technology.

“To me, the danger of this deal is the precedent,” Mr. Samore said. “What’s to stop Russia from making a deal like this?”

Mark Landler is the Paris bureau chief of The Times, covering France, as well as American foreign policy in Europe and the Middle East. He has been a journalist for more than three decades.

For South Korea, U. S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal Exposes a Double Standard

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

President Trump has put Saudi Arabia on the path to enriching uranium on its own soil, a demand South Korea has been making for years.

By Choe Sang-Hun

Reporting from Seoul

For decades, South Korea was an example of the United States’ unyielding stance on nuclear nonproliferation.

In the 1970s, the United States pressured South Korea, a steadfast ally with whom it shared nuclear technology, to give up a clandestine nuclear weapons program. Then, it barred the country from enriching its own reactor fuel. The restriction held firm even after Seoul joined a nonproliferation treaty, accepted rigorous safeguards, and built one of the world’s largest nuclear power industries. Nor did the policy waver as North Korea built a nuclear arsenal on the South’s doorstep.

Now, the Trump administration has apparently shattered that standard. By striking a deal that could lead to Saudi Arabia enriching uranium on its own soil, Washington has prompted an inevitable question in Seoul: Why Saudi Arabia, and not us?

South Korea has long negotiated with the United States for enrichment rights. While its Foreign Ministry declined to comment directly on the U. S.–Saudi accord, it said on Thursday that it was closely monitoring “trends in U. S. foreign policy on the nuclear energy sector” for potential impacts on its own talks. While the deal raises expectations for progress in South Korea’s negotiations with Washington, it could also seed deep friction in the seven-decade-old alliance if Washington continues to ignore Seoul’s demands.

“It is clear that the Trump administration is willing to make major geopolitical bargains with less emphasis on international norms and institutions,” said Leif-Eric Easley, an international studies professor at Ewha Womans University in Seoul.

On Thursday, President Trump said the agreement is contingent on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel, putting its immediate future in doubt.

Still, the contrast between Washington’s dealings with Saudi Arabia and South Korea exposes a stark double standard in American nuclear policy. Washington appears to have paved the way for enrichment rights for Saudi Arabia for power plants it has yet to build, while denying them to South Korea, which already operates 26 reactors and plans to build more to meet surging energy demands for the A. I. revolution. It has exempted Saudi Arabia from intrusive inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency, which South Korea has long submitted to to assure the international community that no technology is diverted to weapons projects.

Many in South Korea find this American concession especially jarring given the geopolitical risks. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia has openly warned that his kingdom would build a bomb if Iran did. By contrast, South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, has repeatedly promised that Seoul will not pursue nuclear weapons, choosing instead to rely on the U. S. security guarantees for deterrence as North Korea expands its nuclear arsenal.

“The danger of a breakout by Seoul is likely lower because of its continuous close coordination with Washington on extended deterrence,” Professor Easley said, adding that unlike in the Middle East, “major war on the Korean Peninsula has been deterred for decades.”

As South Korea was pressured to abandon its weapons program, it signed a treaty with the United States in 1972 that barred enrichment without American consent. Even during a 2015 revision of the agreement, Washington mandated that any enrichment require written bilateral agreement.

Consequently, South Korea imports all of its uranium fuel. Seoul now wants independent enrichment capabilities to secure its fuel supply chain. It also wants to recycle spent fuel to reduce waste storage volume — a massive political headache in a densely populated country with a vocal environmental movement.

The U. S.-Saudi deal will likely take center stage when South Korea and the United States resume talks to implement the comprehensive investment and security agreement struck by Mr. Trump and Mr. Lee in November.

Back then, Washington appeared to address Seoul’s grievances by promising to support a “process that will lead to” civil enrichment of uranium and reprocessing of spent fuel by South Korea. He also approved South Korea’s plan to build nuclear-powered attack submarines, pledging American help to secure uranium fuel for the vessels.

However, the broad wording left critical details unresolved, including whether South Korea could operate enrichment or reprocessing facilities on its own soil and whether those facilities would also supply fuel for nuclear submarines.

Talks aimed at resolving such questions were sidetracked by a separate trade dispute, and working-level negotiations only resumed last month.

South Korea aims to launch its first domestic nuclear submarine within a decade, using low-enriched fuel to ease proliferation fears. But the pathway remains unclear.

In 2004, the I. A. E. A. investigated South Korean scientists for unauthorized enrichment experiments. Today, many in South Korea openly view uranium enrichment as a vital path to “nuclear latency” — the ability to rapidly develop weapons if Mr. Trump’s transactional diplomacy renders the U. S. security guarantee, known as the nuclear umbrella, unreliable.

Despite the South Korean government’s repeated denials of any intent to build atomic weapons, public and political backing for a sovereign nuclear deterrent has increased in recent years, while North Korea’s nuclear threats have escalated. In December, Pyongyang unveiled the hull of what it described as its first nuclear-powered strategic guided missile submarine.

Choe Sang-Hun is the lead reporter for The Times in Seoul, covering South and North Korea.

Why I Sought Out a Taliban Commander I Had Fought

The New York Times July 23, 2026

Essay

First as a Marine and then as a journalist, I spent years tied to Afghanistan. I returned one last time to speak to a former enemy in search of answers, and perhaps closure.

Essay

First as a Marine and then as a journalist, I spent years tied to Afghanistan. I returned one last time to speak to a former enemy in search of answers, and perhaps closure.

Mullah Abdul Rahim Gulab in Marja, Afghanistan, in 2021. Credit... Jim Huylebroek for The New York Times

Supported by

By Thomas Gibbons-Neff

Thomas Gibbons-Neff is a former New York Times reporter who covered the wars in Afghanistan and Ukraine. He traveled to Kabul, Afghanistan, in May.

I’ve had a hand in killing around six people. Maybe seven. I don’t know if one man bled out on the side of the road or was taken to a doctor. I think about him often.

The killings occurred in the winter and spring of early 2010, during one of the largest operations of the Afghanistan war: the battle of Marja. I was the 22-year-old leader of a scout sniper team of seven Marines and one Navy corpsman.

It is a strange thing, having killed people in a conflict that spanned 20 years and was ultimately lost. The sum of such an intense expenditure of human lives and trauma left Afghanistan much as it was in 2001, before any American boots touched the ground.

Killing in war often boils down to an us-or-them mentality, a defensible position common to infantry combat. But we were also directed to “win hearts and minds,” the U. S. strategy meant to earn the population’s trust and isolate the Taliban. Trying to build good will while engaging in gunfights beside people’s homes was profoundly confusing. The killing wasn’t detached; it felt deeply personal.

Patrols required a constant assessment of friend or foe, and long hours staring through high-powered optics trying to determine the intent and mannerisms of our enemies. Rarely did we see them with a rifle in their hands. Killing fell on our own instincts and an ever replenishing set of fears. Should we shoot this man? Should we not? What if we don’t? Will our friends die because of our hesitation?

We also had a twisted culture in which killing earned you respect, as if shooting Afghans was the ultimate proof that you were competent. So we killed people. I killed people. These decisions to pull the trigger were the final steps of our part in a strategy that was doomed before I even deployed.

The Taliban, with their exclusion of women from public life and violent treatment of ethnic minorities, fractured Afghan society. During its 20-year occupation, the United States often used this as a justification to prolong the war, even as it rarely addressed its strategic and moral failures or the pain and loss it was causing so many Afghans.

My journalism career — which began after I left the Marine Corps — revolved around trying to understand why this bloody cycle continued. Reporting was a way to roll back time and understand what I had done and what role I played in a conflict that was far from over. The more I saw, the more I learned, the more my contribution to this mess in my early 20s left me with a sense of shame.

Covering war also meant sustained proximity to violence, victims and trauma, and from time to time the public dishonesty that all but inevitably accompanies conflict. I had lived through enough in the Marine Corps. I was already past my fill of that. I resigned from my job, exhausted.

But in May, with a little over two weeks remaining at The New York Times before returning to school to become an English teacher, I landed in Afghanistan. I had come to speak with the people I once fought against: the Taliban.

My thinking was straightforward. Even if the Pentagon would not undertake any significant reflection for these recent decades of war, I could, at a minimum, hold myself accountable for my part in a half-baked strategy that left tens of thousands of Afghans and Americans dead.

I brought souvenirs from a gift shop near my home in Rhode Island, which I would present to a few Taliban officials whom I have known for nearly a half decade now. Hearts and minds, after all, though this time as a guest not an occupier.

Ultimately, I wanted to talk to Mullah Abdul Rahim Gulab, a Taliban commander whom I met by chance in 2021, just months after Kabul fell to the Taliban. But we had also fought against one another in February 2010 in southern Afghanistan.

I knew he would have a version of the battle in Marja that was different from mine. Maybe he had stories with his own heroes and dead friends that I could appreciate and respect, ones that he also couldn’t stop thinking about. Maybe I could feel bad for him and not just feel bad for living while my friends died.

When I landed in Kabul in May, a Taliban deputy minister at the ministry of information and culture named Muhajer Farahi wanted to talk to me after he saw the request I submitted to speak to Mr. Gulab.

We had not met before. But sitting across from me in his office, Mr. Farahi told me his reasons for fighting the United States were simple: He wanted the Americans out of his home.

He spoke slowly and quietly, and avoided eye contact. His English was good. He made clear that his time in Farah Province in southwestern Afghanistan during the war, or jihad, as the Taliban refer to their 20 year military campaign, was difficult.

“We were on the right side,” he said. “We were fighting for our faith.”

I apologized for his dead friends and the innocent people killed in the war. He looked at me and thought for a moment before reminding me that I was a soldier, a cog in a machine that decided to invade his country and stay. It was as close as I would get to a pardon.

He wanted to discuss other things. Mostly he was curious about the number of Americans he had killed, and was still perplexed that even though he watched roadside bombs detonate under our armored vehicles, our casualty announcements from the Pentagon were relatively low. He assumed the United States lied about its death tolls.

I explained the complicated web of emergency care that was a quick helicopter flight away. He didn’t seem convinced. Instead he said something that most Talibs have echoed when discussing my time as a Marine: Don’t try to invade again.

I assured him that the United States appeared to have moved on, but he raised the latest wars in which the country had embroiled itself.

“You haven’t learned,” he said. “Look at Iran and Gaza — you are fighting for the Israelis. You don’t care about human rights.” He blamed the American people for voting a long line of presidents into power who started and continued the so-called forever wars.

As I walked into the blinding light of downtown Kabul, I felt what could only be described as a strange sense of relief. I had been lectured, yes, but on the edges it felt as if there was some acknowledgment of our humanity.

That felt like enough, for now. It was time to talk to Mr. Gulab.

When I interviewed Mr. Gulab in 2021, I didn’t disclose that I had been a Marine. I questioned him as a reporter about his fighting days. He confirmed things I knew: how he and his peers would drop their weapons and greet us as friends on the streets, and that they relied on children to track our footprints to our makeshift outposts.

These had been hard facts for me to confront back in 2010, and still resonated when spoken in hindsight by a victorious insurgent, a hometown fighter who leveraged cunning to defeat us, even though we were far better armed than his band of 20 men. His tactics had formed a puzzle I navigated on every patrol so that I could survive the day. Some of my friends didn’t.

When I first met Mr. Gulab, I walked to a mud brick wall in Marja as a journalist. As a Marine more than a decade before, I had shot a young man in the head in this exact spot. I remembered the last glimpse of his face before the crack of my bolt-action rifle. My brain didn’t compute that I had killed him until later, when someone told me they had found his body dragged behind a corner with his weapon.

Mr. Gulab and I are roughly the same age, in our late 30s. He joined the Taliban because two of his brothers were killed fighting. One of them is his WhatsApp profile picture.

I joined the Marines because my dad was a Vietnam veteran who rarely spoke about the war, and because I was a short kid who grew up in a nice town and went to a nice public high school and wanted to prove myself.

In May, when I reached Mr. Gulab again, this time by phone, I told him the truth about my background: I wasn’t just a journalist, I had fought in Marja as a Marine. He said he had realized that when we first met, given the specificity of my questions.

He wondered what I wanted now: “What’s the point in talking again?”

Mr. Gulab had won his war, and closed that chapter with the United States long before I did. Now he was preparing to fight another conflict, this time against Pakistan. He led a large Afghan Army unit from a base that is still known as Camp Dwyer, where I had flown from in 2010 to fight him and his mujahedeen troops.

The base was named after a British soldier: Lance Bombardier James Dwyer, who was 22 years old when his vehicle ran over a mine two days after Christmas in 2006.

Our conference call began with pleasantries before his reticence lifted, and he was willing to talk about the beginning of the Marja operation. I was curious about his side of our shared experiences, including the fate of a Taliban sniper whom Mr. Gulab would have known, or at least heard about.

That sniper had shot two of my Marines, including my assistant team leader, on the first day of the battle. It was dusk. We were on the roof of a two-story building, the only structure that high for miles. I remember what sounded like a baseball bat hitting uncooked meat. I looked up to see my friend Matt screaming. He had been shot in the arm. A week or so later we drove that sniper into an orchard, where a drone strike presumably killed him. But 16 years later, I still wanted to know for sure.

Mr. Gulab started to speak but was cut off by his minder, who said curtly that sharing such details was illegal. Instead, Mr. Gulab had questions of his own, involving that same sniper. He said he was nearby when my teammates were hit and remembered reports that two “foreigners” had been shot on that roof and fallen off.

“Did they die?” he asked.

I explained that both Marines had survived their wounds but that Matt died in a motorcycle accident back home a little over a year later.

“Why do many American soldiers who fought in Afghanistan and later returned to their country commit suicide?” Mr. Gulab asked. “I have heard this many times. What is the reason?”

It was a question that haunts many of us. I tried to explain how we carried the crushing weight of our own shattered expectations: We had grown up on the nostalgia of World War II, then done something we were supposed to be proud of. Instead, what we got from our politicians and generals were evasions and lies. Our commanders could never articulate how our deployments, and all the violence we committed and the losses we suffered, made anyone safer in the United States.

We were left to figure everything out on our own while they landed lucrative jobs at defense companies and collected big fees on speaking circuits. For some people, it was too much to handle.

Mr. Gulab’s years after the war had been nothing like that, he said. “Our mujahedeen are the opposite, because of the jihad they carried out and because of the friends they lost, they are very happy, because our jihad had a clear goal.”

While the Taliban had won the war, winning the peace had brought its own difficulties: Afghanistan remained in an economic crisis and isolated from much of the world.

“Regarding your apology,” he said, “I should say that at that time our jihad was for the sake of Allah, and we were not worried about being killed or wounded. We are also not upset about our friends who were killed or wounded, because all of us wished to be martyred or injured on the path of jihad. Since the conditions at that time were wartime conditions, civilians were often killed or wounded.”

I wished that I, too, could accept the deaths of my friends and the results of my own actions instead of inhabiting a fog of anger and bitterness over wasted youth. Mr. Gulab let me know that such sentiments existed in Afghanistan, too.

“Regarding the mujahedeen who were killed by your side, I do not know whether they or their families would forgive you,” Mr. Gulab said. “Those civilians may not forgive the foreign forces, but for me personally, I have my own authority and I have forgiven you.”

I first set foot in Afghanistan as a 20-year-old lance corporal in 2008. The Taliban were shadows in a tree line then, and characters that appeared in my nightmares as I tried to stay alive. In August 2021, I watched them shake hands with a squad of U. S. Marines as the Afghan Army evaporated, Kabul fell and my war was finally, fully lost.

Now my one-time enemy generously offered a kind of coda to a line I wrote in my journal on that first deployment 18 years ago: “It’s hard to explain this place and I feel it’s going to take the rest of my life to figure out what happened here.”

Boarding my flight back to the United States, I realized a pervasive sadness lingered in the corners of my mind. I was tired, as if litigating my war again had somehow restarted it. Mr. Gulab and I were, at one point in our lives, two people, barely men at the time, fighting for vastly different reasons. Maybe it was enough that I saw him now more, in some twisted way, as a friend than my enemy.

Some days later in Rhode Island, as I walked my dog on a muggy New England night, my phone vibrated.

Mr. Gulab had texted me in Pashto: “Have you arrived at your home?” he asked.

I said I had.

“It’s good to hear that you arrived safely.”

In May, I returned to Kabul to say goodbye to my colleagues before leaving The New York Times. But I also wanted one final conversation with Mullah Abdul Rahim Gulab — a Taliban commander I’d fought against in 2010 and met face-to-face in 2021. Above all, I felt I owed readers the story that underpinned everything I’ve written for the paper: my own history and participation in the violence of the Afghan war.

@Thomas Gibbons-Neff Thank you for your moving story, full of lessons for us all. You sum up your central lesson when you say near the end, "Maybe it was enough that I saw him now more, in some twisted way, as a friend than my enemy." May I suggest that yes, it is enough at least for me. And no, it is not twisted at all.

Yaqoob Akbary and Safiullah Padshah contributed reporting.

Why Lettuce Is Always Making People Sick

Wired July 22, 2026

Salad is usually synonymous with healthy eating. Except now, as the US grapples with an expanding outbreak of cyclosporiasis that’s sickened more than 7,100 people in Michigan alone, likely caused by iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms.

In fact, leafy greens are frequently implicated in instances of foodborne illness. There was a 2022 multistate E. coli outbreak tied to romaine served on Wendy’s sandwiches and 173 cases of norovirus linked to Illinois eatery D. C. Cobb’s. In 2021, BrightFarms recalled packaged salad greens sold in several states after 31 people got salmonella. And in 2019, a total of 167 people were infected with E. coli after eating romaine harvested from the Salinas Valley region in California. This isn't even the first cyclospora outbreak linked to lettuce: In 2020, Fresh Express salad kits were linked to more than 700 cases of people afflicted with the parasite.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that produce is responsible for almost half of the reported foodborne illness cases, with leafy vegetables topping the list. So what is it that makes lettuce a major source of America’s foodborne tummy troubles?

One big reason is simply because lots of people eat it. Lettuce is the second-most-consumed vegetable in the US behind potatoes. (The latest outbreak ensures potatoes will remain the king of US veggies. Plus, french fries.) Wraps, subs, tacos, you name a fast food sandwich and it’s almost certainly got lettuce on it. Salad-slinging chains are fixtures across the US. Grocery store coolers are stocked with salad kits, on top of the unadorned heads of iceberg lettuce and containers of spinach.

Those ready-to-eat salads and blends of spring mix pose a particularly acute risk because they contain multiple types of leafy greens, which can come from different farms and locations. If one type of lettuce in the mix is contaminated, it can contaminate the whole bag. And because that contaminated lettuce gets packaged into lots and lots of bagged salad, it has the potential to spread germs far and wide.

How lettuce is grown can also expose it to a wide array of pathogens. A 2025 study by researchers at Cornell University who studied E. coli outbreaks in romaine lettuce found that a lot of contamination originates from irrigation with untreated surface water applied through overhead spray irrigation systems. There are ways to lower that risk, including switching to irrigation systems that do not directly touch the leaves, but that would require upgrades and downtime.

Lettuce’s satisfying crunch is also what makes it prone to pesky pathogens. Since it’s eaten raw—really, who wants wilted lettuce?—there’s no opportunity to cook off any lingering contaminants. Like other raw fruit and produce, leafy greens don’t go through what’s known as a “kill step”—heating, pasteurization, or freezing—which is designed to eliminate pathogens during the food manufacturing process.

The texture of lettuce is an additional factor in its ability to spread disease.“Many lettuce types have a lot of crevices and folds,” says Jeanne Marrazzo, CEO of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. “It’s very easy for these tiny pathogens to get in there.”

Even prewashing procedures at manufacturing facilities don’t always remove microbes, which can cling tightly to leaves. In the case of cyclospora, the parasite has thick outer walls, making it highly resistant to most food sanitizers. Experts say vigorous washing that involves scrubbing is the best way to get rid of cyclospora.

“If you don't wash these products well, you're going to end up ingesting whatever is on the lettuce,” says Amira Roess, an epidemiologist at George Mason University.

The White House Is Trying to Figure Out What to Do About Chinese AI

Wired July 22, 2026

The Trump administration is split over how to respond to the rapid rise of China’s leading AI models, according to multiple people familiar with deliberations.

The debate is broadly divided between parts of the White House, which has pushed for stricter controls on Chinese AI that may soon rival the most powerful US models, and the Commerce Department, which has viewed those restrictions as unworkable.

The conundrum has become the latest flash point for the administration over AI, after China’s Moonshot AI lab last week released its Kimi K3 model that rivals the top US models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

In recent days, senior White House officials have discussed possible measures to stop China’s AI labs from developing their models by training them on US models, a practice known as distillation, the people say.

The White House is expected to take some sort of presidential action after Anthropic last month alleged the Chinese tech company Alibaba had carried out the “largest known distillation attack” against it to date. This action is not currently expected to take the form of an executive order, according to one of the people.

A White House spokesperson did not comment on the reporting in this story.

The White House has been taking distillation attacks especially seriously. It announced on Wednesday that Moonshot had developed Kimi K3 by distilling Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 model, and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent told Fox Business that covert distillation could lead to sanctions, describing it as “IP theft.”

While proposals have been making the rounds inside the White House, no formal request for input has been transmitted yet to the Commerce Department, which has its own ideas, according to two people familiar with deliberations.

The Commerce Department has increasingly emerged as an influential part of the intra-administration split over AI, in part because it oversees export controls through the Bureau of Industry and Security.

Lutnick has contemplated ways to create incentives for top US labs to create their own open weight models to counterbalance China, and has spoken with leaders at a number of AI labs in recent weeks, the people add.

Lutnick appears to be straddling a middle ground of regulation—he imposed export controls on Anthropic to bring them to heel—but has been more freewheeling than Cairncross, one of the people said.

Earlier this month, the biggest AI issue for the administration was Anthropic’s Claude Mythos and Fable 5 models, because of their ability to find vulnerabilities in government systems and critical infrastructure.

But policy headaches with AI have only escalated with the rise of so-called open weight models from China—models that have few to no safeguards to prevent hacking government systems and can be downloaded and used by anyone.

The Odyssey’s Success Is Inspiring Unprecedented Levels of Cope

Wired July 22, 2026

For months, Elon Musk and the right-wing cranks he caters to on X have whipped themselves into a raging froth over the supposed desecration of an ancient Greek poem by one of the most successful movie directors alive.

Now that their manufactured backlash has bombed, they’re searching for ways to cope with the reality that they are increasingly divorced from popular opinion.

Christopher Nolan’s artistic crimes in bringing The Odyssey to the screen, according to Musk and others in a furor, were instances of what they called “historical inaccuracy” in a lavish fantasy teeming with monsters, witches, and undead spirits—mainly the casting of Lupita Nyong'o, who is Black, as Helen of Troy, and Elliot Page, who is trans, as Sinon. The grand total of approximately 10 minutes of screen time between these actors in a three-hour saga, combined with the general hysteria over “wokeness” in Hollywood, a rejection of Americanized dialog, and lingering misogyny regarding scholar Emily Wilson’s 2017 translation of Homer’s epic (the first by a woman), resulted in countless teeth-gnashing posts and calls for a boycott that never materialized.

Instead, the mythic drama hauled in a staggering $264 million as it opened this past weekend, sailing toward continued box office dominance and, in all likelihood, a slew of awards. A few conservative commentators, including Ben Shapiro—no fan of DEI or “woke” values—acknowledged it as a landmark achievement. But while some who had predicted its doom knew enough to move on from this battle to other fronts in the culture war, many sank deeper into denial.

“BREAKING,” blared one anonymous X account on Monday. “The Odyssey is FAKING ticket sales by buying up theaters/seats (Fraud) to make the movie look like a success (already $400 million in the hole) moviegoers are reporting having to take terrible seats (because full) but when they show up the theaters are mostly empty.” The post included screenshots of unverifiable anecdotes from Reddit about quiet cinemas and no-show ticket holders.

What Universal Pictures, the studio behind the film, would stand to gain by spending millions beyond a $250 million production budget and $125 million in marketing costs to astroturf a flop was not exactly clear. Then again, these are the same conspiracists who find it suspicious that the critics’ reviews tend to all be published at the same time.

Musk, for his part, seemed to be inspired by an X user who posted three minutes of AI-generated scenes in which characters from The Odyssey are all white and speak in British accents. Commenting on the clip, which at best resembles a montage from a hokey 1970s adaptation, the richest man in the world declared: “Before this year ends, Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

Those familiar with Musk know that when he vows to reach a milestone by year’s end, it basically never happens. The promise of a Grok-animated Odyssey, though minor compared to most of his ambitions—he even speculated in 2025 that the xAI model might “discover new technologies” within several months—is sure to fall by the wayside as well. Not only is it a tiresome idea with zero appeal to the mainstream moviegoer (who has or will soon see Nolan’s version), it’s also unoriginal: The AI studio Fountain 0 is planning the online release of an artificially generated feature titled Odyssey: The Fall this summer.

Moreover, both ill-conceived projects misunderstand the lesson that the entertainment industry seems to be taking from Nolan’s latest blockbuster. At a moment when executives imagine that AI is the key to cutting costs and turbocharging output, the director has shown once again that the practical craft of filmmaking beats out what he himself has disparaged as “slop.”

So, will this aggrieved little cadre of internet reactionaries ever be able to accept that they don’t understand what audiences want? Or that they have deluded themselves, thanks to skewed algorithms and bogus amplification, into thinking they possess an influence they never had? Please. They’re not capable of conceding a loss. And there’s always another outrage down the road.

China’s Open AI Models Are Challenging Silicon Valley’s Playbook

Wired July 22, 2026

The AI industry is not quite experiencing a DeepSeek 2.0 moment, but it feels very close. The leading Chinese AI labs have been on a roll lately, releasing a series of almost cutting-edge open-source models. Z. ai released GLM 5.2 in June, Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 last week, and Alibaba released Qwen 3.8 this Monday.

Silicon Valley and Washington started talking about the models immediately, especially K3, which is widely seen as the best of the bunch. David Sacks, a venture capitalist and AI adviser to President Donald Trump, called the performance of Moonshot’s model “concerning.” Earlier this week, Commerce Secretary Scott Bessent suggested the US might impose sanctions on Chinese AI companies.

On Wednesday, Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, alleged that the Trump administration has “information that Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic’s Fable for the development of its K3 model,” which he said amounted to “stealing proprietary US technology and undermining American research” and was “unacceptable.” (Moonshot AI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The new Chinese models have a few things in common: Third-party benchmarks show that they perform nearly as well as the best Western models; they are optimized for agentic coding tasks (the hottest thing in AI this year); and they are or will soon be released with open weights, making them accessible and transparent.

But perhaps the biggest parallel between the current moment and January 2025—when the world was shocked by DeepSeek’s R1 model—is that it reaffirms how American and Chinese AI labs are taking diverging paths when it comes to being open or closed.

When it first burst onto the scene, DeepSeek challenged the premise that only closed-source models built with billions of dollars of investment in compute infrastructure and training could achieve frontier performance. But since then, Western AI labs have continued developing AI the same way, and now American frontier models feel more roped-off than they were a year ago.

Anthropic said for months that its latest Mythos model was so dangerously good at hacking that only approved collaborators could use it. When it was finally released more widely, the White House responded by issuing broad export controls, which forced Anthropic to take Mythos and its less capable sister model, Fable 5, offline temporarily. OpenAI similarly delayed the release of GPT 5.6 after it received a request from the White House.

In China, meanwhile, the situation looks very different. Chinese startups and tech giants have doubled down on open source: Anyone with a good enough computer environment can now download an open-weight model, run it locally, add customizations, and overall enjoy a much greater degree of freedom than OpenAI and Anthropic would ever allow. In many ways, the open versus closed debate is more entangled with the US versus China debate than ever before.

There are a lot of reasons why Chinese labs have chosen a business strategy built atop open-source models. Being the newer, smaller fish in the AI field, making their models free and open can help Chinese firms attract more users, collaborators, and media spotlight. It also puts them in a separate lane of competition from the one that OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, SpaceX, and other deep-pocketed giants are in.

Earlier this year, rumors spread that Alibaba might be considering joining the closed-source race after it rearranged its corporate AI model development teams. But the tech giant announced on Monday that it would again release the latest version of Qwen—its line of open-source models beloved by the global tech community—with open weights, signaling to customers and the public it is not pivoting away yet.

Perhaps the strongest validation of the Chinese approach is the models themselves. Chinese labs have produced what are widely considered the world's best open-source AI models, showing that American companies no longer have an exclusive hold on building the most capable systems.

Arena AI, a crowdsourced model evaluation platform, now ranks K3 as the best model when it comes to web development tasks and number four in agentic tasks, just below Anthropic’s Fable and Opus 4.8, as well as OpenAI’s GPT 5.6. Artificial Analysis, an independent AI benchmarking company, ranks K3 in the third spot in its intelligence index.

Shortly after Moonshot AI released a preview version of K3 on July 16, people around the world began rushing to try it out, consuming so much inference computing resources that the company is temporarily restricting new users from signing up.

As more people start using open-source Chinese models with capabilities nearly on par with that of their Western competitors, some have started questioning whether paying for OpenAI or Anthropic’s offerings is really worth it. The fact that multiple Chinese labs were able to create capable agentic models and were unafraid to release them to the public is poking holes in the popular understanding that OpenAI and Anthropic are miles ahead of the competition.

Just like with DeepSeek, K3 fans are now celebrating it as evidence that Western AI models are overhyped and overprotected. “It is absolutely wild how much love Kimi got,” Rui Ma, founder of the independent research firm Tech Buzz China, said in a social media post, referring to the company’s announcement that demand for K3 had overwhelmed its servers. “Only made possible by the poor comms and decisions from [Silicon Valley] labs in the past year,” she added.

“I think Anthropic has overhyped the risks, or described risks that are coming soon but do not currently proliferate,” says Nathan Lambert, an independent AI researcher in Seattle who recently visited Moonshot AI’s office in China. He admits, though, that just like the rest of the general public, he has little firsthand information about how Mythos really performs. “We rely on a few private companies and a federal government with depleted state capacity to make that judgment call,” he says.

In addition to challenging the mainstream Western narrative about AI, Chinese open-source models are also proving to be a practical commercial replacement for American closed models. They aren’t just talked about on X and benchmarked against other models—they have become a popular and readily usable option for a growing number of Western startups and individual users.

“There's a real shift toward actually using these newest models that started with GLM 5.2,” Lambert says, referring to Z. ai’s model. “​​Even weeks after the GLM 5.2 release, I hear from AI researchers in the Bay Area that they are still using it for a core part of their workflow. Kimi, being a stronger model, will only do more, especially in areas like cybersecurity, where Mythos, Fable, and GPT 5.6 are effectively unusable.”

In fact, this is already happening. On Tuesday, OpenAI disclosed a concerning incident in which its GPT-5.6 Sol model hacked into the production system of Hugging Face, an open-source AI platform. Hugging Face has said it resorted to using the open-source model GLM 5.2 to analyze the cyberattack because other frontier models were refusing to help due to built-in safety guardrails.

Chinese AI models also tend to be cheaper than Western alternatives, but that’s not necessarily their main selling point. While models like K3 charge less for tokens, early tests show that they may require more tokens than Western models to solve the same problems, thus making the cost gap smaller. “In my fairly limited use, [K3] also seemed very token-hungry. It's not obvious to me that this model is actually that cheap to run,” wrote Dean Ball, a former White House AI adviser who recently joined OpenAI as its head of strategic futures, in a social media post in which he also praised K3 as “a very good model.”

Even if they are relatively token-hungry, models like K3 do ultimately challenge a fundamental assumption that has driven OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s strategy for years: that AI labs need infinite funding to scale up their compute capabilities just to make better models. “In the end, open-weight models deter further AI capex,” Ball wrote.

Review: Dyson V10 Konical

Wired July 22, 2026

7/10

I’ve spent the past week living with Dyson’s newest vacuums, and a clear favorite has emerged. But it’s not the one I expected.

I was ready to love the V16 Piston Animal for all the capabilities and suction power it offers, but as I’ve been testing, it’s the the Dyson V10 Konical that has left me most impressed for its performance at this price. Funny enough, when thinking about Dyson’s new lineup. it’s the least flashy offering, and the one I always forget about. The V8 Cyclone revives a longtime favorite, while the V16 packs the highest suction we’ve seen yet, making both easy to remember and exciting to try.

It was easy to let the V10 Konical fade into the background. It has the same power level as the V8 but a slightly higher price tag thanks to the new All Floor Cones cleaner head instead of the older Motorbar style.

When placed side by side, though, the V10 Konical easily justifies its $100 higher price over the V8 Cyclone. It did better than the V8 in almost every test I ran when comparing Dyson’s vacuums side by side, and it did the best when vacuuming up sand on a rug (even better than more expensive Dyson vacuums like the V15 Detect and Gen5Detect). If you’re looking for a good Dyson vacuum that doesn’t cost the better part of a grand, this is the one to get.

The Dyson V10 Konical packs a solid range of features for its price. It packs 150 air watts of power, which is above average for lightweight stick vacs, though it is weaker than most of Dyson’s own stick vacs. Our favored V15 Detect has 240 air watts, for example, but the V10 Konical felt similar on carpet to the V15 Detect, even with the change in suction power. It even felt like it suctioned better when I used it in handheld mode.

Dyson V10 Konical

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

That’s because just suction power alone doesn’t make a vacuum great at sucking up dirt and debris. A great motor and vacuum head design are equally important, if not more so. Dyson says the V10 Konical’s engine has 15 cyclone chambers built into it for air to flow through and create efficient suction. So while the power is lower than the V15, the two vacuums feel much more similar than I expected, since it still has impressive suction for its power and price point.

The V10 also has a seven-cell lithium battery that lasts for 60 minutes, like the more expensive V15 before it. There are three power modes, but there’s no screen on this device—just a built-in light on the mode button that shows you which setting you’re on. There’s green for eco mode, blue for medium mode, and red for max mode. The mode changes the suction level, so eco is great for lighter cleans while max is best for bigger messes; each higher mode uses more battery. The lack of a screen also means you’ll fly blind on battery life, so beware how long you spend on more powerful modes.

The V10 comes with the new All Floor Cones cleaner head, which is similar to the head that comes with the new V16 Piston Animal (though that version can sense messes). The All Floor Cones head has cones on either side to suck up hair and debris; the cone design promises to detangle long hair instead of letting it get stuck around the vacuum head’s bar. So far, I haven’t seen any hair tangled around the cones, so it seems to be working as intended. There’s also a built-in illuminating light to spot dust and debris when you’re vacuuming hard floors, which is a nice bonus.

This vacuum comes with two attachments: a crevice tool and a mini motorized tool that’s designed for cleaning upholstery. Plus, unlike many older Dyson models, including the more expensive V15 or the cheaper (but equally new) V8, you’ll also get fully sealed, five-stage HEPA filters to keep allergens from circulating out of the vacuum and back into the air.

Dyson V10 Konical

It’ll also be compatible with Dyson’s new docking station, the Auto-empty Dok, hopefully out later this year. Only the V10 Konical and the V16 Piston Animal ($980) are currently slated to work with it.

What made me like the Dyson V10 Konical so much was how well it did in my testing rounds. I tested it with sand and cereal on rugs, followed by litter on hardwood, and then carpeted stairs and bedrooms. It did better than many Dysons in its overall score, beating the V15 Detect, V16 Piston Animal, and V8 Cyclone with its score.

My scoring criteria ran 1 through 4 on five tests—sand, cat litter, Cheerios, general vacuuming, and handheld mode—with 4 representing the best performance and 1 being the lowest. The V10 Konical walked away with a 14 out of 20, while the V15 came behind it with a 12 out of 20. The V10 came in second overall out of five Dyson vacuums, with only the Gen5Detect beating it with a score of 17. The V10 pulls ahead of the Gen5Detect if you’re looking for add-ons, though, as the V10 will be compatible with Dyson’s self-emptying docking station that will release later this year.

While testing, I was particularly impressed with how well it picked up sand for its lower suction power, and it did a great job sucking up an intentional mess of Cheerios I created. I was less impressed with the hard floor results, but since the V10 doesn’t work with the Fluffy Optic head like Dyson’s high-end vacuums, it was never going to be as effective as vacuums that can switch to a head made for that surface. Still, it’s not bad—it was still able to vacuum up the litter I scattered on hard floors as a test. It just needed a couple of passes instead of a single pass to get it all, and it didn’t shove it into a pile like the cheaper V8 Cyclone did. The V10 does well in handheld mode and on carpet and rugs, and it felt a little easier to push around on a low-pile rug than the V8 did with its Digital Motorbar head.

Overall, I’d recommend this vacuum if you’re set on a Dyson and have a home full of mostly carpets and rugs. It’s a better buy than going for the cheaper V8, and I found it a better all-around experience than some of the more expensive Dyson vacuums out there. I still wouldn’t call it better than the Shark PowerDetect, but if you’re set on a Dyson, this is the best buy on the affordable end of Dyson’s scale.

Which Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 or Flip8 Phone Should You Buy?

Wired July 22, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Samsung has steadily improved its foldables, but the eighth annual update includes a fresh face, the Z Fold8, which features the long-rumored wide form factor. It slots in between the flagship Z Fold8 Ultra, which is the successor to last year’s Fold7, and the smaller Flip8, which succeeds the Flip7. Is the newcomer an awkward middle child or the glue that holds Samsung's folding family together? Samsung also has a couple of new smartwatches, the Galaxy Watch Ultra2 and Watch9.

The new phones are available for preorder, but before you get yours, let’s dig into the details to help you decide which of Samsung’s folding phones to buy. I’ll break down the key differences and similarities, so you can make an informed choice. And remember, Samsung sells many other smartphones, and we highlight the ones worth looking at in our Best Samsung Phones guide.

Let’s take a quick peek at what the eighth-generation Samsung Galaxy Z foldables have in common this year.

Although Samsung’s foldables all feature exterior and foldout screens in completely different sizes, they all boast Samsung’s Dynamic AMOLED 2X technology, so you get a 120-Hz refresh rate, support for HDR, and higher peak brightness than ever before (up to 3,000 nits), making it easy to read your screen, even in direct sunlight. They also have features designed to filter blue light and reduce eye strain.

The Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 have a special Flex Titanium layer that reduces the visible crease and provides extra strength, flexibility, and resilience. The titanium-alloy film should help the displays last longer, but also means they are flatter and smoother than before, with an anti-reflective finish that reduces glare.

All three phones have Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 processor inside, with 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB or 512 GB of storage. You can also get the Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 with 16 GB of RAM and 1 TB of storage. They are all IP48 water- and dust-resistant and feature Samsung’s Advanced Armor Aluminum frame, which is scratch-resistant and durable enough to survive minor drops. The Fold8 Ultra and Fold8 support fast charging at up to 45 watts and fast wireless charging at 20 watts; the Flip8 is slightly slower for both. All three support Wireless PowerShare to top up wireless earbuds and other devices. Connectivity includes Wi-Fi 7 and Ultra Wideband (UWB).

Aside from the sizes, the camera systems are very different, but here are all the specs, so you can see exactly where they diverge.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra is the biggest and best foldable that Samsung offers. If you crave the largest screen available but want to fold it away and have something that feels close to a regular smartphone when closed, this is it. The 6.5-inch cover display and slimmed-down design are slick but won’t turn heads. Open it up and you get an expansive 8-inch screen that feels like two 6.5-inch displays side by side.

Everything is smoother and stronger, with Samsung's usual raft of annual refinements. Both displays boast Samsung’s latest tech and a silky smooth adaptive refresh rate that also saves power. Speaking of which, the battery is significantly bigger than the Fold7 at 5,000 mAh, and it supports faster wired and wireless charging than its predecessor. The only slight disappointment is the lack of magnetic Qi2, which is such a handy feature for easy docking and perfect wireless charging alignment.

What truly makes the Fold8 Ultra “ultra” is the camera system. It’s a top-tier combo of a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and a 10-megapixel telephoto lens that supports 3X optical zoom. Both the main and ultrawide can shoot 8K video, and you’ll find plenty of AI assistance in your photo and video editing options.

Who it’s for: The flagship fan who wants the best of the best and doesn’t mind spending to get it.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Fold8 is where things get interesting. So far, the best folding phones have all been either book-style like the Fold8 Ultra, or much smaller flip phones, like the Flip8 below, but the Fold8 strikes an interesting middle ground. It’s much shorter than the Fold8 Ultra at 124 mm compared to 158 mm, but it’s also wider at 161 mm compared to 143 mm unfolded (82 to 73 mm when folded).

This form factor gives you a 7.6-inch inner display with a 4:3 (landscape) or 3:4 (portrait) aspect ratio, a more natural format for some media. While the unfolded screen isn’t miles away from the Ultra’s, using the Fold8 when closed will take some getting used to; even though it’s only millimeters of difference, it looks short and squat. It’s also a little more pocket-friendly, and at 201 grams it’s the lightest large-screen foldable on the market.

Performance, display tech, and most of the rest of the spec sheet match the Fold8 Ultra, though the battery is slightly smaller at 4,800 mAh. The glaring difference is the camera system, which consists of a pair of 50-megapixel lenses (wide and ultrawide) and drops the telephoto lens altogether, though it does still offer 10X digital zoom. It can still record in 8K, and Samsung has included features such as dual recording and my FanCam, a post-video editing feature where you can tap a subject in footage and generate a reframed clip that keeps them centered for social-ready content without the need for manual cropping.

Who it’s for: Fun and adventurous folks seeking something a little bit different.

Samsung

Samsung

The Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 is the lightest and thinnest flip phone in the world thanks to its redesigned chassis. It’s the perfect option for folks who miss smaller phones, as it flips shut to slide easily into any pocket or bag. You get a 4.1-inch cover screen, but it flips open to convert into a 6.9-inch candy bar, and the main screen has Samsung’s top display tech.

It’s tougher and more durable than ever, and it boasts the same excellent chipset and top-end performance as its two bigger siblings. The smaller, 4,300-mAh battery is likely enough for similar stamina, since the screens are so much smaller, though the wired and wireless charging are a touch slower. You also get a more basic camera system, comprising a 50-megapixel main shooter backed by a 12-megapixel ultrawide, and video recording tops out at 4K, though that’s plenty for most folks.

Who it’s for: People who prize portability, but still want a fun, flip design that's satisfying to slam shut.

Life is easier when you buy your new phone unlocked, because you can jump carriers to find better deals and easily switch to international eSIMs when you travel. The Galaxy Z phones sold through Samsung’s website are always unlocked.

The best place to buy a Galaxy Z phone is Samsung. com, especially since some colors are exclusive to the storefront. Always check out the promotions to make sure you snag any deals and consider trading in your old model for a decent discount. You get a six-month trial of Google AI Pro with these phones.

Whichever Samsung Galaxy Z foldable you decide on, you might want to buy it with the Galaxy Card, because you can earn 5 percent cash rewards on all in-store or online purchases made directly from Samsung in the US. Other benefits include 3 percent cash rewards on purchases using Samsung Wallet, 2 percent cash rewards on streaming service subscriptions, and 1 percent cash rewards on everything else with the physical card.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra2 succeeds the Samsung Watch Ultra and promises to be more accurate, faster, and smoother, thanks to the Snapdragon Wear Elite chipset inside. It also has the brightest display in a smartwatch at up to 5,000 nits. It’s still titanium, but both the watch case and the band are thinner and lighter. Under the hood, there’s specialized pro-level sport tracking, hydration guidance, and depth measurement for divers.

The Watch9 boasts the same chipset, a 3,000-nit display, and a 20 percent battery bump over the Watch8 to 390 mAh. It tracks your vitals, warns about any deviation from your usual baseline, and gives you a personalized fitness score and recommendations to improve your health.
